These studies highlight the importance of evaluation protocols
in continual learning, while our experiments focus on online
memory adaptation under fixed resource budgets.

We evaluate online lifelong variants of
BigCodeBench

retrieval using only preceding experience. Memory is updated after the
current task has been evaluated, without access to future tasks.
The language-model backbone remains frozen throughout each run.
BigCodeBench.
We use BigCodeBench Full v0.1.4 in the
Instruct
format,
comprising
1,140
coding problems. Each method makes a single
pass through the same deterministic sequence: the 992 problems in
Full excluding Hard, followed by the 148 problems in the Hard subset.
Within these two groups, we preserve the order of the pinned Full and
Hard dataset files, respectively; no random shuffling is applied.
The memory bank is carried across the two groups without resetting.
For each problem, the agent generates one solution, which is sanitized
and evaluated using BigCodeBench’s official execution-based evaluator
inside a Docker worker. A problem succeeds only when the evaluator
returns
pass
; generated-code failures and execution timeouts
count as unsuccessful outcomes. Evaluator infrastructure errors
invalidate the run. We report pass@1 over all 1,140 problems, counting
each problem once. Memory is updated after evaluation, and previously
evaluated problems are not revisited. The local deployment uses
Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. The API deployment uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash with thinking explicitly disabled.
Both deployments use temperature zero. Reference solutions and unit
tests are excluded from the model’s memory and input prompts.
ALFWorld.
We use Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as the frozen backbone, with temperature
zero and top-
p
p
equal to one. A complete run contains
574
episodes: 300 training episodes selected by task-type-stratified
sampling, all 140 validation-seen episodes, and all 134
validation-unseen episodes. The phases run in this order. The base
seed is 42; the sampling and ordering routines use seeds 42, 43, and
44 for the three phases, respectively. Within each phase, game paths
are sorted, shuffled within task-type groups using the phase seed,
and selected by round-robin traversal of the groups. The resulting
ordered episode manifest is fixed and shared across methods, and
the runner checks that the environment follows this order.
Each selected episode is executed once. An episode succeeds when

won

The success rate reported here is the total number of successful
episodes divided by
574
, including all three phases; it is

across phase boundaries and is updated after every completed episode,
including validation-seen and validation-unseen episodes. Thus, this
is an online lifelong protocol rather than evaluation with memory
frozen after training. Expert trajectories are excluded from memory.

article.headline: 资源受限终身智能体：学习记忆价值提升成功率
article.lede: TokenWorth 从在线执行反馈学习查询相关的记忆价值，在六个 LifelongAgentBench 设置中成功率最
article.problem: 终身智能体在生成、交互与记忆预算同时受限时，现有记忆机制可能失效，部分复杂方法甚至不如无记忆智能体。此时单次检索决策影响更大，相关但不有用的记忆会挤占稀缺上下文。核心问题从“检索相关经验”转为“判断哪些经验值得保留与复用”。
article.method: TokenWorth 是一个轻量在线记忆框架，用带先验正则的线性基评分器捕捉稳定的记忆效用，并用 RFM 残差学习查询相关的非线性修正。它把学到的记忆价值同时用于当前检索和有界记忆库的准入、替换与淘汰，且不更新主干、不重放任务、不做反事实执行或额外语言模型调用。
article.results: 在三个 LifelongAgentBench 环境与本地/API 两种部署的六个组合中，TokenWorth 成功率均为最高：本地 DB 65.0%（最强基线 33.0%）、OS 59.4%（54.6%）、KG 36.7%（30.7%）；API DB 62.2%（32.2%）、OS 73.2%（70.2%）、KG 36.7%（32.0%）。输出 token 相对无记忆 Standard 在本地 DB/OS/KG 分别降低 9.3%/51.5%/18.7%，API 分别降低 31.6%/58.3%/21.3%。DB 消融中完整方法 65.0%，仅基评分器 64.2%，基评分器加固定度量 RFM 为 63.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 在推理成本和交互轮次受限的真实部署中，这提示终身智能体的关键不只是扩大记忆，而是把有限记忆预算分配给真正有用的经验。
article.limitations: 反馈只来自被选中的记忆，论文承认其因果贡献无法识别。实验只在固定严格预算下评估，未声称跨预算鲁棒；API BigCodeBench 上 50.6% 也略低于 RAG 的 50.9%。

email_papers.title: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents
email_papers.abstract: Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions. However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory in a query-agnostic manner, which can incur unnecessary preprocessing cost and discard details that later prove essential. Recent studies have begun shifting memory processing toward runtime adaptation, but typically specialize in particular operations or fixed processing schemes, leaving flexible control over performance, cost, and latency largely underexplored. To address this challenge, we present MemPilot, a flexible framework that orchestrates on-demand memory curation under different performance--cost--latency preferences. Specifically, we optimize a multi-step LLM policy via reinforcement learning to iteratively choose between retrieving from query-agnostic memory and delegating query-specific curation of raw multimodal history to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. The policy jointly controls evidence amount, curation instructions, model selection, and visual access, enabling fine-grained allocation of runtime computation. To optimize this policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by separately estimating each objective's advantage before aggregation. Moreover, we introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step rollouts. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance--cost--latency trade-offs across optimization preferences, with preference sweeps yielding broader frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines.

Abstract
Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions.
However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory in a query-agnostic manner, which can incur unnecessary preprocessing cost and discard details that later prove essential.
Recent studies have begun shifting memory processing toward runtime adaptation, but typically specialize in particular operations or fixed processing schemes, leaving flexible control over performance, cost, and latency largely underexplored.
To address this challenge, we present
MemPilot
, a flexible framework that orchestrates on-demand memory curation under different performance–cost–latency preferences.
Specifically, we optimize a multi-step LLM policy via reinforcement learning to iteratively choose between retrieving from query-agnostic memory and delegating query-specific curation of raw multimodal history to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs.
The policy jointly controls evidence amount, curation instructions, model selection, and visual access, enabling fine-grained allocation of runtime computation.
To optimize this policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by separately estimating each objective’s advantage before aggregation.
Moreover, we introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step rollouts.
Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance–cost–latency trade-offs across optimization preferences, with preference sweeps yielding broader frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines.

Introduction
As large language model (LLM) agents evolve toward persistent, long-horizon interaction, memory becomes increasingly central to preserving and reusing past experience
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
.
However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory from interaction histories in a query-agnostic manner, and relying solely on such pre-query construction can be wasteful and lossy, as it cannot reliably anticipate future query needs
(
Xu et al., 2025
;
Fang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026c
)
.
To mitigate this limitation, a growing line of work moves memory adaptation to runtime through query-time evidence distillation, on-demand memory construction, and adaptive memory strategies
(
Yan et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2026d
)
.
Despite this progress, flexible orchestration of runtime memory adaptation remains underexplored, particularly when adapting runtime computation to query needs and multimodal evidence while balancing performance, cost, and latency
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
.
This raises a key challenge:
how can runtime multimodal memory curation be adaptively orchestrated with controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs?
Unfortunately, addressing this challenge is non-trivial due to three key limitations of existing approaches to runtime memory adaptation.
1
Runtime memory control remains structurally rigid
: existing methods typically rely on hand-designed operations or fixed processing pipelines, with efficiency control hard-wired into predefined modules, budget tiers, or heuristics
(
Yin and Tang, 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Yu et al., 2026a
)
, leaving few degrees of freedom for query-specific adaptation and making fine-grained trade-off optimization difficult.
2
Trade-off optimization remains incomplete
: existing approaches often target only a subset of efficiency objectives, such as token usage or monetary cost, while user-facing latency is rarely treated as an explicit optimization objective
(
Liu et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026d
)
.
3
Existing methods largely assume a fixed processing backend for runtime memory adaptation
, overlooking substantial variation in curation quality, cost, and latency across heterogeneous models and limiting adaptation to query difficulty and evidence modality, thereby constraining the achievable trade-off space
(
Yu et al., 2026a
;
Yan et al., 2025a
)
.
Collectively, these limitations call for a more flexible framework that can orchestrate runtime memory operations and processing backends according to both query needs and optimization preferences.
Building on these observations, in this work we introduce
MemPilot
, a flexible framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under different performance–cost–latency preferences.
At a high level, MemPilot follows a simple design principle: retain query-agnostic memory, compatible with off-the-shelf agent memory systems, for efficient access, while preserving raw interaction history for query-specific runtime curation.
Specifically, at inference time, a multi-step LLM policy constructs a query-adaptive orchestration trajectory by iteratively choosing between retrieving from the query-agnostic memory bank and delegating curation of the raw history to heterogeneous LLMs and vision-language models (VLMs), whose distinct capabilities naturally offer different quality, cost, and latency profiles.
Rather than relying on hand-crafted pipelines or discrete budget tiers, the policy adaptively determines how much evidence to process, how it should be curated, which model to invoke, and whether visual evidences are needed, exposing fine-grained controls over runtime computation trade-offs.
We optimize this policy with reinforcement learning under different performance, cost, and latency preferences. To better handle the resulting multi-objective optimization, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by estimating each objective’s advantage separately before weighted aggregation.
We further introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation, which estimates the marginal contribution of individual curation steps for fine-grained credit assignment.
Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks show that MemPilot achieves favorable performance–cost–latency trade-offs across different optimization preferences. Fine-grained preference sweeps further reveal broader trade-off frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines, while behavioral analyses show that MemPilot adaptively reallocates runtime computation as optimization preferences change.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce
MemPilot
, a systematic framework for preference-aware runtime memory orchestration that jointly controls memory access, query-specific curation, heterogeneous model delegation, and visual evidence usage. By unifying these decisions within a multi-step policy, MemPilot enables fine-grained performance–cost–latency control without relying on fixed processing pipelines, predefined budget tiers, or a fixed processing backend.
•
To optimize the orchestration policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling and introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment in multi-step rollouts, enabling stable and effective optimization.
•
Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance–cost–latency frontiers across preferences, with analyses revealing shifts in model selection, visual access, and computation allocation as preferences change.
2
Related Work
2.1
Agent Memory and Runtime Adaptation
LLM agents increasingly rely on memory mechanisms to preserve and reuse information from long-term interaction histories
(
Zhong et al., 2024
;
Packer et al., 2023
)
.
Most existing text-centric systems construct memory before future queries are known, using either hand-designed mechanisms for extraction and organization
(
Chhikara et al., 2025
;
Xu et al., 2025
;
Kang et al., 2025
;
Fang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026c
)
or learned policies for memory construction, updating, and retrieval
(
Yan et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Yu et al., 2026b
;
Yue et al., 2026
)
.
Beyond text-centric memory, recent work has extended agent memory to multimodal interactions, maintaining structured representations over textual, visual, and other sensory experiences
(
Feng et al., 2026a
;
Wang and Chen, 2025
;
Long et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026b
)
.
Despite increasingly adaptive and multimodal memory designs, they still construct memory in a largely query-agnostic manner.
A growing line of work instead shifts memory processing toward runtime adaptation.
GAM
(
Yan et al., 2025a
)
performs just-in-time research over stored memory and raw history, while BudgetMem
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
learns query-aware runtime extraction under different computation budgets.
MemGen
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
and AdaMEM
(
Zhang et al., 2026d
)
dynamically generate or refresh memory guidance according to evolving reasoning states, whereas MemRL
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
adapts the utility of stored experiences from interaction feedback.
More recent work further explores query-time evidence distillation and deferred memory construction
(
Yin and Tang, 2026
;
Yu et al., 2026a
)
.
However, these approaches typically specialize in a particular form of runtime adaptation or follow a predefined processing pattern.
MemPilot instead learns to orchestrate heterogeneous multimodal memory curation at runtime under controllable performance–cost–latency preferences.
2.2
LLM Routing
LLM routing aims to match different queries with suitable models based on their heterogeneous capabilities and costs.
Early approaches route queries through model cascades or select models based on estimated query difficulty
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Ding et al., 2024
)
.
More recent work improves routing through preference learning
(
Ong et al., 2025
)
, contrastive objectives
(
Chen et al., 2024
)
, and graph-based modeling
(
Feng et al., 2024
)
, while further extending routing to multi-agent settings
(
Yue et al., 2025
)
and unified routing frameworks
(
Feng et al., 2026b
)
.
Moving beyond one-shot routing, several methods employ reinforcement learning to enable multi-step model selection and orchestration
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Qian et al., 2025
;
Feng et al., 2026c
)
.
These advances highlight the potential of LLM routing as a general paradigm for adaptively allocating heterogeneous model computation according to task demands and resource constraints.
3
Methodology
In this section, we first formulate on-demand memory orchestration as a multi-step decision process (Section
3.1
). We then instantiate the factorized curation and delegation decisions that enable query-adaptive runtime control (Section
3.2
). Finally, we introduce resource-aware reward modeling for optimizing quality–cost–latency trade-offs with fine-grained credit assignment (Section
3.3
).
Figure 1

Overview of MemPilot.
(a)
The orchestrator iteratively retrieves compressed memories or delegates query-specific curation of raw multimodal histories to heterogeneous LLMs/VLMs. Factorized controls govern evidence retrieval, curation strategy, visual access, and model selection, with accumulated evidence guiding subsequent decisions and final answering.
(b)
Objective-wise advantage decoupling enables controllable trade-offs among quality, cost, and latency, while prefix-based answer probing estimates each step’s marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment.

Benchmarks and Metrics.
We mainly evaluate MemPilot in multimodal settings involving both textual and visual interaction histories. Specifically, we use five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks: Mem-Gallery

Implementation Details
MemPilot is implemented based on VeRL

(
Yang et al., 2025
)
as the default orchestrator policy. To disentangle gains from RL-enhanced answer generation, we additionally report a decoupled-answer evaluation where the curated context is passed to a separate, non-RL-trained answer model, using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. External LLMs and VLMs are accessed through OpenRouter
2
2
2
https://openrouter.ai

A.2

(
Zhang et al., 2025c

for semantic retrieval. Unless otherwise specified, the query-agnostic memory bank is constructed with LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024

at a 0.4 compression ratio for policy training and main evaluation. We further examine compatibility with memory banks produced by other agent memory systems in Section
4.6
. We retrieve at most five evidence items per step for both MemPilot and applicable baselines. Since memory items from different systems can vary substantially in length, we directly compare monetary cost and latency rather than memory-item counts. Remaining hyperparameters are provided in Appendix
A.5
.
For training, we adopt a 7/1/2 train/validation/test split. We merge the training portions of Mem-Gallery, WorldMemArena, and H2HMem into a joint training set and evaluate in-domain performance on their held-out test sets. We further use MemLens and MemEye exclusively for out-of-domain evaluation to assess generalization to unseen memory distributions. The same data protocol is applied to all applicable baselines, with detailed dataset statistics provided in Appendix
A.4
. For the main comparison, we evaluate three representative MemPilot preferences:
Perf
,
Bal
, and
Cost
, prioritizing answer quality, balanced quality–resource trade-offs, and inference cost, respectively. Additional preference settings are explored in Section
4.4
.

As shown in Table
1
, MemPilot spans distinct quality–cost regimes across both models and benchmarks. The results reveal several consistent trends across methods and settings.
(1) Text-centric systems achieve low cost largely by avoiding additional multimodal processing and runtime curation, but this often comes with lower answer quality.
In comparison, MemPilot-Bal generally achieves stronger overall quality at moderate cost, while MemPilot-Cost reaches similarly low-cost regimes on most datasets.
(2) Runtime adaptation does not necessarily translate into controllable trade-offs.
Although GAM, AgeMem, and Mem-T adapt memory processing at inference time, they largely expose a fixed operating regime rather than explicitly controlling the quality–cost balance. In contrast, MemPilot spans multiple operating points. MemPilot-Perf achieves the best L-J score across all five benchmarks under both models, while MemPilot-Bal substantially lowers cost and provides a distinct intermediate quality–cost trade-off.
(3) Multimodal memory processing can be costly without adaptive allocation.
MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse often incur substantially higher inference cost without consistently translating that expense into better answer quality. In contrast, MemPilot selectively invokes external curation and achieves stronger performance at much lower cost in most settings, with the same trend extending to MemEye and MemLens.
Overall, MemPilot provides controllable quality–cost trade-offs rather than a single performance-oriented operating point.
MemPilot-Perf prioritizes answer quality, MemPilot-Bal offers a balanced operating point, and MemPilot-Cost further reduces resource usage with greater quality sacrifice. We analyze latency and finer-grained performance–cost–latency frontiers in Section
4.4
.

Performance–cost.
As shown in Figure
2
(a), MemPilot forms a stronger frontier across a broad cost range and largely envelopes the competing methods. Compared with trade-off-aware baselines such as LightMem, BudgetMem, and OmniSimpleMem, MemPilot reaches higher quality as additional computation is allocated, while also covering competitive low-cost operating points. Most conventional memory systems expose only a fixed quality–cost point, highlighting the additional flexibility provided by learned runtime orchestration. Multimodal systems such as MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse generally incur much higher cost due to visual processing, whereas MemPilot reduces unnecessary multimodal computation through on-demand curation and selective model delegation.
Performance–latency.
Figure
2
(b) shows a similarly broad quality–latency frontier. MemPilot spans lightweight to performance-oriented configurations, whereas most baselines expose only a narrow region or a single operating point. Even among runtime-adaptive methods, the achievable latency range remains limited. MemVerse achieves competitive quality at relatively low latency, but lacks explicit trade-off control and incurs substantially higher monetary cost in Figure
2
(a). This further highlights that cost and latency capture complementary resource constraints.
Overall, MemPilot provides a broader, more controllable performance–cost–latency frontier through adaptive runtime orchestration, enabling flexible computation allocation under resource preferences.
4.5
How Does MemPilot Allocate Runtime Computation?
To better understand how MemPilot realizes different trade-offs, we analyze its learned runtime curation behavior in Figure
3
. Panels (a) and (b) show that as the optimization preference shifts toward lower cost or lower latency, the policy adjusts multiple control dimensions in a coordinated manner rather than relying on a single knob. Moving from left to right, MemPilot generally reduces the number of policy steps, the frequency of
Curate
actions, image access, and policy output tokens. At the same time, evidence count also changes adaptively, indicating that the policy does not simply retrieve less information, but learns to reconfigure how memory is accessed and processed under different resource preferences.
Panel (c) further shows that model selection is a key mechanism behind this adaptation. Under higher-cost settings, MemPilot relies more heavily on stronger VLMs and LLMs, while lower-cost settings shift computation toward cheaper model groups. Together, these results show that MemPilot learns a coherent allocation strategy over curation depth, modality access, and routed model capacity, which explains its ability to realize controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs.

Ablation Study of Core Design Choices.
We ablate four key components of MemPilot to examine their contributions to runtime orchestration and policy optimization, with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. As shown in Table
2
, removing LLM/VLM delegation reduces the average Judge score from 37.40 to 14.58, highlighting the importance of adaptive external curation. Removing marginal utility or retrieval–instruction decoupling causes similarly large degradation, demonstrating the value of fine-grained credit assignment and separating evidence retrieval from curation instructions. Objective-wise advantage decoupling is also important for multi-objective training, with its removal reducing the Judge score to 21.94. Although all ablated variants consume less inference cost, their substantial quality losses indicate that simply reducing runtime computation does not yield a desirable trade-off.

Compatibility with Off-the-Shelf Memory Banks.
To examine whether MemPilot depends on a particular query-agnostic memory construction, we replace its default memory bank with off-the-shelf agent memory banks and evaluate the performance–cost frontiers without retraining using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. Figure

The resulting frontiers are clearly separated: the default bank occupies the lower-cost regime, SimpleMem provides an intermediate profile, while A-MEM incurs higher cost but reaches stronger performance. Each memory bank thus induces a distinct operating regime, while MemPilot improves performance as additional runtime computation is allocated. This demonstrates compatibility with diverse upstream memory systems while preserving their distinct performance–cost characteristics through runtime orchestration.
5
Conclusion
We presented
MemPilot
, a framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under controllable performance–cost–latency preferences. MemPilot formulates runtime memory adaptation as a multi-step decision process, combines query-agnostic memory with raw interaction history, and adaptively delegates curation to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. We further introduced resource-aware policy optimization with objective-wise advantage decoupling and prefix-based marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment. Experiments across multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate that MemPilot achieves favorable trade-off frontiers while adapting computation to different optimization preferences. We hope this work encourages agent memory systems to move beyond performance-only optimization toward resource-aware runtime adaptation.

Latency Reward.
We use a deterministic latency proxy rather than the observed wall-clock latency of individual API requests, which can vary substantially with network conditions and transient serving load. LLM inference latency is roughly influenced by fixed per-request overhead, input-dependent prefill computation, and autoregressive output decoding. Rather than modeling the full hardware- and serving-dependent latency profile, we adopt a deliberately simplified affine proxy that summarizes these effects with a fixed overhead and average per-token contributions for input and output over the operating range considered in our experiments. A.4
Evaluation Details
Memory preprocessing and indexing.
We serialize each multimodal conversation in chronological order and partition it into approximately 256-token text chunks. Dialogue turns are treated as atomic units: a turn is never split across chunks, and its attached images, image identifiers, and captions remain associated with the same chunk. An oversized individual turn is retained as a single chunk. For WorldMemArena
(
Liu et al., 2026a
)
, the memory available to each question is additionally restricted to the cumulative conversation prefix visible at its corresponding checkpoint.
We construct separate dense indexes for the raw and compressed memory corpora. Query-agnostic compression is performed independently for chunk text and image captions using LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
with a default compression rate of 0.4, while memory and image identifiers remain unchanged. Document embeddings are computed offline using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
(
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, normalized, stored in float16 format, and reused throughout evaluation. At runtime, only the policy-generated retrieval query is encoded, after which evidence is ranked by embedding similarity. The compressed-memory and raw-memory indexes are searched independently, with at most five retrieved items per curation operation. Image captions participate in textual retrieval, whereas image pixels are made available only when an image-capable external model is selected. Reference answers are never used during preprocessing, indexing, or retrieval.
Benchmarks and data splits.
Our in-distribution evaluation covers Mem-Gallery
(
Bei et al., 2026
)
, the lifelong subset of WorldMemArena
(
Liu et al., 2026a
)
, and both the dyadic and multiparty variants of H2HMem
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
. Each dataset is split at the conversation level into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test data, ensuring that questions derived from the same conversation never appear in different splits. WorldMemArena is additionally stratified by category and scenario. The source datasets are split independently before their training and validation portions are merged, and their source identities are preserved for dataset-wise reporting.
For out-of-distribution evaluation, we use the complete open-answer portion of MemEye
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
, containing 371 questions across eight scenarios, and the official 32K memory-agent subset of MEMLENS
(
Ren et al., 2026
)
. MemEye’s multiple-choice variant is excluded. MEMLENS answer-refusal questions are removed, leaving 173 of the 195 agent-subset questions. Answer-refusal questions are likewise excluded from Mem-Gallery and H2HMem. For H2HMem, we additionally remove dialogues without usable memory content and Conflict Detection instances whose reference labels cannot satisfy the benchmark’s required standalone Yes/No answer format. Neither OOD benchmark contributes data to policy training or model selection.

Inference.
We evaluate one deterministic trajectory per question using greedy decoding with temperature 0. The maximum prompt and response lengths are both 4,096 tokens. Each trajectory permits at most six sequential curation rounds and at most two concurrent independent curation operations. All policy-facing memory-access settings are kept identical to those used during the corresponding training run.
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
We additionally evaluate semantic answer correctness using
openai/gpt-4o-mini
. We preserve each benchmark’s official judge role, correctness rubric, score semantics, and output convention. The only sample-dependent inputs presented to the judge are the predicted answer and the ground-truth reference answer.
Minor answer-only adaptations are applied when an official prompt requires information unavailable to common baseline outputs. Specifically, we remove the question field from all judge inputs; remove Key Memory Points from WorldMemArena because they evaluate evidence coverage rather than final-answer correctness; convert H2HMem’s session-batched evaluation into itemwise evaluation; and remove the previous answer from MEMLENS Knowledge Update prompts because correctness is determined by the current reference answer. Policy–answer model decoupling.
For controlled comparisons that separate memory orchestration from answer-generation ability, we optionally remove the trained policy’s final answer while retaining the query and the memory evidence collected along its curation trajectory. This information is provided to a separately specified, untrained answer model using a benchmark-specific QA prompt. Policy reasoning, routing arguments, system instructions, and reference answers are excluded from this prompt. The replacement model’s cost and latency are added to the corresponding resource totals, but its common final-answer invocation is not counted as a routed external-model invocation.

B.1
Per-Benchmark Runtime Computation Allocation
Figure
5
provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the runtime-allocation analysis in Section
4.5
. The overall behavior is consistent across all five benchmarks. As stronger cost or latency preferences are imposed, MemPilot generally reduces policy steps,
Curate
actions, visual access, and policy-generation tokens, indicating coordinated adaptation across multiple control dimensions.
Model routing exhibits an equally consistent shift. High-resource settings rely heavily on larger LLMs and VLMs, whereas tighter cost preferences progressively move curation toward lighter models. At the lowest displayed cost point, all five benchmarks route exclusively to LLMs below 70B. Meanwhile, individual controls such as evidence depth and image access need not change monotonically, showing that MemPilot reallocates computation jointly rather than uniformly shrinking every decision dimension. These results confirm that the aggregate behavior observed in the main text is broadly consistent across datasets while retaining dataset-specific curation patterns.
B.2
Per-Benchmark Ablation Results
Table
6
provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the ablation study. The full MemPilot configuration consistently achieves the highest Judge score across all five benchmarks. Among the ablations, removing objective-wise advantage decoupling generally preserves the strongest performance, yet still causes clear degradation on every dataset, confirming its role in multi-objective policy optimization. Removing LLM/VLM delegation, marginal utility, or retrieval–instruction decoupling leads to substantially larger drops, with similar trends observed on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Although all ablations reduce inference cost, the accompanying quality degradation remains pronounced, indicating that the complete design yields a more effective quality–cost trade-off rather than merely consuming additional computation.

B.3
Memory-Bank Compatibility Across Benchmarks
We further report per-benchmark results for the memory-bank compatibility analysis in Figure
6
. Across all five benchmarks, replacing the default memory bank with SimpleMem
(
Liu et al., 2026c
)
or A-MEM
(
Xu et al., 2025
)
preserves clear performance–cost frontiers without retraining, confirming that MemPilot is not tightly coupled to a particular query-agnostic memory construction. Different memory banks occupy distinct cost regimes while retaining similar improvements as runtime computation increases. The default bank generally provides more cost-efficient operating points, whereas A-MEM incurs higher overall cost but often reaches a higher performance ceiling, particularly on WorldMemArena, MemEye, and MemLens. SimpleMem typically lies between these regimes and remains competitive on Mem-Gallery and H2HMem. These results suggest that MemPilot preserves its runtime orchestration behavior across diverse memory banks while retaining the distinct performance–cost characteristics of their upstream memory representations.

Appendix D
Limitations and Future Work
While MemPilot provides flexible runtime memory orchestration, several aspects could be further improved:
•
Privacy-aware delegation.
Runtime curation may send retrieved interaction history to external models, which can raise privacy concerns for sensitive memories. Future work could incorporate privacy-aware routing, local processing, or access-control mechanisms while remaining orthogonal to MemPilot’s core orchestration design.
•
Preference calibration.
MemPilot controls trade-offs through predefined optimization preferences. Future work could study more user-friendly ways to map high-level deployment preferences to reward coefficients, making trade-off specification easier across applications.
•
Deployment-aware latency modeling.
We use a proxy latency estimator during training to avoid instability from transient network and serving fluctuations. Future work could instead optimize directly against measured latency in a controlled system-level sandbox with stable networking and serving conditions.
Appendix E
Broader Impact
MemPilot advocates a broader shift in agent memory from performance-oriented optimization toward explicit and controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs. In practical deployments, the highest-performing memory configuration is not always the most desirable, as different users and applications may place substantially different values on monetary cost and response latency. This mirrors modern commercial LLM services, which increasingly offer model tiers spanning different capability, cost, and latency profiles (e.g., GPT-5.6-Sol/Terra/Luna), allowing users to choose operating points that best match their needs. We believe agent memory systems should provide similar flexibility rather than committing to a single performance-oriented configuration. This becomes particularly relevant for multimodal agents, where accessing and processing visual evidence can introduce substantially different resource demands. More broadly, treating memory curation as adaptive computation allocation may encourage tighter integration between agent memory, model routing, and resource-aware decision making, enabling future long-horizon agents to become more efficient, responsive, and deployment-aware.

Judge Prompt: MemEye (Open-Ended)
You are an impartial judge evaluating the memory capabilities
of an AI assistant on a question-answering task.
Your task is to compare the Assistant’s Answer against the
Ground Truth and assign a score of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, or 1.
Important Principles.
1.
Semantic equivalence over surface form.
The assistant may use different wording, synonyms, or sentence
structure. As long as the meaning matches the Ground Truth,
it should receive full credit.
Do NOT penalize for stylistic differences.
2.
Numeric / counting questions are binary.
If the Ground Truth is a specific number (e.g., “3”),
the answer is either exactly right (score 1) or wrong (score 0).
There is no partial credit for being off by one.
3.
Negation + correction questions.
Some Ground Truth answers first negate a premise and then
provide the correct information
(e.g., “No — it was May 18-22, not May 15-19”).
The assistant must get BOTH the negation AND the corrected
fact right for full credit.
4.
Identity / “Who is” questions.
The Ground Truth may describe a person by role, actions,
or relationships rather than by name.
The assistant’s answer is correct if it identifies the same
unique person, even if it uses a name instead of a description
or vice versa.
5.
Answer the thing that was asked.
Judge whether the assistant answered the requested attribute
or type of information. If the question asks for a category,
role, relationship, time, count, ordering, or specific item,
an answer giving a different type of information is not fully
correct even if it is related.
6.
Wrong entity beats related entity.
If the answer names the wrong person, object, brand, place,
event, or option, do not give high scores just because it
is on-topic. Being from the right semantic domain is not enough.
7.
Multi-item questions require set matching.
Full credit requires all required items and no incorrect extras.
If only some required items are correct, partial credit
may be appropriate.
8.
Ordering / chronology questions require
the correct item.
If the question asks which item was first, last, middle,
earlier, later, before, or after, the selected item must
match the Ground Truth.
A different plausible item is still wrong.
9.
Do not over-reward fluent explanations.
Extra detail is helpful only if it stays consistent with
the Ground Truth.
Confident wording or elaboration should not increase the
score when the core fact is wrong.
10.
Contradicted relations or orderings
are usually zero.
If the question asks about a relationship such as before/after,
earlier/later, first/last, middle, sequence, relative timing,
or other ordering, and the assistant gives the opposite
relation, denies the relation, or selects the wrong ordered
item, this is usually a clear contradiction and should
normally receive score 0 rather than 0.25.
Scoring Rubric.
Score 0 (Incorrect / Miss):
•
The answer contradicts the Ground Truth.
•
For Yes/No questions: The answer has the wrong polarity
(e.g., says “Yes” when Ground Truth is “No”).
•
For numeric questions: The number is wrong.
•
For attribute-type mismatches: the answer gives the
wrong kind of thing (for example, a brand when the question
asks for a product category, or a related event when the
question asks for the earliest specific item).
•
For relation/order questions: if the answer contradicts
the required before/after, earlier/later, first/last, middle,
or similar relationship, score 0 in the usual case.
•
The answer provides factually wrong information,
hallucinations, or fails to provide any relevant information.
Score 0.25 (Poor / Tangential):
•
The answer touches on the topic but misses the
core entity
or key value required.
•
The answer contains a mix of minor correct details and
significant hallucinations
or wrong associations.
•
The answer is excessively vague to the point of being
useless (e.g., answering “a dog” instead of
“a golden retriever”).
•
For multi-item questions: use 0.25 when the answer is
clearly about the right topic but most of the required
set is wrong.
Score 0.5 (Partial / Vague):
•
The answer captures the
main entity or concept
correctly but misses important supporting details.
•
For negation + correction questions: The polarity is
correct but the corrected fact is missing or wrong,
or vice versa.
•
The answer is too general or misses key qualifiers
present in the Ground Truth.
•
For multi-item questions: use 0.5 when the answer gets
a substantial part of the required set right
(for example, one of two required items is correct and the
rest is wrong or missing).
Score 0.75 (Good / Minor Imperfection):
•
The answer is largely accurate and captures the
core information confidently.
•
It misses only
minor details
(e.g., specific adjectives or secondary details)
that do not alter the main truth.
•
The answer contains all the correct information but
includes unnecessary filler that reduces precision.
Score 1 (Correct / Exact):
•
The answer is accurate, precise, and confident.
•
For Yes/No questions: The polarity matches the
Ground Truth perfectly.
•
For numeric questions: The number matches exactly.
•
For descriptive questions: The answer contains
all
the core information and necessary details
required by the Ground Truth without hallucinations.
•
Semantic equivalence is sufficient — exact wording
is NOT required.
•
For multi-item questions: all required items are
present and there are no incorrect extra items.
Input Data.
Ground Truth:
<reference answer(s)>
Assistant Answer:
<predicted answer>
Output Format.
Output strictly in the following JSON format:
{"score": <0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, or 1>,
"reasoning": "<short explanation>"}
MemLens.
MemLens uses a binary rubric with a task-specific criterion.
Exactly one of the criteria listed below is inserted into
the shared template.
Judge Prompt: MemLens
Now your role is a grading teacher.
Your task is to review and score student answers based on
reference standard answers for a question-answering benchmark.
First, extract the final answer from the student’s solution,
then judge whether the answer is correct.
Score only the final answer; intermediate problem-solving steps
do not need to be correct.
If multiple inconsistent answers are given, or no clear final
answer is stated, assign 0 points.
Only the student’s last clearly stated answer counts.
An item is covered if it is strictly mentioned or unambiguously
implied by semantic equivalence.
This includes numerical equivalence, synonyms, plural/singular
forms, and equivalent date formats.
Do not accept loosely related concepts.
Ignore minor formatting differences, capitalization, punctuation,
and equivalent wording when meaning is unchanged.
The scoring scale has two levels: 1 point and 0 points.
Assign 1 point if the student’s final answer matches the standard
answer under the task-specific criteria below.
Assign 0 points otherwise, including refusal or a claim of
insufficient information except for answer-refusal tasks.
[Task-Specific Criteria]:
<criterion selected for the question type>
Your output format is:
[Scoring Rationale]:
[Score]: x points
[JSON]: {"answer_score": <0 or 1>}
[Current Case]
Standard Answer:
<reference answer(s)>
Student Answer:
<predicted answer>
[Scoring Rationale]:
MemLens Task-Specific Criteria
[IE — Entity / Attribute Extraction]
This is an information extraction question about a concrete
entity, count, attribute, text, object, location, or visual
detail from the provided memory context.
•
Assign 1 point if the student’s response contains
the core information from the standard answer.
Minor wording differences are acceptable, but the essential
information must be present and correct.
•
Assign 0 points if the core information is missing,
contradicted, too vague, refused, or incorrect.
•
For numeric or count answers, require the exact value
unless the standard answer itself is approximate.
[IE — Previous Information Extraction]
This is an information extraction question about previously
mentioned information, spatial relations, counts, or attributes
from earlier conversation/image context.
•
Assign 1 point if the student’s response recovers
the same previous information as the standard answer,
including the correct relation, location, count, or attribute.
•
Minor wording differences are acceptable if they
preserve the same meaning.
•
Assign 0 points if the answer refers to the wrong
previous item, gives the wrong relation/count/location,
is too vague, refuses, or is unsupported.
[KU — Knowledge Update]
This is a knowledge update question testing whether the model
tracks the latest state.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the current
(correct) answer.
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives an outdated answer,
any other incorrect answer, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Yes/No (Entity Resolution)]
This is a yes/no question.
•
Assign 1 point if the student’s final answer is
semantically equivalent to the standard answer
(e.g., “Yes” matches “Yes”, “No” matches “No”),
even if phrased differently
(e.g., “That’s correct” for “Yes”).
•
Assign 0 points if the answer means the opposite,
refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Counting]
This is a counting question.
The standard answer is a specific number.
•
Assign 1 point if the student clearly states the
exact number in any equivalent form
(e.g., “3”, “three”, “3.0”).
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a different number,
a range, an approximation, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Arithmetic]
This is an arithmetic question.
The standard answer is a specific value.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the same value
in an equivalent format
(e.g., “0.5” and “1/2” and “50%”).
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a different value,
an unsupported approximation, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[TR — Duration Comparison (A/B)]
This is a binary choice question.
The student must select one of two options.
•
Assign 1 point if the student clearly selects the
same option as the standard answer, regardless of phrasing.
•
Assign 0 points if the student selects the other option,
refuses, or does not make a clear selection.
[TR — Order Ranking]
This is an ordering question.
The standard answer is an exact sequence of items.
•
Assign 1 point ONLY if the student gives the exact
same sequence in the same order.
•
Assign 0 points if any item is missing, added,
duplicated, misplaced, or if the order is unclear.
[TR — Date Extraction]
This is a date extraction question.
The standard answer is a specific date.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the same date
in any unambiguous equivalent format
(e.g., “Jan 15, 2024” and “2024-01-15” and “15/01/2024”).
•
Assign 0 points if the date is different,
incomplete when a full date is required, ambiguous, or missing.
[AR — Answer Refusal]
•
Assign 1 point if the student explicitly refuses,
says there is not enough information, or indicates the
question is unanswerable from the provided context.
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a substantive
answer, even if hedged.

article.headline: MemPilot：按需编排多模态记忆的智能体框架
article.lede: 用强化学习训练一个多步编排策略，在检索压缩记忆与委派原始多模态历史之间反复选择，换取可调的质量—成本—延迟折中。
article.problem: 现有智能体记忆系统大多以与查询无关的方式预先构建记忆，既产生不必要的预处理开销，又可能丢掉后续查询才需要的细节。近期转向运行时自适应的方案往往只针对单一操作或固定处理流程，且很少把用户可感知的延迟当作显式优化目标，对性能、成本、延迟的灵活控制仍未被充分探索。
article.method: MemPilot 维护双视图记忆：一个与查询无关的压缩记忆库用于快速检索，一份按 256 token 分块、保留原始多模态上下文的交互历史用于运行时策展。编排器是一个多步 LLM 策略，每一步在 Retrieve 与 Curate 之间选择；Curate 进一步分解出检索查询、证据条数、策展指令、调用哪个外部 LLM/VLM、是否附带原始图像等控制量。训练用 GRPO，并对质量、成本、延迟三个目标分别做组内优势归一化再加权聚合，同时用前缀答案探测估计每一步的边际效用，做更细粒度的信用分配。
article.results: 在 Mem-Gallery、WorldMemArena、H2HMem 三个域内基准和 MemEye、MemLens 两个域外基准上，以 Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct 为答案模型时，MemPilot-Perf 在全部五个基准上取得最高 LLM-judge 分数（65.82、63.41、35.97、25.07、27.17），换用 Qwen3.5-9B 答案模型后同样全部最高（67.64、74.09、37.57、21.83、24.28）。MemPilot-Bal 在 Mem-Gallery 上 F1 为 57.26、成本 1.4e-2，MemPilot-Cost 把成本压到 8.2e-3 但 F1 降至 32.67。消融显示五个基准平均 judge 分从 37.40 分别跌至：去掉 LLM/VLM 委派 14.58、去掉边际效用 14.82、去掉目标优势解耦（GDPO）21.94、去掉检索—指令解耦 15.35。
article.why_it_matters: 它把记忆策展从「预先建好、查询时照用」改写成运行时的计算分配问题：同一套策略通过偏好向量在不同质量、成本、延迟的工作点上滑动，并与现成的查询无关记忆库保持兼容。对需要长程多模态交互的智能体部署来说，这提供了比单一性能最优点更贴近实际的配置方式。
article.limitations: 实验中的延迟并非实测墙钟时间，而是由固定开销加每 token 系数的仿射代理估计器给出，作者自己也承认需要稳定的系统级沙箱才能直接对真实延迟优化。此外，Curate 会把检索到的交互历史发给外部模型，存在隐私暴露风险；偏好系数仍需人工设定，且 Cost 偏好下质量下降明显（Mem-Gallery 上 F1 从 57.26 掉到 32.67），说明低成本工作点并不总能保住可用质量。

figure.caption: {Overview of MemPilot.} {(a)} The orchestrator iteratively retrieves compressed memories or delegates query-specific curation of raw multimodal histories to heterogeneous LLMs/VLMs. Factorized controls govern evidence retrieval, curation strategy, visual access, and model selection, with accumulated evidence guiding subsequent decisions and final answering. {(b)} Objective-wise advantage decoupling enables controllable trade-offs among quality, cost, and latency, while prefix-based answer probing estimates each step's marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment.

page_papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
page_papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

Abstract
Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control.
Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface.
In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding.
Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored.
Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

Keywords:
Machine Learning, ICML
1
Introduction
Learning models that can understand and predict the physical world is a long-standing goal of artificial intelligence
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Hafner et al., 2025
;
Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018
)
.
In particular, the emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)
(
Assran et al., 2023
;
Bardes et al., 2024
;
Bardes et al., 2023
;
Ghaemi et al., 2026
;
Skenderi et al., 2025
)
offer a promising approach by predicting in representation space rather than reconstructing observations at the pixel level.
Recent notable developments such as V-JEPA 2
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Maes et al., 2026
)
further extend this idea toward world modeling, where learned latent representations support the prediction of future states and, when conditioned on actions, can be used for planning and control. JEPA-based models have also expanded beyond general-purpose visual representation learning to embodied control and robotics
(
Sun et al., 2026
;
Yan et al., 2026
)
, 3D scene understanding
(
McVay et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Zhu et al., 2026
)
, medical analysis
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Radhachandran et al., 2026
;
Shah et al., 2025
)
, scientific discovery
(
Larey et al., 2026
;
ElSheikh et al., 2026
;
Bardhan et al., 2025
)
, and other domains
(
He et al., 2026
;
Hassan et al., 2026
)
. As JEPAs take on broader roles, their latent spaces increasingly serve as internal states for representing and predicting how the world evolves.
This encouraging shift, on the other hand, also raises a largely overlooked question:
what world has a JEPA learned inside its latent space?
This question is challenging, because unlike generative world models that produce human-observable predictions, JEPAs intrinsically predict in an abstract representation space without a naturally interpretable interface.
When a prediction fails, it is therefore difficult to determine whether the failure arises from the represented state, learned dynamics, missing interactions, or errors accumulated over time. More broadly, predictive performance alone cannot establish whether a model has learned meaningful world structure or relies on shortcuts that succeed within its training distribution
(
Kang et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
Figure 1
:
Evolution and positioning of interpretability for latent-space world models. Despite rapid advances in latent-space world modeling and a rich XAI toolbox, direct interpretation of learned world models remains sparse. Existing efforts largely focus on latent-content probing or isolated analysis and intervention techniques, leaving systematic understanding of latent worlds underexplored.
Currently, few existing approaches to representation interpretability provide a natural starting point for addressing this problem. They can reveal what semantic or physical information is recoverable from learned representations, such as objects, motion, and actions
(
Yuan and Søgaard, 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
)
. However, decodability alone does not establish how this information participates in the model’s internal world. Recovering velocity, for example, does not show how it relates to other variables, shapes latent dynamics, or causally contributes to prediction.
As such, interpreting a latent world model therefore requires moving beyond what its representations encode toward how they function together as a predictive system.
To instantiate this point, Figure
1
situates the gap within the broader landscape of world modeling and interpretability. Although general XAI and mechanistic interpretability offer a rich toolbox
(
Sundararajan et al., 2017
;
Wachter et al., 2017
;
Alain and Bengio, 2017
;
Kim et al., 2018
;
Huben et al., 2024
;
Olah et al., 2020
;
Meng et al., 2022
;
Turner et al., 2023
)
, this toolbox has rarely been applied to learned world models as the primary object of interpretation. Existing XAI studies involving world representations largely pursue different objectives.
Some introduce explicit world structure as a modeling mechanism: TDB
(
Dedieu et al., 2024
)
uses discrete bottlenecks to extract cognitive maps, OOCDM
(
Yu et al., 2024
)
builds object-oriented causal dynamics models, and C-JEPA
(
Nam et al., 2026
)
introduces object-centric latent structure.
Others use world models as an interpretability lens, asking whether Transformers or LLMs develop structured internal representations that resemble world models
(
Rohekar et al., 2025
;
Spies et al., 2025
;
Tehenan et al., 2025
)
. In both cases, the learned world model itself is not the primary object of interpretation. Direct interpretability of learned world models remains scarce. Existing efforts primarily probe what information is encoded in latent representations
(
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ming, 2026
)
or explore individual analysis and intervention techniques
(
Challagundla et al., 2026
;
Hong et al., 2026
)
. Consequently, how latent variables are organized, evolve, and causally support prediction remains largely unexplored.
Our position is therefore:
as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction.
Towards this shift, we envision a four-stage blueprint:
Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act
.
Specifically, Ground connects latent factors to variables in the external world. Structure studies how these factors relate and evolve through the model’s learned dynamics. Verify tests whether the identified factors and structures are causally involved in prediction through controlled interventions. Finally, Act uses this understanding to diagnose failures and improve model behavior. Together, these stages shift the interpretability from identifying information that can be extracted from representations to understanding the internal mechanisms through which a latent world model represents, predicts, and acts upon the world.
In sum, our contribution is to establish a clear formulation of latent-world interpretability for predictive world models and provide a systematic blueprint for studying it. We organize existing efforts through this lens, identify the key gaps that remain, and outline how closing these gaps could enable more informative diagnosis, evaluation, and improvement of predictive world models. Finally, we discuss alternative views and identify priorities for advancing this emerging research agenda.

Linear and nonlinear probes test the decodability of particular variables, while concept-based methods, clustering, sparse representations, and related approaches identify correspondences between latent features and interpretable properties. Despite their methodological differences, these approaches share a common question:

. It characterizes the semantic and physical content accessible from learned representations and provides a natural starting point for JEPA interpretability.
2.3
The Gap: Decoding Is Not Understanding
Decodability establishes that information about a world variable is accessible from a latent state, but not how it is organized or used by the predictive dynamics. This distinction matters for world models, where latent states are transformed over time to predict how the world evolves.
Consider a simple example in which velocity can be accurately decoded from

This establishes that velocity-related information is accessible from the representation, but not how velocity relates to other variables such as object position or contact, or how these variables jointly evolve over time. More importantly, successful decoding does not establish that the predictor actually uses velocity-related information when computing

We therefore distinguish
representational accessibility
from
world-model understanding
. The former concerns what information can be recovered from latent states; the latter concerns how that information is organized, evolves through learned dynamics, and causally contributes to prediction. For action-conditioned models, it also concerns how actions influence this evolution. The next section develops a four-stage blueprint for moving toward such understanding.
Takeaway 1: Decodability is not understanding.
Recovering a world variable from a latent state shows that the information is accessible, but not how it is organized, how it evolves, or whether the predictor causally relies on it.

Takeaway 3: Direct evidence for latent-world interpretability in JEPAs remains sparse.

5
Implications: What Understanding Latent Worlds Enables
In this section, we aim to shift the object of interpretation from representations to latent worlds, changing how world models can be analyzed and evaluated.
If the internal variables, relations, and dynamics of a JEPA can be grounded and causally verified, they can help explain model successes and failures, assess when predictions should be trusted, and guide improvements in model behavior.
To achieve this goal, we highlight four implications below.
5.1
Diagnosing where prediction failures arise
A prediction error alone reveals little about what went wrong inside a world model. Consider a robot pushing a cup near the edge of a table. If the model predicts that the cup will remain on the table but it instead falls, several internal failures could produce the same observed error. The latent state may fail to represent that the cup is near the edge (
state representation
); the predictor may represent the state correctly but fail to capture the dynamics of losing support (
dynamics
); it may fail to model the interaction among the robot, cup, and table (
interaction
); or initially correct predictions may drift during multi-step prediction (
rollout
).
Latent world understanding could make these failure modes distinguishable. Grounded factors can reveal whether the relevant state information is present, while recovered relations and transitions can expose where the predicted evolution departs from the expected dynamics. Causal analysis can further identify which internal mechanisms contribute to the failure. Thus, these capabilities could turn interpretability into a tool for localizing errors within the predictive process.
5.2
Distinguishing learned world models from shortcuts
Strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply that a model has captured the underlying structure of the world. Similar performance may arise from meaningful physical structure or from correlated cues such as background texture and camera motion. Latent world interpretability provides a way to distinguish these possibilities by examining whether verified internal mechanisms remain predictively relevant as such correlations change.
A model whose predictions consistently depend on stable world relevant factors across objects, scenes, and environments provides stronger evidence of having captured transferable world structure. Conversely, if prediction depends strongly on factors tied to incidental properties of the training distribution, the apparent world modeling capability may be more fragile than performance suggests. This distinction could provide a more informative basis for assessing what kind of world knowledge a JEPA has actually acquired.
5.3
Explaining generalization and its limits
Understanding latent worlds may also help explain why some predictive models generalize across environments while others fail under distribution shift. Rather than treating generalization only as an empirical property measured on downstream benchmarks, latent world analysis allows us to examine which parts of the internal model remain stable as the environment changes.
For example, latent factors that remain stable across changes in object appearance while varying systematically with geometry or dynamics may support transfer across visually different environments
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
. Conversely, factors that change strongly with background, camera viewpoint, or other task-irrelevant properties may reveal likely sources of out-of-distribution failure
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Sun et al., 2024
)
. Studying these invariances and dependencies could connect the internal organization of a latent world to the conditions under which its predictions remain reliable
(
Poudel et al., 2024
)
.
Takeaway 4: Similar predictive performance can hide fundamentally different internal worlds.
Latent-world analysis can distinguish where failures arise, whether predictions rely on transferable world structure or shortcuts, and which internal mechanisms remain stable under distribution shift.
5.4
From post-hoc explanation to decision-bounded interpretation
The consequences of latent world understanding become particularly important when model predictions are used for planning and control. In this setting, an inaccurate internal world can affect not only what the model predicts, but also which actions an agent chooses. Interpretability could provide an additional basis for assessing predictions before they are used for decision making, for example by identifying whether relevant state variables are represented reliably or whether the predicted dynamics are consistent with previously verified mechanisms.
This perspective also broadens the role of interpretability in safety. Rather than explaining failures only after an action has been taken, latent world analysis could help assess predictions before they are used for action. For agents that use JEPA predictions for planning and control, interpretability could reveal whether a prediction depends on internal variables and dynamics that have been reliably identified and verified, or on patterns known to be unstable under similar conditions. Such information could provide a signal for deciding when a model’s prediction should be trusted.
6
Alternative Views and Limitations
We consider several alternative views that challenge our position and help clarify its scope.
One possible view is that decoding may sometimes be sufficient. This is indeed the case for many interpretability questions. If the goal is to determine whether a JEPA representation contains information about object identity, motion, geometry, or another property, a well-designed probe may provide all the evidence that is needed. The need for deeper analysis arises when the question concerns the internal predictive world: how represented information is organized, how it participates in prediction, or whether the model causally relies on it. These questions require evidence beyond decodability. Our blueprint is intended for precisely this setting, where representation-level interpretation is a useful starting point but not the end of the analysis.
A deeper concern is whether human-defined variables provide the right ontology for interpreting a latent world. A JEPA need not decompose its internal computation into familiar concepts such as position, velocity, or contact
(
Chawla et al., 2026
)
. Its representations may instead be distributed, nonlinear, relational, or task-dependent, and some predictive factors may have no simple human-interpretable counterpart. Grounding should therefore not presuppose a one-to-one correspondence between human concepts and individual neurons or latent directions. Instead, such concepts can serve as reference points for discovering testable correspondences involving subspaces, nonlinear structures, or distributed representations. Cases in which the model’s internal organization departs from human-defined variables may themselves reveal how it represents the world differently from our chosen description.
Another concern is that interventions in latent space may not always be valid. We agree that simply changing a latent factor is not sufficient to establish a causal relationship. A latent representation may encode multiple properties together, so changing a factor associated with velocity, for example, could unintentionally change other properties as well. The modified representation may also no longer correspond to a plausible state of the world. In either case, a change in prediction would be difficult to attribute to the intended intervention. An important challenge for Verify is therefore to develop interventions that change the target factor while preserving other relevant information and keeping the resulting latent state plausible. Determining how to construct and validate such interventions is an important direction for future research.
More broadly, interpretability may not be necessary for building reliable world models. Robust prediction and control can also be pursued through behavioral evaluation, uncertainty estimation, robustness training, and out-of-distribution testing without examining internal representations. Latent world interpretability should not replace these approaches. Its value is complementary: behavioral evaluation can reveal whether and under what conditions a model fails, while internal analysis may help identify the mechanisms behind those failures and distinguish models that achieve similar performance through different internal strategies. This additional evidence may be particularly useful when predictive models are used for planning and control, where prediction failures can directly affect subsequent decisions and actions.
Taken together, these considerations highlight important challenges of latent world interpretability. They also clarify where the proposed blueprint applies and where its assumptions and methods require further validation.
Takeaway 5: Going beyond decoding does not mean abandoning decoding or behavioral evaluation.
Decoding remains sufficient for representation-level questions, while latent-world understanding is needed for claims about predictive mechanisms. Such claims require valid interventions and should complement, rather than replace, behavioral evaluation.
7
Call to Action
In aggregate, the aforementioned discussions indicate that realizing latent-world interpretability inevitably requires redirecting research efforts beyond isolated applications of existing interpretability tools toward a systematic research program centered on the variables, structures, dynamics, and causal mechanisms of learned worlds. To help shape future research, we highlight four priorities toward this goal.
Build controlled testbeds and evaluation criteria.
A first priority is to develop settings in which latent world interpretations can be tested against known properties of the world. Environments with known objects, physical variables, interactions, and dynamics provide a basis for evaluating whether recovered latent structure reflects the underlying system. Evaluation should go beyond decoding accuracy to test whether interpretations remain stable across contexts, whether recovered relations and dynamics are consistent with observed behavior, and whether causal claims hold under controlled changes. Such testbeds will not capture the full complexity of real-world prediction, but they can provide a foundation for evaluating latent world interpretations systematically.
Study how latent worlds emerge and differ across models.
Latent world interpretability should examine how internal predictive structure develops through learning. The organization learned by a JEPA may depend on its architecture, training objective, data, model scale, and stage of training
(
Richens et al., 2025
)
. Comparing models along these dimensions could reveal when world-relevant factors and dynamics begin to emerge, whether similar structures arise across models, and which design choices lead to more stable or reusable internal structure. This would extend interpretability to studying how latent worlds form and evolve.
Connect interpretation to model behavior and design.
Interpretations should be tested against meaningful differences in prediction, generalization, failure modes, and downstream planning or control. Such connections can also inform model design. If particular internal structures are consistently associated with more reliable prediction or better generalization, they may provide useful evidence for comparing architectures, training objectives, or other design choices.
Interpretability could thereby serve not only to analyze trained models, but also to understand which design choices lead to better predictive world models.
Scale latent world analysis to realistic settings.
Methods developed in controlled environments must eventually be tested on natural video, long-horizon prediction, and embodied agents operating in complex environments. Doing so will require tools for extracting and comparing internal states, tracing predictive computation over time, performing controlled interventions, and analyzing rollouts across model families.
Shared infrastructure and evaluation protocols could make these analyses more reproducible and make it easier to compare findings across models and studies.
8
Conclusion
This Perspective aims to establish latent-world understanding as a central goal for interpreting predictive world models. We note that decodability is not understanding: accessible information does not reveal how it is organized, evolves, or causally supports prediction. Building on this observation, we envision the Ground–Structure–Verify–Act blueprint as a path toward this goal, and as a framework for shaping future research on latent-world interpretability. We call for future interpretability efforts to move beyond isolated representation-level analyses toward systematically understanding, validating, and acting on the internal worlds learned by predictive models.
