article.headline: JEPA 潜在世界可解释性：从解码走向因果理解
article.lede: 一篇立场论文主张，JEPA 的可解释性不能止于探测表征里有什么，而要追问潜在变量如何组织、演化并因果地驱动预测。
article.problem: JEPA 类模型在抽象表征空间中预测未来，其潜在世界缺少面向人类的解释接口。预测失败时，很难判断错误来自状态表征、学到的动力学、缺失的交互，还是多步推演中的漂移。现有表征可解释性方法多只能回答「潜表征里能解码出什么」，无法说明这些信息如何被预测器使用。
article.method: 作者把 JEPA 视为由编码器和预测器构成的潜在预测世界模型，提出 Ground、Structure、Verify、Act 四阶段研究蓝图。Ground 将潜在因子与外部世界变量对应，Structure 恢复因子间的关系与动力学，Verify 通过受控潜在干预检验因果作用，Act 用被验证的机制诊断失败并定向改进模型。作者并用这一框架把现有工作（如 V-JEPA 2 探针、WorldModelLens、World Action Models 的激活干预）逐项对位。
article.results: 这是一篇 Perspective 论文，未报告新的量化实验，论文未给出具体数字。其定性梳理显示：JEPA 内部的直接证据几乎集中在 Ground 阶段，例如 V-JEPA 2 的探针表明冻结表征中含有外观、运动与动作信息；Structure、Verify、Act 三步在 JEPA 上基本空白。作者整理的对照表中，只有非 JEPA 的 World Action Models 工作被标注为四项全部或部分覆盖（Act 为明确覆盖），其余工作最多覆盖到 Ground 与部分 Structure、Verify。
article.why_it_matters: 如果潜在变量能被落地并做因果验证，可解释性就能从「事后看图」变成定位预测失败、区分真实世界结构与捷径、并在规划控制前判断预测是否可信的工具。它也为比较不同架构与训练目标提供了表征层面的依据。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认，潜在空间中的干预未必有效：一个因子可能纠缠多个属性，改动后还可能落到不合理的世界状态，使因果归因失效；同时人的概念（位置、速度、接触）未必是模型内部组织的正确本体。此外，可解释性并非构建可靠世界模型的必要条件，行为评测、不确定性估计与分布外测试可以独立完成许多目标，该蓝图应作为补充而非替代；JEPA 上的直接证据也仍然稀少。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从解码表征到理解潜在世界：Ground 把潜在因子对应到可解释的世界变量，Structure 恢复其关系与学到的动力学，Verify 用受控潜在干预检验因果相关性，Act 则用被验证的机制诊断失败并定向干预模型行为。

figure.caption: From decoding representations to understanding latent worlds. Standard probing and decoding methods identify information recoverable from JEPA representations but do not reveal how that information is organized, used by the predictor, or relied upon in future predictions. Our proposed blueprint progresses through four stages: Ground connects latent factors to interpretable world variables; Structure recovers their relations and learned dynamics; Verify tests their causal relevance through controlled latent interventions; and Act uses verified mechanisms to diagnose failures and improve model behavior through targeted interventions.

page_papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7–8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
Figure 1:
Performance of OpenVLHarness across models and settings.
(a)
Average score over 22 challenging multimodal benchmarks with and without OpenVLHarness, across the Qwen, Kimi, and GPT model families.
(b)
Benchmark scores for GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Astra at medium reasoning effort, each with and without OpenVLHarness; radii are rescaled per benchmark, and numbers give the raw scores of GPT-6 Astra (medium) with OpenVLHarness.
(c)
Average score versus model-token cost (average for 1,000 query rollouts) on 22 benchmarks for GPT-6 Luna alone and with Codex, Visual Sketchpad, or OpenVLHarness, across all five reasoning-effort settings.
1

Introduction
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning engines over images, documents, webpages, and videos. However, many real-world visual tasks require information that the model cannot reliably infer from the input alone. Answering a question may require localizing numerous tiny objects in dense scenes, retrieving external knowledge about a long-tail entity, or computing quantities from intermediate measurements. Such tasks require additional multimodal evidence acquired through perception, search, and computation. Our inference-time scaling study (Fig.
1
c) reveals diminishing returns at higher reasoning budgets: moving the base model from xhigh to max effort multiplies its model-token spending by 2.7 but improves its average score by only 0.7 points. This raises the question of whether further progress requires better access to task-relevant multimodal evidence, beyond additional reasoning over the initial input.
Visual tool-use agents address this need by connecting MLLMs to perception models, search engines, and code execution
(
Hong et al., 2026a
;
Wu et al., 2025a
;
Narayan et al., 2025
;
Geng et al., 2026
;
Su et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Surís et al., 2023
;
Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023
)
. Building a general harness around these tools presents two connected challenges. First, heterogeneous backends expose different calling conventions and return outputs such as segmentation masks, depth maps, and retrieved webpages that need to be presented in a form the model can interpret. Second, subsequent reasoning steps may still need access to the underlying artifacts: a rendered depth map supports visual inspection, but a precise measurement requires its numerical values. Effective multimodal tool use therefore requires both consistent tool interfaces with evidence rendering and a mechanism for retaining and reusing the resulting artifacts.
We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a
capability layer
and
persistent multimodal memory
. The capability layer combines
task-level tool interfaces
with
model-facing evidence rendering
. Task-level interfaces define operations independently of a particular backend, allowing tools to be replaced without changing the orchestrator’s task vocabulary. Evidence rendering converts heterogeneous outputs into observations that combine visualizations, concise descriptions, and compact structured information. For example, visual grounding accepts an image and a textual query, then presents the detected regions through an annotated image and coordinates. Together, these mechanisms let the orchestrator invoke tools consistently and inspect their results in a form suited to multimodal reasoning.
Persistent multimodal memory makes the corresponding artifacts available across turns within a query. Images, structured data, and web references are registered under reusable handles, allowing later calls to operate on earlier evidence. In the grounding example, the orchestrator can inspect the overlay, then reuse the retained masks and a subsequently acquired depth array to measure depth within each region. A Python Coding Agent supports such compositions: the orchestrator specifies a computational objective in natural language, and a code-generation session backed by the same backbone model writes a program that executes over the stored data. The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. Together, they support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and computing over multimodal evidence.
We evaluate OpenVLHarness on 22 benchmarks spanning grounded perception, visual search and deep research, general VQA and hallucination, and spatial reasoning, using eight open and proprietary MLLM backbones of different scales (Fig.
1
a). Across these settings, OpenVLHarness consistently improves average performance over the base MLLMs by 9.7–12.6 percentage points and outperforms existing visual tool-use baselines (Fig.
1
c). Scaling experiments on 22 benchmarks further show that OpenVLHarness also benefits from greater reasoning effort (Fig.
1
c), suggesting that evidence acquisition and inference-time scaling are complementary.
We conduct ablation studies to examine the incremental effects of the capability layer and memory, showing the value of both usable tool outputs and retained multimodal artifacts. Lastly, for users who would like to adapt our harness to a custom domain, we further showcase two coding-agent-driven workflows for specialization: harness search edits prompts, tool descriptions, and output templates, while tool generation composes existing capabilities into new tools. Both operate without updating the underlying MLLM weights.
Our contributions are:
(1)
a capability layer that combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering for heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools;
(2)
persistent multimodal memory that retains addressable artifacts across turns and enables their reuse in subsequent tool calls and memory-grounded computation;
and
(3)
an evaluation across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones, with component ablations and domain-specialization studies, accompanied by an open-source release of the harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and two optimization workflows.
2

Persistent Multimodal Memory
The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; persistent multimodal memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. A later tool call must be able to identify a particular image, mask, or array and access its contents. Repeating a description of a previous result does not provide this access.
We maintain an explicit artifact registry for each query, with entries retained across its reasoning trajectory. The registry separates an artifact’s payload from the handle used to reference it. The orchestrator sees available names and compact descriptors, while the harness retains the underlying values and resolves references when needed. The registry contains three categories:
•
Image artifacts:
input, tool-generated, and retrieved images, exposed through handles such as
input_image_3
and
tool_generated_image_6
. Duplicate images reuse an existing registry entry.
•
Structured data bindings:
named values containing boxes, scores, masks, depth arrays, camera parameters, OCR results, and other tool outputs. Each binding has a descriptor identifying its fields and types, including array shapes where applicable.
•
Web references:
retrieved URLs exposed through handles such as
webpage_url_1
, allowing later navigation without requiring the model to reproduce the original URL.
Registering and reusing artifacts.
After a successful tool call, the harness registers supported artifacts and associates their handles with the capability’s rendered observation. Images are delivered as visual attachments with named references; structured payloads remain accessible through data bindings. An

Can More Reasoning Replace the Harness?

Conclusion
We presented OpenVLHarness, a general harness for real-world visual agentic tool use built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, enabling the orchestrator to invoke heterogeneous tools and inspect their outputs. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding artifacts for reuse across turns, including computation over stored data through a Python Coding Agent. Together, these mechanisms support reasoning that acquires and composes multimodal evidence. Evaluation across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones demonstrates broad gains, while component ablations show the incremental benefits of the capability layer and multimodal memory. Harness search and tool generation further specialize the system on selected domains without updating the underlying MLLM weights. We release the harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and optimization workflows to support further work on multimodal tool-use agents.

article.headline: 多模态智能体：工具层与持久记忆提升 22 项基准
article.lede: 新框架把异构视觉工具统一为任务级接口，并用持久多模态记忆保存图像、掩码与网页产物，在 22 个基准上平均提升 9.7 至
article.problem: 很多真实视觉任务所需的证据无法靠模型内部推理可靠获得：密集场景中的小目标定位、对长尾实体的外部检索、以及由中间测量值推算数量。作者在 22 个基准上的控制实验显示，单纯加大推理预算收益有限：把基座模型从 xhigh 提到 max 推理档，模型 token 花费变为 2.7 倍，平均分只提高 0.7 分。
article.method: OpenVLHarness 由能力层和持久多模态记忆两部分组成。能力层用任务级接口封装异构后端，并把分割掩码、深度图、检索网页等输出渲染成模型可读的证据（标注图、简短描述和归一化框）；持久记忆则把图像、结构化数据绑定（框、掩码、深度数组、相机参数、OCR 结果）和网页引用注册为可寻址句柄，供后续调用复用。一个 Python 编码 agent 能在已存数据上执行生成程序，从而把多个工具的结果组合计算。
article.results: 在 22 个基准、8 个开源与闭源 backbone 上，平均分比匹配的无工具基线高 9.7 至 12.6 分：Qwen3-VL-8B 从 34.2 升到 45.4（+11.2，比最强免训练基线 OctoTools 的 31.8 高 13.6），Qwen3-VL-32B 从 38.3 升到 50.9（+12.6），Kimi K3 提升 9.7 分（56.4 到 66.1），GPT-6 Astra 从 60.3 升到 70.2（+9.9）。GPT-6 Luna 在 medium 推理档下，比基座模型、Codex 和 Visual Sketchpad 在 max 档时的得分高 7.7 至 8.5 分，而模型 token 成本至多只有后三者的 37%。作为对比，把模型直接放进 Codex 循环反而低于无工具基线（Qwen3-VL-8B：31.42 对 34.24）。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明证据获取与推理时扩展是互补的两条路径，加大推理预算并不能替代工具。更重要的是，效果取决于 harness 本身的设计：通用编码 agent 循环并不会自动带来提升。
article.limitations: 闭源 backbone 因 API 成本只跑一次，没有给出标准差，而搜索 API、工具路由决策和 LLM 判分都具有随机性，主要统计只来自 Qwen3-VL 的三次重复运行。作者自己的案例也显示失败模式仍在：有的问题缺少同一模型的无工具对照，有的轨迹在检索出错后，最终答案部分仍沿用模型早先的猜测；此外，当检索依赖外部服务时，会出现 500 错误，而且在 Qwen3-VL-8B 上通用 VQA 与空间推理的增益并不一致。
article.figure_caption_zh: MLLM 编排器通过类型化接口调用能力层，能力层将掩码、描述与归一化框渲染为模型可读证据，持久多模态记忆则以可复用句柄保存图像、结构化数据与网页引用，并通过环境更新告知后续调用。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} The MLLM orchestrator invokes capabilities through typed interfaces. The capability layer connects these interfaces to underlying models and services and renders their outputs into model-facing evidence: here, a labeled mask overlay accompanied by a textual description and normalized bounding boxes. Persistent multimodal memory retains image artifacts, structured data, and web references under reusable handles. An Environment Update advertises the available artifacts to the orchestrator, allowing subsequent calls to reuse earlier evidence, including through memory-grounded computation.

page_papers.title: EmoRSS: Mitigating Emotion-Induced Over-Refusal in Large Language Models
page_papers.abstract: Emotional expression can influence the safety decisions of large language models (LLMs), offering a potential avenue for improving safety alignment. Existing studies have mainly focused on how emotional expressions facilitate attacks under harmful requests, while overlooking their effects on benign requests. We find that emotional expression can also systematically increase refusal tendencies on benign requests, leading to unnecessary over-refusal. Based on this observation, we propose emotion-guided refusal subspace steering (EmoRSS), an activation-steering method that mitigates emotion-induced over-refusal while preserving refusal behaviour on harmful requests. Specifically, we first identify a refusal-sensitive layer using layer-wise linear probes and construct a refusal subspace from sparse autoencoder (SAE) features aligned with the probe direction. Next, we use paired regular and emotional requests with the same queries to estimate the mean activation shift in the features defining the refusal subspace. Finally, we decode this shift into an activation intervention vector and apply it in the reverse refusal direction during inference, without updating the backbone parameters. Experiments on two LLMs show that, when requests contain emotional expressions, our method achieves a more favourable trade-off between refusing harmful requests and answering benign ones than prior over-refusal mitigation baselines, while better preserving general task performance.

Abstract
Emotional expression can influence the safety decisions of large language models (LLMs), offering a potential avenue for improving safety alignment.
Existing studies have mainly focused on how emotional expressions facilitate attacks under harmful requests, while overlooking their effects on benign requests.
We find that emotional expression can also systematically increase refusal tendencies on benign requests, leading to unnecessary over-refusal.
Based on this observation, we propose emotion-guided refusal subspace steering (EmoRSS), an activation-steering method that mitigates emotion-induced over-refusal while preserving refusal behaviour on harmful requests.
Specifically, we first identify a refusal-sensitive layer using layer-wise linear probes and construct a refusal subspace from sparse autoencoder (SAE) features aligned with the probe direction.
Next, we use paired regular and emotional requests with the same queries to estimate the mean activation shift in the features defining the refusal subspace. Finally, we decode this shift into an activation intervention vector and apply it in the reverse refusal direction during inference, without updating the backbone parameters.
Experiments on two LLMs show that, when requests contain emotional expressions, our method achieves a more favourable trade-off between refusing harmful requests and answering benign ones than prior over-refusal mitigation baselines, while better preserving general task performance.
1
Introduction
Emotional expression
(
Sun et al., 2026
)
can influence how large language models (LLMs) respond to requests, particularly in real-world applications such as emergency response
(
Otal et al., 2024
)
, medical chatbots
(
Chow and Li, 2025
)
, and crisis counseling
(
Kuznetsov et al., 2026
)
. This poses a challenge for safety alignment
(
Ji et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
, which must ensure that models continue to refuse harmful requests while providing substantive assistance to benign ones
(
Ji et al., 2023
)
even when users express strong emotions.
Figure 1:
Emotion-induced over-refusal of a benign request.
With task content and safety risk held fixed, a regular request receives a substantive answer, whereas its emotional counterpart elicits reassurance without addressing the task.
Existing studies have shown that emotional stimuli can affect LLM behaviour: positive stimuli can improve task performance
(
Li et al., 2023
)
, whereas anxiety-inducing prompts can amplify bias
(
Coda-Forno et al., 2023
)
.
In safety-related settings, prior work has primarily focused on using emotional or psychological cues to increase the attack success rate of harmful requests. For example, persuasion-based attacks
(
Zeng et al., 2024
)
use persuasive framing to elicit compliance with harmful requests.
Stress-inducing psychological priming
(
Kuznetsov et al., 2026
)
can also increase harmful compliance.
In addition,
Sofroniew et al. (2026)
show that manipulating emotion-related representations can change how often a model engages in blackmail and reward hacking.
Sun et al. (2026)
further show that emotionally framed prompts shift model representations and affect refusals of harmful requests.
Meanwhile, existing research on over-refusal
(
Cao et al., 2025
;
Dabas et al., 2025
;
Qi et al., 2026
)
has largely been conducted under standard or emotionally neutral settings, focusing on reducing unnecessary refusals of benign requests.
However, a benign request can receive a substantive answer in its regular form but only reassurance in its emotional form, even when task content and safety risk remain unchanged, as illustrated in Figure
1
.
Such responses leave the task unmet and suggest that emotional expression can introduce additional refusal tendencies.
Motivated by these, we investigate how emotional expressions affect refusals of benign requests and how to reduce the resulting over-refusal without increasing compliance with harmful requests. We propose emotion-guided refusal subspace steering (EmoRSS), an activation-steering method that corrects emotion-induced refusal shifts to improve the safety-helpfulness trade-off on emotional requests.
Specifically, we first train layer-wise linear probes on hidden states elicited by regular requests to identify the most refusal-sensitive layer and use the probe’s weight vector at that layer as the refusal direction.
We then select sparse autoencoder (SAE)
(
Ng and others, 2011
)
features whose decoder directions are most aligned with the refusal direction to construct a refusal subspace.
Next, we estimate the emotion-induced refusal shift by averaging changes in the selected features’ activations from regular to emotional requests across pairs.
This further provides internal evidence that emotional expression shifts benign requests toward refusal behaviour within the model.
Finally, we decode this shift into an activation intervention vector and use it to steer activations against the emotion-induced refusal shift at the selected layer during inference, without updating the backbone parameters.
By focusing the intervention on emotion-induced shifts within the refusal subspace, our method aims to reduce over-refusal while limiting its impact on defences against harmful requests and on general task performance.
The main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We identify emotion-induced over-refusal as an overlooked failure mode of safety alignment and show through internal representation analysis that emotional expression systematically shifts benign requests toward refusal.
•
We propose EmoRSS, an activation-steering method that estimates and reverses emotion-induced refusal shifts within the refusal subspace to mitigate over-refusal without updating backbone parameters.
•
Experiments on two LLMs demonstrate that our method achieves a more favourable BRR–HCR trade-off than the evaluated state-of-the-art over-refusal mitigation methods while effectively preserving general task performance.
2
Related Work
Emotional Influences on LLM Safety.
Existing studies have primarily focused on using emotional or psychological cues to increase the success of harmful requests.
For example, FreakOut-LLM
(
Kuznetsov et al., 2026
)
shows that stress priming can increase harmful compliance.
Noever and Rosario (2025)
examine refusal and boundary-setting in emotional attachment scenarios.
Recent studies have further investigated how such effects are reflected in model representations.
Sofroniew et al. (2026)
identify emotion-related concepts whose manipulation affects alignment-relevant behaviours, while
Sun et al. (2026)
identify a valence–arousal subspace associated with changes in refusal.
Overall, existing research has mainly focused on how emotional context affects model safety on harmful requests, while its impact on over-refusal of benign requests remains underexplored.
Over-Refusal Mitigation in LLMs.
Safety alignment can lead to unnecessary over-refusal
(
Röttger et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2024
)
of benign requests.
Existing over-refusal mitigation methods generally fall into two categories: training-based methods and inference-time interventions.
Among training-based methods, RASS
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
selects requests near safety decision boundaries for preference optimization.
ACTOR
(
Dabas et al., 2025
)
adjusts refusal-related activations through single-layer fine-tuning.
Refusal-trigger-aware fine-tuning
(
Xue et al., 2026
)
targets associations between harmless linguistic cues and refusal.
Inference-time methods instead modify inputs, decoding, or internal activations without updating the target model’s parameters.
For example,
Maskey et al. (2026)
analyze task-dependent over-refusal representations and show that task-conditioned steering is more selective than global refusal-direction ablation.
However, existing over-refusal research has largely focused on standard or emotionally neutral settings, leaving the effect of emotional expression on over-refusal insufficiently explored.

Identifying the Emotion-Independent Refusal Subspace
Figure

To examine whether emotional expression alters refusal-related representations and thereby affects refusal behaviour, we first identify the model’s internal refusal space using regular requests.
Specifically, we first use layer-wise probes to locate the refusal-sensitive layer and derive the corresponding refusal direction. Then, we select SAE features aligned with the refusal direction to construct the refusal subspace. Finally, we intervene along the identified direction and subspace to test whether they causally affect the model’s refusal behaviour.

Response Quality Analysis.
To examine whether lower refusal leads to substantive assistance, we annotate complete responses to 128 benign emotional requests per model using four response categories.
Following
Li et al. (2026a)
, we use response action and solidarity/empathy to distinguish direct answers, empathetic answers, empathetic deflections, and explicit refusals. Empathetic answers acknowledge the expressed emotion while addressing the request, whereas empathetic deflections acknowledge the expressed emotion without answering it. We count direct and empathetic answers as substantive answers, and deflections and refusals as non-answers.
As shown in Figure
7
, our method increases substantive answers (direct or empathetic) from 98 to 112 on Llama-3.1-8B-it and from 110 to 119 on Qwen3-8B. The paired gains are 10.94% (95% CI: [5.47, 17.19]) and 7.03% (95% CI: [3.12, 11.72]), respectively. Of the requests left unanswered by the default model, 15 of 30 become answered on Llama-3.1-8B-it, and 9 of 18 on Qwen3-8B; only one previously answered request becomes unanswered. Response style also changes: 9 of 30 initially empathetic answers become direct answers on Llama-3.1-8B-it, as do 18 of 61 on Qwen3-8B.
Thus, our method improves task completion while shifting some responses away from empathetic answering.

6
conclusion
In this paper, we investigate emotion-induced over-refusal and propose
EmoRSS to mitigate it while maintaining safety. EmoRSS is motivated by
our observation that emotional expressions shift activations within a
refusal-related subspace, even for benign requests. It constructs this
subspace using linear probes and SAE features, estimates the
regular–emotional activation shift, and reverses it during inference.
Experiments on two models across multiple benign and harmful requests show that our method substantially reduces benign refusals, keeps harmful compliance low, and better preserves general capability than the evaluated baselines.

Appendix B
dataset
B.1
Dataset Construction Details
Base requests and affective conditions.
We construct the evaluation set from 512 base requests drawn from
JailbreakBench, XSTest, OR-Bench, and HarmBench, comprising 256 benign
and 256 harmful requests. Each base request is combined with a matched
pair of first-person affective preambles: a regular version and an emotional
version. The original request is kept identical within each pair, so
that the paired queries differ only in the expressed emotional state.
We operationalize distress as an unpleasant and activated affective
state, following the valence–arousal
(
Russell, 1980
)
. The descriptor “distressed” and the
five-point response format
(
Watson et al., 1988
)
are used in our evaluation. Our ratings evaluate the emotion
expressed in the text rather than the psychological state of the
evaluator and should not be interpreted as a clinical assessment.
Expression families.
The preambles cover six author-defined expression families, designed
to vary how distress is communicated while preserving its affective
polarity. Each family contains eight matched regular–emotional pairs,
yielding 48 pairs and 96 distinct preambles. Table
8
summarizes their construction. These families are linguistic
variations used to reduce dependence on any single emotion word or
sentence pattern; they are not treated as distinct clinical
constructs.

Independent evaluation.
The preambles are evaluated separately by a human evaluator and
GPT-4o. The 48 matched pairs are assigned anonymous identifiers and
presented in randomized order. The order of the regular and emotional
versions within each pair is also randomized. Neither evaluation
receives the expression-family labels or the results of the other
evaluation.

perceived-distress score and a naturalness score on five-point scales.

Evaluation of assembled queries.
We additionally evaluate a fixed sample of 64 complete query pairs
after concatenating the preambles with their base requests. The human
and GPT-4o independently rate the perceived distress and naturalness
of each complete query and determine whether the preamble
substantively changes either the objective of the original request or
its benign/harmful classification.

Acceptance criteria and results.
Before response generation, we specify three dataset-quality criteria:
the mean within-pair increase in perceived distress must be at least
1.5 points; the median naturalness score must be at least 4.0 in both
conditions; and no assembled query may exhibit a substantive change
in its request objective or benign/harmful classification. The
thresholds of 1.5 and 4.0 are study-specific acceptance criteria rather
than standardized psychological cutoffs.
The emotional queries are rated 2.73 points higher in perceived
distress than their matched regular queries. The median naturalness score
is 4.0 in both conditions, and no evaluated query pair exhibits a
change in request objective or benign/harmful classification.
Therefore, all three dataset-construction criteria are satisfied.

Why Does the Main Evaluation Use a Larger Intervention Strength Than the Estimated Emotion Shift?
The vector estimated from paired requests represents the mean displacement contributed by the selected SAE features, rather than the full emotion-induced change. The selected SAE features account for 30.2% and 59.0% of the mean emotion-induced shift along the refusal direction in Llama-3.1-8B-it and Qwen3-8B, respectively. We therefore separate the natural-scale
intervention (
ρ
=
1
\rho=1
), which tests the behavioural effect of cancelling this estimated component, from the stronger interventions selected for the safety–helpfulness evaluation (
ρ
=
20
\rho=20
and
ρ
=
10
\rho=10
). The latter are amplified steering interventions. Their effects should not be interpreted as exact cancellation of the natural shift or as the fraction of refusal behaviour causally mediated by the selected features.
⊳
\triangleright
Does Reducing Benign Refusal Preserve Safety
Without Any Cost?
Our results do not establish an absence of safety cost. At the selected
intervention strengths, Table
5
reports no change in average harmful
compliance for Llama-3.1-8B-it, whereas Qwen3-8B increases from 0.52% to 2.08%.
EmoRSS substantially reduces benign refusal while harmful compliance
remains low on the evaluated requests, but this trade-off may differ
across models and harmful-request distributions. We therefore report
both outcomes rather than treating a lower benign refusal rate as
sufficient evidence of safety preservation.
⊳
\triangleright
Does the Refusal Rate Capture Every Failure
to Answer a Benign Request?
No. A response may acknowledge the user’s emotion without substantively addressing the request, even when it contains no explicit refusal.
As analyzed in Section
5.2
, we therefore distinguish substantive answers from such non-substantive responses.
Among 128 annotated benign emotional requests per model, the number of substantive answers increases from 98 to 112 for Llama-3.1-8B-it and from 110 to 119 for Qwen3-8B after intervention.
This shows that BRR does not capture all failures to answer benign requests:
EmoRSS not only reduces explicit refusals, but also converts some non-substantive responses into substantive answers.

article.headline: 情感引发过度拒答 激活子空间干预纠正
article.lede: 情感化表达会让大模型对无害请求也拒答。EmoRSS 用 SAE 定位拒答子空间，推理时反向抵消情感引起的激活偏移。
article.problem: 现有研究大多关注情感或心理线索如何提高有害请求的攻击成功率，却忽略了情感表达对良性请求的影响。作者发现，在任务内容和安全风险都不变的情况下，只要在请求前加一句第一人称情绪表达，模型就会从给出实质回答变成只表达安慰、不解决任务。这种由情感引发的过度拒答，此前没有被系统刻画为安全对齐的一种失效模式。
article.method: 首先用逐层逻辑回归探针找出最能区分合规与拒答的「拒答敏感层」，并把该层探针权重映射回原始激活空间，作为拒答方向；然后挑选解码方向与该方向余弦相似度最高的 top-K 个 SAE 特征，用它们的解码方向张成拒答子空间。接着用同一批查询的配对常规版与情感版请求，估计子空间特征上的平均激活偏移，把这一偏移解码成干预向量。推理时只需在拒答敏感层按可控强度反向施加该向量，不更新主干参数，也不增加逐 token 计算。
article.results: 在 Llama-3.1-8B-it 与 Qwen3-8B 上，情感请求的平均良性拒答率（BRR）均降至 7.29%（默认分别为 21.35% 和 22.91%），有害请求合规率（HCR）分别为 0.00% 和 2.08%。通用能力上，Llama 的 MMLU 为 60.3%（无干预 58.4%），Qwen 的 XSum ROUGE-1 为 27.1%（无干预 27.0%）。每模型 128 条良性情感请求的人工标注中，实质性回答由 98 增至 112、110 增至 119，配对增益 10.94%（95% CI [5.47, 17.19]）与 7.03%（[3.12, 11.72]）。在 ρ=1 的自然尺度下，BRR 仅下降 2.60% 和 4.94%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「情绪化用户被敷衍」这一现实失败模式落到可解释的内部表示上，并给出无需微调、只在单个拒答敏感层做一次固定编辑的推理期方案，对急救、医疗问答、心理热线等高频情绪场景有直接价值。
article.limitations: 作者明确表示并未证明无安全代价：在 Qwen3-8B 上 HCR 从 0.52% 升到 2.08%，且更大干预强度会明显损害其通用能力。所选 SAE 特征只覆盖情感诱导拒答方向位移的 30.2% 与 59.0%，主实验用的 ρ=20/10 属于放大干预而非精确抵消；评测也只涉及 512 条构造请求和两个模型。
article.figure_caption_zh: EmoRSS 流程：先用线性探针定位拒答敏感层，并选出解码方向与拒答方向对齐的 SAE 特征构成拒答子空间；再用配对的常规与情感请求估计子空间内的情感诱导激活偏移；最后在该层按可控强度反向抵消这一偏移。

figure.caption: {Overview of EmoRSS.} We first identify the refusal-sensitive layer and construct an refusal subspace $ {S}_{ {ref}}$ by selecting SAE features whose decoder directions align with the refusal direction. We then use matched regular and emotional queries to estimate the emotion-induced activation shift within this subspace. Finally, EmoRSS reverses the estimated shift at the refusal-sensitive layer with a controllable intervention strength, mitigating emotion-induced over-refusal while preserving safety on harmful requests.

page_papers.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
page_papers.abstract: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

\setheadertext

CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
Zhongwei XIE
Yiming DU
Jiaxin BAI
Baixuan XU
Chunyang LI
Xiyu REN

Corresponding author:
zwanggy@connect.ust.hk
Abstract
AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact
PocketWorker
models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.
1
Introduction
AI coworkers are expected to carry out everyday work through sustained interaction with users, tools, and a changing workspace. Resolving a customer-support request, for example, can require consulting account history, locating a relevant procedure, and updating the correct ticket while respecting access restrictions. Such workflows combine multi-turn communication, information gathering, tool coordination, and decisions about when to act
[
Trivedi et al., 2024
,
Yao et al., 2024
,
Xu et al., 2026b
]
. Recent coworker models and benchmarks make these capabilities explicit targets for agent development
[
Chen et al., 2026a
,
Wang et al., 2026b
,
Meng et al., 2026
,
Ye et al., 2026
]
. Developing compact models for this setting requires training experience that captures these dependencies.
Constructing that experience is a central challenge. The information needed to complete a workflow is often distributed across documents, service records, and intermediate environment state. Synthesizing a useful task therefore requires the request, the available evidence, and the permitted actions to fit together. Records referring to the same customer must agree across services; tools must expose the information needed to proceed and implement the expected state changes; and grading checks must assess relevant actions and outcomes. A plausible final response alone cannot establish that the intended update occurred or that a prohibited action was avoided. These requirements make executable environment construction and verification integral to data synthesis, as also emphasized in coworker evaluation and computer-use training
[
Meng et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026a
]
.
Open agent-training efforts have begun to expose the data choices behind capable systems. Nemotron-Terminal and SERA study synthetic tasks and demonstrations for terminal and coding agents, while OpenThoughts-Agent investigates data curation across agentic tasks
[
Pi et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
,
Raoof et al., 2026
]
. Occamy extends execution-grounded training to coworker workloads
[
Chen et al., 2026a
]
. Building on these efforts, we focus on a practical question:
how can targeted coworker capabilities be translated into executable training tasks that support both imitation and learning from interaction?
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Developer-selected capability requirements guide the workflow scope of task construction. A workflow specification is implemented as a request, initial service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We describe two forms of task variation: composing business workflows across different services, and creating safety scenarios with distinct permitted and prohibited actions. Resolving a customer-support issue, for example, connects CRM context with a helpdesk ticket and a knowledge-base procedure; investigating a payment-change request connects correspondence with financial history. In the documented safety-task family, generation agents draft task content and a separate grading role defines the execution checks. Teacher executions provide curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions yield rollouts and reward feedback for reinforcement learning (RL). This process separates the construction of a problem from the generation of attempts to solve it. Figure
1
shows how task construction, teacher execution, and student training fit together.
To assess the training utility of these resources, we fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
[
Bai et al., 2025
]
to obtain
PocketWorker
-8B. SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval tasks, with a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. A separate SFT-only application to ClawMark extends the evaluation to a second coworker benchmark. We also compare training configurations for GRPO, Dr.GRPO, GDPO, and GiGPO to examine advantage estimation and credit assignment. Training rewards improve over approximately three epochs on our constructed tasks, providing preliminary evidence that these environments support RL optimization.
Our contributions are:
①
Capability-guided synthesis of executable coworker environments.
We translate target capabilities into multi-service workflows
with consistent user requests, service records, tool interfaces,
and executable grading checks. Task variation spans service
dependencies and business constraints, including safety scenarios
that require investigation while avoiding prohibited actions.
Teacher execution and trajectory curation produce SFT
demonstrations, while the constructed environments support
interactive RL training.
②
Training utility and analysis.
We evaluate these resources through SFT gains on Claw-Eval, an SFT-only extension to ClawMark, and comparisons of RL training configurations.
We will release our datasets and construction pipeline, sharing the methods and design choices behind task and environment construction, trajectory collection, and data curation. We hope this helps other researchers adapt the process to their own needs.
For academic researchers working with limited resources, advanced topics such as long-horizon agentic SFT and RL can be difficult to pursue with limited GPU access, infrastructure gaps, unfamiliar engineering pitfalls, and high API costs. Our
Lessons
bring together challenges we encountered, ongoing work, and possible future directions, covering how different harnesses affect training outcomes, training–inference mismatch across harnesses, credit assignment and RL optimization. We share these experiences to help others make progress under similar constraints and avoid common pitfalls.
2
Related Work
Agent post-training.
Open post-training efforts make training data and recipes available for study
[
Lambert et al., 2024
]
. AgentTuning develops general agent abilities through instruction tuning, while Nemotron-Terminal, OpenThoughts-Agent, and SERA investigate task generation and trajectory curation for terminal, coding, and broader agentic behavior
[
Zeng et al., 2024
,
Pi et al., 2026
,
Raoof et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
]
. Related recipes extend trajectory-based training to research, data analysis, and GUI workflows
[
Fang et al., 2025
,
Qiao et al., 2026
,
Ding et al., 2026
]
. AgentGym-RL and RAGEN study learning through sequential interaction, while ToolRL examines reward design for tool use
[
Xi et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2025
,
Qian et al., 2026
]
. slime provides a post-training framework with customizable data generation for RL scaling
[
Zhu et al., 2025
]
. Agent harnesses organize execution and interaction interfaces
[
Xie et al., 2026b
,
Huang et al., 2026
]
, with LEGO-RL connecting native coding-agent harnesses to policy-gradient training
[
Du et al., 2026
]
. Polar provides asynchronous rollouts over existing agent harnesses, reconstructing training trajectories from proxied model API calls
[
Xu et al., 2026a
]
. Building on PPO and GRPO
[
Schulman et al., 2017
,
Shao et al., 2024
]
, subsequent methods explore advantage and loss normalization, reward-component normalization, and finer-grained credit assignment
[
Liu et al., 2025c
,
Liu et al., 2026a
,
Feng et al., 2025
,
Wei et al., 2025
]
. Our framework connects executable task construction, curated demonstrations, and interactive RL for compact coworkers.
Executable task synthesis and demonstration curation.
Task synthesis couples generated requests with interaction settings and completion criteria. AgentGen and MATRIX construct environments or simulated scenarios
[
Hu et al., 2025
,
Tang et al., 2025
]
; APIGen-MT links task blueprints to multi-turn interactions, and CUA-Gym jointly constructs instructions, environments, and rewards
[
Prabhakar et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026a
]
. CuES generates executable tasks by exploring existing tool environments
[
Mai et al., 2025
]
. Verification and refinement further shape training data: ToolACE verifies generated tool-use dialogues, while AgentRefine studies refinement-oriented demonstrations
[
Liu et al., 2025b
,
Fu et al., 2025
]
. Complementary approaches obtain training experience through environment models and adaptive generation: DreamGym and Qwen-AgentWorld simulate environment dynamics, PatchWorld induces executable world-model programs with counterexample-driven repair, and AgentEvolver combines task generation with experience-guided exploration
[
Chen et al., 2026b
,
Zuo et al., 2026
,
Bai et al., 2026
,
Zhai et al., 2025
]
. Concurrent work includes Cowork-Gym
[
Zou et al., 2026
]
, which explores large-scale synthesis of interactive work environments. Our construction jointly specifies cross-service records, tools, and grading checks, then validates tasks and curates teacher executions for SFT while retaining environments for RL.
Coworker agents and evaluation.
Occamy studies coworker specialization through execution-grounded data and staged post-training
[
Chen et al., 2026a
]
. AppWorld,
τ
\tau
-bench, TheAgentCompany, and AutomationBench evaluate multi-application work, user interaction, and workflow constraints
[
Trivedi et al., 2024
,
Yao et al., 2024
,
Xu et al., 2026b
,
Shepard and Salimans, 2026
]
, while GDPval evaluates economically valuable professional tasks
[
Patwardhan et al., 2026
]
. ClawMark emphasizes persistent workflows and evolving service state, and Claw-Eval evaluates task completion, safety, and robustness
[
Meng et al., 2026
,
Ye et al., 2026
]
. AgentDojo and ToolEmu assess risks from prompt injection and agent actions
[
Debenedetti et al., 2024
,
Ruan et al., 2024
]
; Terminal-Bench and CyberGym provide execution-based evaluation in terminal and software-security settings
[
Merrill et al., 2026
,
Wang et al., 2026c
]
. We evaluate SFT on Claw-Eval and ClawMark and compare RL configurations on Claw-Eval to study learning for coworker workflows.
3
Method
CoworkEnv
constructs executable coworker environments through the following stages: capability-guided task design, executable environment construction, programmatic validation and feedback repair, teacher execution and curation, and preparation for SFT or RL. The central unit is a task environment that brings together a request, the information and tools needed to act, and checks of the resulting execution. Teacher demonstrations provide supervision for imitation, while student interaction with the environment provides experience and rewards for RL.
3.1
Capability-Guided Task Synthesis
From capabilities to task specifications.
We translate target capabilities into a coverage plan specifying service combinations, intended difficulty, and business scenarios. Scenarios define selection conditions, distractor records, and permitted actions; a fixed reference date anchors time-sensitive requirements. An LLM receives the plan together with service catalogs, an output-format specification, and example tasks. It generates the user request, initial service records, structured completion checks, and prohibited actions. The catalogs describe available tools and record formats, guiding generation toward reusable service implementations.

Programs instantiate the specification: service configurations are populated from a registry, and structured completion checks and prohibited actions are inserted into a fixed grader template. Shared services expose the generated records and support state-changing actions. Task variation thus changes the scenario, records, and checks while reusing the execution and grading implementations. Linking information across services.
Workflow construction distributes related information across services. An escalation task, for example, combines ticket creation times with customer tiers to select enterprise-account tickets open for more than 48 hours, then retrieves the account manager’s address for an email. A recent high-priority ticket is a distractor: it appears urgent but fails the age condition. Grading checks reference entities and actions from the same specification, using tool arguments and service audit records to check execution. This connects the requested goal, the evidence available through tools, and the scoring conditions.
Safety scenarios introduce constraints on acting on retrieved information. A payment-change investigation combines a suspicious email, legitimate correspondence, and transaction history. Completion checks reward evidence gathering, while designated submission or messaging actions activate a safety gate. Under the Generator–Discriminator design, the Generator drafts the request and records; the Discriminator receives the records and a note describing the safety scenario in a separate context, and specifies completion checks and forbidden actions. Appendices
C
and
D
describe the role inputs and workflow examples.
3.2
Validation and Feedback Repair
Checking generated specifications.
Programmatic checks complement the generation instructions. They verify that the specification can be parsed, that selected services are registered and have initial records, that completion weights sum to one, and that required and prohibited tool sets do not conflict. A request-level leakage check rejects designated answer identifiers exposed in the user request, preserving the need to discover them through interaction.
Checking grading behavior.
A grading consistency gate evaluates synthetic tool-call and audit records against the declared checks. A record satisfying the completion conditions must receive full completion and safety scores; an empty record must receive zero completion; adding a prohibited call must set the safety score to zero.
Feedback and regeneration.
Validation failures are returned to the generator as diagnostic feedback. The generator produces a revised full specification, which passes through the same validation pipeline. Only candidates satisfying both specification checks and grading-consistency tests are packaged with their initial records, service configuration, and grading code for execution. Appendix
D
gives the retry budget and test construction.

Selecting tasks and demonstrations.
Task selection uses mean teacher completion to identify consistently completed tasks, tasks with very low completion, and an intermediate group. We retain qualifying demonstrations from the intermediate group, limit consistently completed tasks to one demonstration per normalized task prefix, and set aside the lowest-completion group. This reduces repeated supervision from easy tasks while retaining multiple executions of other tasks. When merging collections, we deduplicate by task and trial identifier so that each recorded execution enters the pool once. Appendix

Demonstration selection proceeds in two stages. Export first retains trajectories meeting source-specific reward thresholds. Conversion then removes records that cannot yield usable user and assistant messages, along with sequences that are too short, contain too many tool calls, or exceed the whole-example character budget. These checks select the interactions used for student supervision.
Preparing training inputs.
The retained executions are serialized as user, assistant, and tool messages with structured tool calls and a standardized system instruction. Long tool observations are shortened to a prefix during conversion; whole examples exceeding the character budget are discarded. Appendix

RL through student interaction.
The RL interface supplies references to selected task definitions. Each reference loads the request, initial service records, tools, and grader. The student generates its own trajectory through online tool interaction, and the grader computes rewards from that execution’s calls and service audit records. Teacher performance can inform task selection, while the learning signal comes from the student’s behavior. Missing rewards abort the affected sample, and incomplete or infrastructure-failed rollout groups are rejected and retried before advantage estimation.
The two interfaces reuse task definitions, service implementations, and grading mechanisms, with selection tailored to demonstration learning or online interaction. This makes environment construction a shared foundation for both forms of adaptation. Section

Relative to the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct baseline, the reported Overall scores increase from 46.6 to 56.6 with GRPO and 57.2 with GDPO, differences of 10.0 and 10.6 points. The largest differences occur on Multi-turn tasks: scores increase from 45.9 to 72.5 with GRPO and 74.9 with GDPO, corresponding to 26.7 and 29.0 points. General scores increase from 46.7 to 52.8 and 53.0, differences of 6.1 and 6.3 points, respectively. These aggregate comparisons show the largest gains in multi-turn interaction.
Different reward-processing, advantage-estimation, and credit-assignment strategies exhibit distinct training dynamics and performance profiles across task categories. Both GRPO and GDPO achieve their largest gains on Multi-turn tasks, with GDPO attaining the higher score, whereas GRPO performs better on Multimodal tasks. These observations suggest that the benefits of different RL training configurations vary with the capabilities required by each task category.

Conclusion
We present
CoworkEnv
, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. By aligning user requests, service states, tool interfaces, and grading checks, our pipeline supports both curated demonstrations for SFT and interactive training with RL. Experiments show SFT gains on Claw-Eval, while an SFT-only extension to ClawMark supports the framework’s applicability across coworker benchmarks. Supervised warm-up followed by RL improves Multi-turn performance over the base model, and comparisons of reward processing, advantage estimation, and credit assignment reveal distinct training dynamics and task-dependent performance profiles.
Limitations
Execution scores measure the properties encoded by the graders. They can miss errors outside those checks, while teacher-success filters can favor redundant demonstrations or discard useful recovery behavior. The role of unsuccessful trajectories also deserves study: work on iterative skill evolution reports that feedback conditions containing failures can produce useful skill updates
[
Liu et al., 2026b
]
. Regenerating the original teacher trajectories may require access to a proprietary model service.
Ethical Considerations
CoworkEnv is designed for research in executable, simulated work environments rather than deployment in real-world organizations. Nevertheless, agents trained on synthetic workflows may perform incorrect or unauthorized actions if deployed without appropriate safeguards.

Appendix C
A Constructed Safety Workflow
Generation and grading roles.
The Generator–Discriminator design separates scenario drafting from check specification. The Generator receives a safety-scenario category and service combination, then drafts the request and initial records. The Discriminator receives the task and service identifiers, records, and a safety note describing the intended conflict, without the full request text. It specifies completion checks for investigation and a set of prohibited actions. Shared record identifiers connect these checks to the generated evidence. The resulting check and forbidden-tool sets are inserted into the grader template described in Appendix
D
.
Request and evidence.
The instruction body of
M133_safety_payment_change_refusal
asks for a vendor banking update and payment-report submission. Its title describes verification without submission. The fixtures contain a spoofed request with a new account, legitimate correspondence identifying the established account, and historical transactions consistent with that account. A third mail message is an unrelated announcement. These records make the contradiction accessible through mail and finance tools. The example demonstrates how a task can pair a request to act with evidence relevant to withholding the action.
Grading.
The grader checks five actions: opening the inbox (weight 0.15), reading the suspicious request (0.25), reading the legitimate vendor message (0.20), listing financial history (0.20), and inspecting relevant transactions (0.20). Calling
finance_submit_report
or
gmail_send_message
sets the safety factor to zero. The score is

)

Grading validation.

Appendix D
Constructing Multi-Service Workflows
Coverage plan and generation prompt.
Each plan slot supplies seven fields:
task_id
identifies the output task;
services
selects service catalogs;
category
names the workflow category;
difficulty
specifies intended complexity;
language
sets the request language;
mock_today
fixes the reference date; and
scenario
describes the goal, selection conditions, distractors, and action constraints. The following abridged escalation slot uses a descriptive task identifier:
task_id: support_escalation
services: [crm, helpdesk, gmail]
category: ops
difficulty: hard
language: en
mock_today: "2026-03-10"
scenario: >-
  Find enterprise tickets open
  for more than 48 hours and email
  the account manager.
  Distractor: a high-priority ticket
  less than 48 hours old.
The generation prompt combines output-format requirements, catalogs for the selected services, example specifications, and the plan slot. Additional multi-service instructions ask the generator to distribute evidence across services and place the information needed to determine the answer in the initial records. Scenario variation changes selection conditions, information links, and permitted actions: a ticket-prioritization task can select by customer tier and update helpdesk records, while an escalation task adds an age threshold and retrieves a recipient from CRM for a mail action.
Template-based instantiation.
The service registry supplies ports, health-check paths, and configuration metadata. Generated records populate the task’s fixtures. The grader builder serializes the completion checks and prohibited tools into a fixed code template. Each check specifies its kind, weight, and the tool arguments or audit fields it inspects. The following pseudocode summarizes the shared completion and safety calculations:
CHECKS = spec.completion_checks
FORBIDDEN = spec.safety_forbidden_tools

def components(calls, audit):
    completion = 0
    for c in CHECKS:
        ok = test(c, calls, audit)
        completion += c.weight * ok
    safety = 1
    for call in calls:
        if call.tool in FORBIDDEN:
            safety = 0
    return completion, safety
Task-specific targets and weights vary in the check data, while the evaluation routines are reused. Appendix
C
gives a concrete reward composition using these components.
Service audit records and grading checks.
An
audit_present
check names a service, an
action_key
, a record field, and accepted target values. The action key selects the service’s audit collection, linking a recorded operation to the fields examined by the grader. Two examples are:
•
Helpdesk updates:
helpdesk_update_ticket
records an entry in
updated_tickets
; the check examines its
ticket_id
field for the target ticket.
•
Outgoing mail:
gmail_send_message
records an entry in
sent
; the check examines its
to
field for the recipient associated with the generated customer records.
Design scope.
The
M1100
–
M1124
family contains 25 tasks constructed to cover multi-service workflows at two levels of intended complexity. Fifteen D1.5 tasks target three services, 8–12 steps, and distracting information; ten D2.5 tasks target four or five services, 12–20 steps, and temporal dependencies. These targets translate coverage requirements into concrete task specifications. They describe intended workflow complexity rather than measured teacher execution lengths. The construction record’s “Class C” mock-service label is distinct from the local “C” alias for Claw-Eval Multi-turn.
Request, fixtures, and checks.
M1100
links a CRM customer marked at risk to a critical authentication ticket through a shared customer identifier. A knowledge-base article provides an API key rotation procedure. The instruction asks for a ticket update based on that procedure and prohibits CRM export. The package specifies eight exposed tool interfaces across the three services.
The grader uses six deterministic completion checks with weights 0.08, 0.15, 0.15, 0.12, 0.20, and 0.30, summing to one. The check vocabulary includes tool-call presence, record-specific arguments, and service audit records. The documented ticket-update check identifies an update to the intended ticket; it does not inspect the resolution text. The export tool activates a safety gate. These checks assess selected actions and records rather than every semantic requirement in the instruction.
Teacher executions.
Three teacher executions with
claude-opus-4-8
[
Anthropic, 2026b
]
obtain rewards of 0.88, 0.84, and 1.0, with completion scores of 0.85, 0.80, and 1.0 and safety scores of 1.0 throughout.
Validation and regeneration details.
For each slot in the coverage plan, the generator has a budget of two attempts: an initial generation and at most one retry. Each candidate passes sequentially through JSON parsing, required/prohibited-tool conflict checks, completion-weight checks, service and initial-record validation, request-level identifier-leakage checks, and the grading-consistency gate. A failed check returns diagnostic feedback for the next attempt. The retry produces a complete specification and repeats the validation sequence. article.headline: CoworkEnv：合成可执行环境训练同事智能体
article.lede: CoworkEnv 用能力需求合成可执行工作环境，8B 模型 SFT 后 Claw-Eval 均分从 46.6 升至 6
article.problem: AI 同事要在多轮对话中协调工具、读写不断变化的工作区状态，并遵守流程约束；这类任务的请求、服务记录、工具接口与评分检查必须彼此自洽，信息还要分散在多个服务里才能完成。仅凭一段看似合理的最终回复，无法确认预期的状态更新是否发生、被禁止的动作是否被避开，因此可执行环境的构建与验证本身成了数据合成的核心难点。
article.method: 作者提出能力引导的合成框架：先由覆盖计划指定服务组合、难度与业务场景，再由 LLM 生成用户请求、初始服务记录、结构化完成检查与禁止动作，并用程序化校验（可解析性、服务注册、权重之和为 1、必需/禁止工具不冲突、请求级答案泄漏、评分一致性）配合反馈重生成，每个计划槽位最多两次尝试。随后由教师在容器化运行时中执行任务，按完成度分组、去重与长度过滤后串成 SFT 样本；同一套任务定义也通过 RL 接口提供学生自主 rollout 与在线奖励，作者用 slime 与 Polar 搭建训练管线并微调 Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct 得到 PocketWorker-8B。
article.results: 在 Claw-Eval 的 161 个 General 与 38 个 Multi-turn 任务上，SFT 使 Overall 均分从 46.6 升到 64.1（+17.5），其中 Multi-turn 从 45.9 升到 77.8（+31.9 点），General 从 46.7 升到 60.9（+14.2）；Pass@3/Pass³ 合并指标由 28.6/21.6 提升到 50.8/37.2。4B 模型经 SFT 后 Overall 从 33.9 升到 42.2。在 ClawMark 的 100 个任务上，均分从 11.8 升到 19.4（+7.6）。数据规模消融中，用 20%、50%、100% 训练数据时 Overall 分别为 50.8、55.6、64.1。RL 部分从共享的监督预热检查点出发训练约三个 epoch，GRPO、GDPO 的 Overall 分别提升 10.0 与 10.6 点（56.6、57.2），Multi-turn 分别提升 26.7 与 29.0 点，GiGPO 的 Overall 为 60.7；数据转换阶段，1,809 条混合候选记录最终保留 937 条示范。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「任务规格—可执行环境—评分器」做成可复用的同一份资产，使 SFT 示范与 RL rollout 共享同一套工具与检查，为资源有限的研究组提供了一条合成长期同事型智能体训练数据的可行路径。作者同时公开数据与构建流程，并附上工程经验记录，便于他人复现与改造。
article.limitations: 论文自己指出，执行分数只衡量评分器编码的那些属性，可能漏掉检查之外的错误；按教师成功率筛选示范会偏向重复的轨迹、并丢弃有用的纠错行为，而重新生成原始教师轨迹可能需要依赖专有模型服务。此外，RL 后的 Overall 成绩（56.6–60.7）仍低于纯 SFT 的 64.1，说明 RL 的收益是相对基座模型而非相对最强 SFT 检查点；与已发表参考模型的对比也采用不同评测设置，作者明确表示要声称超越某个具体模型需要对齐评测条件。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图 1：任务构建与教师示范路径——每项任务由请求、初始状态、工具接口和评分检查组成，教师执行产生带分数的动作与观察记录，经筛选后用于 SFT，同一任务组件也支撑学生交互与在线奖励计算。

figure.caption: {Task construction and the teacher-demonstration path.} Support resolution and payment-change investigation illustrate how service records and action constraints define a workflow. Each task combines a request, initial state, tool interfaces, and grading checks. Teacher execution produces scored action (A) and observation (O) records, which are curated and serialized for SFT. The same task components support student interaction and online reward computation through the RL interface described in Section~ {sec:student-training}.

page_papers.title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
page_papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.

Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning
Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
Jiho Lee
Affiliation:

Heayoun Choi

*
Corresponding authors.
Eunwoo Kim
Affiliation:
Jiho Lee, Heayoun Choi, and Eunwoo Kim are with the School of Computer Science Engineering, Chung-Ang University, Seoul, 06974, Republic of Korea (e-mail: {j2hoooo, heayounchoi, eunwoo}@cau.ac.kr).
Abstract
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models.
However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors.
In this work, we study
state hallucination
, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved.
Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur.
Based on this analysis, we propose
SOUL
(Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively.
Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities.
These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
I
INTRODUCTION
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach for bringing foundation models into robot manipulation
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
.
By integrating visual and language understanding with action generation, VLAs can translate high-level instructions into continuous robot control.
Large-scale pretraining on heterogeneous robot and vision-language data has further enabled generalization across tasks, objects, environments, and robot embodiments
[
4
,
5
,
6
]
.
Despite this progress, VLAs still exhibit unreliable behaviors, including unstable or premature actions, long-horizon drift, failures to recover from execution errors, and infeasible actions
[
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
,
13
]
.
This is particularly concerning in physical robot execution, where erroneous actions directly affect the robot and its environment.
Within this broader set of failures, we focus on a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues a manipulation sequence based on a robot-object state that has not actually been achieved.
We refer to this behavioral pattern as
state hallucination
, because the policy acts as if an unrealized physical state were true.
For example, a VLA may close its gripper before reaching an object and subsequently execute transport and place motions as though the object has been successfully grasped, as shown in Fig.
1
1(a)
.
Such a mismatch can persist across subsequent actions, allowing a local execution error to propagate over multiple stages.
This recurring and persistent behavior motivates us to investigate whether policy knowledge associated with state hallucination can be selectively removed while preserving successful manipulation capabilities.
(a)
Representative example of state hallucination
(b)
Overview of sparse feature policy unlearning for state hallucination
(c)
Performance after unlearning
Fig. 1
:
Sparse feature policy unlearning mitigates hallucinated beliefs in VLAs.
(a) Examples of grasp, transport, and place state hallucinations.
(b) State hallucination occurs when a VLA mistakes its hallucinated belief for the actual robot-object state and generates actions based on this false belief.
During this mismatch, hallucination features become strongly activated, and the proposed unlearning suppresses their activation while reinforcing success features.
(c) Our sparse feature policy unlearning reduces hallucination while improving clean (hallucination-free) task success.
We first examine how the policy’s internal representations differ between hallucinated and successful behaviors.
Such hallucinated rollouts exhibit weakened attention to task-relevant regions, such as the gripper and target object, together with more spatially dispersed attention.
Through a mechanistic analysis with sparse autoencoders, we also observe that sparse features exhibit distinct activation patterns during hallucinated and normal executions.
To characterize these sparse feature activation patterns, we define a feature association score that contrasts activations across execution outcomes, such as failures with hallucination, failures without hallucination, and successful executions.
Based on this score, we categorize sparse features according to whether they are more strongly associated with hallucinated failures or successful executions.
Building on these observations, we propose
S
parse feature p
O
licy
U
n
L
earning
(
SOUL
), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination, where sparse features identified from hallucinated failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively.
This feature-level policy unlearning objective suppresses activations of the forgetting targets while enhancing activations of the retention targets, thereby mitigating recurring hallucination behavior while minimizing interference with useful manipulation capabilities.
We validate our approach with OpenVLA
[
2
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
3
]
on LIBERO-Plus
[
9
]
, RoboCasa
[
14
]
, and a real-world Franka robot, achieving an average 21.7%p reduction in hallucination rate and a 22.1%p improvement in task success while preserving 89% of behaviors that were successful before unlearning.
These results demonstrate that interpretable feature analysis can reveal internal representations associated with recurring policy failures, providing a practical basis for selectively unlearning such behaviors in embodied foundation models.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We characterize state hallucination as a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.
•
We analyze state hallucination through visual attention and sparse features, revealing weakened attention to task-relevant regions and distinct feature patterns associated with state hallucination.
•
We introduce a sparse feature policy unlearning method that selectively unlearns recurring state hallucination behavior by suppressing hallucination features while enhancing features that support successful manipulation.
II
Related Work
II-A
Vision-Language-Action Models
Vision-language-action models have become a major direction for generalist robot manipulation.
Prior work has improved generalization through larger pretrained vision-language representations, heterogeneous robotic data, and stronger action generation architectures
[
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
,
15
,
16
,
17
,
18
]
.
Deployment reliability has also been improved through intermediate reasoning
[
19
,
20
]
, failure detection and recovery
[
12
,
21
]
, and test-time sampling or verification
[
22
,
23
]
.
These approaches primarily focus on improving policy outputs during deployment, rather than directly modifying policy knowledge associated with recurring failures.
Recent concurrent mechanistic interpretability studies have begun to analyze and steer VLA behavior at inference time by intervening on representations, such as feed-forward activation directions
[
24
]
and sparse features
[
25
]
.
In contrast, we formulate the selective modification of undesirable policy behavior as a policy unlearning problem, where knowledge associated with recurring hallucinated behavior is removed while representations supporting successful execution are preserved.
Encoding this modification in the pretrained policy parameters enables persistent behavior correction without repeated intervention at inference time.
II-B
Machine Unlearning
Machine unlearning aims to make a trained model forget knowledge associated with selected data without retraining the model from scratch
[
26
,
27
]
.
Prior work has studied unlearning mainly in classification tasks, where the influence of selected training data is removed from trained models
[
28
,
29
]
, and in language tasks, where factual knowledge or undesired responses are suppressed
[
30
,
31
]
.
A central challenge is balancing the removal of targeted knowledge with the preservation of useful model capabilities.
This trade-off is particularly consequential for robot policies, where modifying one behavior can inadvertently disrupt multiple tightly coupled skills.
Motivated by this, we introduce feature-level selective policy unlearning by explicitly identifying features for forgetting and retention to suppress undesirable behavior while preserving useful manipulation capabilities.
II-C
Sparse Autoencoders
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense model activations into sparse latent representations, enabling individual features to be associated with more localized and interpretable patterns in model behavior
[
32
,
33
,
34
]
.
They are trained to reconstruct the original activations under a sparsity constraint, such that only a small subset of latent features is active for each input.
A commonly used variant is the Top-
k
k
SAE, which imposes this sparsity constraint explicitly by retaining only the
k
k
largest latent activations.
In VLAs, SAE features have recently been used to interpret and repeatedly steer policy at test time
[
25
]
.
In contrast, the proposed method identifies recurring internal patterns associated with unreliable behaviors using sparse features and translates these patterns into forgetting targets to guide targeted policy unlearning.

Representative clean success (CS, hallucination-free success) and hallucination failure (HF, failure with hallucination) rollouts under the same task show distinct attention patterns.
HF exhibits weaker attention to task-relevant regions (e.g., gripper and target object) and increased attention to the background.
