4.2
Implementation Details
MemPilot is implemented based on VeRL
1
1
1
https://github.com/volcengine/verl
, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
as the default orchestrator policy. To disentangle gains from RL-enhanced answer generation, we additionally report a decoupled-answer evaluation where the curated context is passed to a separate, non-RL-trained answer model, using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. External LLMs and VLMs are accessed through OpenRouter
2
2
2
https://openrouter.ai
, with the heterogeneous model pool specified in Appendix
A.2
. We segment raw interaction histories into 256-token chunks and use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
(
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
for semantic retrieval. Unless otherwise specified, the query-agnostic memory bank is constructed with LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
at a 0.4 compression ratio for policy training and main evaluation. We further examine compatibility with memory banks produced by other agent memory systems in Section
4.6
. We retrieve at most five evidence items per step for both MemPilot and applicable baselines. Since memory items from different systems can vary substantially in length, we directly compare monetary cost and latency rather than memory-item counts. Remaining hyperparameters are provided in Appendix
A.5
.
For training, we adopt a 7/1/2 train/validation/test split. We merge the training portions of Mem-Gallery, WorldMemArena, and H2HMem into a joint training set and evaluate in-domain performance on their held-out test sets. We further use MemLens and MemEye exclusively for out-of-domain evaluation to assess generalization to unseen memory distributions. The same data protocol is applied to all applicable baselines, with detailed dataset statistics provided in Appendix
A.4
. For the main comparison, we evaluate three representative MemPilot preferences:
Perf
,
Bal
, and
Cost
, prioritizing answer quality, balanced quality–resource trade-offs, and inference cost, respectively. Additional preference settings are explored in Section
4.4
.

As shown in Table
1
, MemPilot spans distinct quality–cost regimes across both models and benchmarks. The results reveal several consistent trends across methods and settings.
(1) Text-centric systems achieve low cost largely by avoiding additional multimodal processing and runtime curation, but this often comes with lower answer quality.
In comparison, MemPilot-Bal generally achieves stronger overall quality at moderate cost, while MemPilot-Cost reaches similarly low-cost regimes on most datasets.
(2) Runtime adaptation does not necessarily translate into controllable trade-offs.
Although GAM, AgeMem, and Mem-T adapt memory processing at inference time, they largely expose a fixed operating regime rather than explicitly controlling the quality–cost balance. In contrast, MemPilot spans multiple operating points. MemPilot-Perf achieves the best L-J score across all five benchmarks under both models, while MemPilot-Bal substantially lowers cost and provides a distinct intermediate quality–cost trade-off.
(3) Multimodal memory processing can be costly without adaptive allocation.
MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse often incur substantially higher inference cost without consistently translating that expense into better answer quality. In contrast, MemPilot selectively invokes external curation and achieves stronger performance at much lower cost in most settings, with the same trend extending to MemEye and MemLens.
Overall, MemPilot provides controllable quality–cost trade-offs rather than a single performance-oriented operating point.
MemPilot-Perf prioritizes answer quality, MemPilot-Bal offers a balanced operating point, and MemPilot-Cost further reduces resource usage with greater quality sacrifice. We analyze latency and finer-grained performance–cost–latency frontiers in Section
4.4
.

Performance–cost.
As shown in Figure
2
(a), MemPilot forms a stronger frontier across a broad cost range and largely envelopes the competing methods. Compared with trade-off-aware baselines such as LightMem, BudgetMem, and OmniSimpleMem, MemPilot reaches higher quality as additional computation is allocated, while also covering competitive low-cost operating points. Most conventional memory systems expose only a fixed quality–cost point, highlighting the additional flexibility provided by learned runtime orchestration. Multimodal systems such as MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse generally incur much higher cost due to visual processing, whereas MemPilot reduces unnecessary multimodal computation through on-demand curation and selective model delegation.
Performance–latency.
Figure
2
(b) shows a similarly broad quality–latency frontier. MemPilot spans lightweight to performance-oriented configurations, whereas most baselines expose only a narrow region or a single operating point. Even among runtime-adaptive methods, the achievable latency range remains limited. MemVerse achieves competitive quality at relatively low latency, but lacks explicit trade-off control and incurs substantially higher monetary cost in Figure
2
(a). This further highlights that cost and latency capture complementary resource constraints.
Overall, MemPilot provides a broader, more controllable performance–cost–latency frontier through adaptive runtime orchestration, enabling flexible computation allocation under resource preferences.
4.5
How Does MemPilot Allocate Runtime Computation?
To better understand how MemPilot realizes different trade-offs, we analyze its learned runtime curation behavior in Figure
3
. Panels (a) and (b) show that as the optimization preference shifts toward lower cost or lower latency, the policy adjusts multiple control dimensions in a coordinated manner rather than relying on a single knob. Moving from left to right, MemPilot generally reduces the number of policy steps, the frequency of
Curate
actions, image access, and policy output tokens. At the same time, evidence count also changes adaptively, indicating that the policy does not simply retrieve less information, but learns to reconfigure how memory is accessed and processed under different resource preferences.
Panel (c) further shows that model selection is a key mechanism behind this adaptation. Under higher-cost settings, MemPilot relies more heavily on stronger VLMs and LLMs, while lower-cost settings shift computation toward cheaper model groups. Together, these results show that MemPilot learns a coherent allocation strategy over curation depth, modality access, and routed model capacity, which explains its ability to realize controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs.

Ablation Study of Core Design Choices.
We ablate four key components of MemPilot to examine their contributions to runtime orchestration and policy optimization, with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. As shown in Table
2
, removing LLM/VLM delegation reduces the average Judge score from 37.40 to 14.58, highlighting the importance of adaptive external curation. Removing marginal utility or retrieval–instruction decoupling causes similarly large degradation, demonstrating the value of fine-grained credit assignment and separating evidence retrieval from curation instructions. Objective-wise advantage decoupling is also important for multi-objective training, with its removal reducing the Judge score to 21.94. Although all ablated variants consume less inference cost, their substantial quality losses indicate that simply reducing runtime computation does not yield a desirable trade-off.

To examine whether MemPilot depends on a particular query-agnostic memory construction, we replace its default memory bank with off-the-shelf agent memory banks and evaluate the performance–cost frontiers without retraining using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. Figure

The resulting frontiers are clearly separated: the default bank occupies the lower-cost regime, SimpleMem provides an intermediate profile, while A-MEM incurs higher cost but reaches stronger performance. Each memory bank thus induces a distinct operating regime, while MemPilot improves performance as additional runtime computation is allocated. This demonstrates compatibility with diverse upstream memory systems while preserving their distinct performance–cost characteristics through runtime orchestration.
5
Conclusion
We presented
MemPilot
, a framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under controllable performance–cost–latency preferences. MemPilot formulates runtime memory adaptation as a multi-step decision process, combines query-agnostic memory with raw interaction history, and adaptively delegates curation to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. We further introduced resource-aware policy optimization with objective-wise advantage decoupling and prefix-based marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment. Experiments across multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate that MemPilot achieves favorable trade-off frontiers while adapting computation to different optimization preferences. We hope this work encourages agent memory systems to move beyond performance-only optimization toward resource-aware runtime adaptation.

A.4
Evaluation Details
Memory preprocessing and indexing.
We serialize each multimodal conversation in chronological order and partition it into approximately 256-token text chunks. Dialogue turns are treated as atomic units: a turn is never split across chunks, and its attached images, image identifiers, and captions remain associated with the same chunk. An oversized individual turn is retained as a single chunk. For WorldMemArena
(
Liu et al., 2026a
)
, the memory available to each question is additionally restricted to the cumulative conversation prefix visible at its corresponding checkpoint.
We construct separate dense indexes for the raw and compressed memory corpora. Query-agnostic compression is performed independently for chunk text and image captions using LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
with a default compression rate of 0.4, while memory and image identifiers remain unchanged. Document embeddings are computed offline using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
(
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, normalized, stored in float16 format, and reused throughout evaluation. At runtime, only the policy-generated retrieval query is encoded, after which evidence is ranked by embedding similarity. The compressed-memory and raw-memory indexes are searched independently, with at most five retrieved items per curation operation. Image captions participate in textual retrieval, whereas image pixels are made available only when an image-capable external model is selected. Reference answers are never used during preprocessing, indexing, or retrieval.
Benchmarks and data splits.
Our in-distribution evaluation covers Mem-Gallery
(
Bei et al., 2026
)
, the lifelong subset of WorldMemArena
(
Liu et al., 2026a
)
, and both the dyadic and multiparty variants of H2HMem
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
. Each dataset is split at the conversation level into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test data, ensuring that questions derived from the same conversation never appear in different splits. WorldMemArena is additionally stratified by category and scenario. The source datasets are split independently before their training and validation portions are merged, and their source identities are preserved for dataset-wise reporting.
For out-of-distribution evaluation, we use the complete open-answer portion of MemEye
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
, containing 371 questions across eight scenarios, and the official 32K memory-agent subset of MEMLENS
(
Ren et al., 2026
)
. MemEye’s multiple-choice variant is excluded. MEMLENS answer-refusal questions are removed, leaving 173 of the 195 agent-subset questions. Answer-refusal questions are likewise excluded from Mem-Gallery and H2HMem. For H2HMem, we additionally remove dialogues without usable memory content and Conflict Detection instances whose reference labels cannot satisfy the benchmark’s required standalone Yes/No answer format. Neither OOD benchmark contributes data to policy training or model selection.

Inference.
We evaluate one deterministic trajectory per question using greedy decoding with temperature 0. The maximum prompt and response lengths are both 4,096 tokens. Each trajectory permits at most six sequential curation rounds and at most two concurrent independent curation operations. All policy-facing memory-access settings are kept identical to those used during the corresponding training run.

Minor answer-only adaptations are applied when an official prompt requires information unavailable to common baseline outputs. Specifically, we remove the question field from all judge inputs; remove Key Memory Points from WorldMemArena because they evaluate evidence coverage rather than final-answer correctness; convert H2HMem’s session-batched evaluation into itemwise evaluation; and remove the previous answer from MEMLENS Knowledge Update prompts because correctness is determined by the current reference answer. Policy–answer model decoupling.
For controlled comparisons that separate memory orchestration from answer-generation ability, we optionally remove the trained policy’s final answer while retaining the query and the memory evidence collected along its curation trajectory. B.1
Per-Benchmark Runtime Computation Allocation
Figure
5
provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the runtime-allocation analysis in Section
4.5
. The overall behavior is consistent across all five benchmarks. As stronger cost or latency preferences are imposed, MemPilot generally reduces policy steps,
Curate
actions, visual access, and policy-generation tokens, indicating coordinated adaptation across multiple control dimensions.
Model routing exhibits an equally consistent shift. High-resource settings rely heavily on larger LLMs and VLMs, whereas tighter cost preferences progressively move curation toward lighter models. At the lowest displayed cost point, all five benchmarks route exclusively to LLMs below 70B. Meanwhile, individual controls such as evidence depth and image access need not change monotonically, showing that MemPilot reallocates computation jointly rather than uniformly shrinking every decision dimension. These results confirm that the aggregate behavior observed in the main text is broadly consistent across datasets while retaining dataset-specific curation patterns.
B.2
Per-Benchmark Ablation Results
Table
6
provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the ablation study. The full MemPilot configuration consistently achieves the highest Judge score across all five benchmarks. Among the ablations, removing objective-wise advantage decoupling generally preserves the strongest performance, yet still causes clear degradation on every dataset, confirming its role in multi-objective policy optimization. Removing LLM/VLM delegation, marginal utility, or retrieval–instruction decoupling leads to substantially larger drops, with similar trends observed on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Although all ablations reduce inference cost, the accompanying quality degradation remains pronounced, indicating that the complete design yields a more effective quality–cost trade-off rather than merely consuming additional computation.

Appendix D
Limitations and Future Work
While MemPilot provides flexible runtime memory orchestration, several aspects could be further improved:
•
Privacy-aware delegation.
Runtime curation may send retrieved interaction history to external models, which can raise privacy concerns for sensitive memories. Future work could incorporate privacy-aware routing, local processing, or access-control mechanisms while remaining orthogonal to MemPilot’s core orchestration design.
•
Preference calibration.
MemPilot controls trade-offs through predefined optimization preferences. Future work could study more user-friendly ways to map high-level deployment preferences to reward coefficients, making trade-off specification easier across applications.
•
Deployment-aware latency modeling.
We use a proxy latency estimator during training to avoid instability from transient network and serving fluctuations. Future work could instead optimize directly against measured latency in a controlled system-level sandbox with stable networking and serving conditions.
Appendix E
Broader Impact
MemPilot advocates a broader shift in agent memory from performance-oriented optimization toward explicit and controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs. In practical deployments, the highest-performing memory configuration is not always the most desirable, as different users and applications may place substantially different values on monetary cost and response latency. This mirrors modern commercial LLM services, which increasingly offer model tiers spanning different capability, cost, and latency profiles (e.g., GPT-5.6-Sol/Terra/Luna), allowing users to choose operating points that best match their needs. We believe agent memory systems should provide similar flexibility rather than committing to a single performance-oriented configuration. This becomes particularly relevant for multimodal agents, where accessing and processing visual evidence can introduce substantially different resource demands. More broadly, treating memory curation as adaptive computation allocation may encourage tighter integration between agent memory, model routing, and resource-aware decision making, enabling future long-horizon agents to become more efficient, responsive, and deployment-aware.

Semantic equivalence over surface form.
The assistant may use different wording, synonyms, or sentence

it should receive full credit.
Do NOT penalize for stylistic differences.
2.
Numeric / counting questions are binary.
If the Ground Truth is a specific number (e.g., “3”),
the answer is either exactly right (score 1) or wrong (score 0).
There is no partial credit for being off by one.
3.
Negation + correction questions.
Some Ground Truth answers first negate a premise and then
provide the correct information
(e.g., “No — it was May 18-22, not May 15-19”).
The assistant must get BOTH the negation AND the corrected
fact right for full credit.
4.
Identity / “Who is” questions.
The Ground Truth may describe a person by role, actions,
or relationships rather than by name.
The assistant’s answer is correct if it identifies the same
unique person, even if it uses a name instead of a description
or vice versa.
5.
Answer the thing that was asked.
Judge whether the assistant answered the requested attribute
or type of information. If the question asks for a category,
role, relationship, time, count, ordering, or specific item,
an answer giving a different type of information is not fully
correct even if it is related.
6.
Wrong entity beats related entity.
If the answer names the wrong person, object, brand, place,
event, or option, do not give high scores just because it
is on-topic. Being from the right semantic domain is not enough.
7.
Multi-item questions require set matching.
Full credit requires all required items and no incorrect extras.
If only some required items are correct, partial credit
may be appropriate.

Ordering / chronology questions require
the correct item.
If the question asks which item was first, last, middle,
earlier, later, before, or after, the selected item must
match the Ground Truth.
A different plausible item is still wrong.

Do not over-reward fluent explanations.
Extra detail is helpful only if it stays consistent with
the Ground Truth.
Confident wording or elaboration should not increase the
score when the core fact is wrong.
10.
Contradicted relations or orderings
are usually zero.
If the question asks about a relationship such as before/after,
earlier/later, first/last, middle, sequence, relative timing,
or other ordering, and the assistant gives the opposite
relation, denies the relation, or selects the wrong ordered
item, this is usually a clear contradiction and should
normally receive score 0 rather than 0.25.

from earlier conversation/image context.
•
Assign 1 point if the student’s response recovers
the same previous information as the standard answer,
including the correct relation, location, count, or attribute.
•
Minor wording differences are acceptable if they
preserve the same meaning.
•
Assign 0 points if the answer refers to the wrong
previous item, gives the wrong relation/count/location,
is too vague, refuses, or is unsupported.
[KU — Knowledge Update]
This is a knowledge update question testing whether the model
tracks the latest state.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the current
(correct) answer.
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives an outdated answer,
any other incorrect answer, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Yes/No (Entity Resolution)]
This is a yes/no question.
•
Assign 1 point if the student’s final answer is
semantically equivalent to the standard answer
(e.g., “Yes” matches “Yes”, “No” matches “No”),
even if phrased differently
(e.g., “That’s correct” for “Yes”).
•
Assign 0 points if the answer means the opposite,
refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Counting]
This is a counting question.
The standard answer is a specific number.
•
Assign 1 point if the student clearly states the
exact number in any equivalent form
(e.g., “3”, “three”, “3.0”).
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a different number,
a range, an approximation, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[MSR — Arithmetic]
This is an arithmetic question.
The standard answer is a specific value.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the same value
in an equivalent format
(e.g., “0.5” and “1/2” and “50%”).
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a different value,
an unsupported approximation, refuses, or does not clearly answer.
[TR — Duration Comparison (A/B)]
This is a binary choice question.
The student must select one of two options.
•
Assign 1 point if the student clearly selects the
same option as the standard answer, regardless of phrasing.
•
Assign 0 points if the student selects the other option,
refuses, or does not make a clear selection.
[TR — Order Ranking]
This is an ordering question.
The standard answer is an exact sequence of items.
•
Assign 1 point ONLY if the student gives the exact
same sequence in the same order.
•
Assign 0 points if any item is missing, added,
duplicated, misplaced, or if the order is unclear.
[TR — Date Extraction]
This is a date extraction question.
The standard answer is a specific date.
•
Assign 1 point if the student gives the same date
in any unambiguous equivalent format
(e.g., “Jan 15, 2024” and “2024-01-15” and “15/01/2024”).
•
Assign 0 points if the date is different,
incomplete when a full date is required, ambiguous, or missing.
[AR — Answer Refusal]
•
Assign 1 point if the student explicitly refuses,
says there is not enough information, or indicates the
question is unanswerable from the provided context.
•
Assign 0 points if the student gives a substantive
answer, even if hedged.

article.headline: MemPilot：按需编排多模态记忆的智能体框架
article.lede: 用强化学习训练一个多步编排策略，在检索压缩记忆与委派原始多模态历史之间反复选择，换取可调的质量—成本—延迟折中。
article.problem: 现有智能体记忆系统大多以与查询无关的方式预先构建记忆，既产生不必要的预处理开销，又可能丢掉后续查询才需要的细节。近期转向运行时自适应的方案往往只针对单一操作或固定处理流程，且很少把用户可感知的延迟当作显式优化目标，对性能、成本、延迟的灵活控制仍未被充分探索。
article.method: MemPilot 维护双视图记忆：一个与查询无关的压缩记忆库用于快速检索，一份按 256 token 分块、保留原始多模态上下文的交互历史用于运行时策展。编排器是一个多步 LLM 策略，每一步在 Retrieve 与 Curate 之间选择；Curate 进一步分解出检索查询、证据条数、策展指令、调用哪个外部 LLM/VLM、是否附带原始图像等控制量。训练用 GRPO，并对质量、成本、延迟三个目标分别做组内优势归一化再加权聚合，同时用前缀答案探测估计每一步的边际效用，做更细粒度的信用分配。
article.results: 在 Mem-Gallery、WorldMemArena、H2HMem 三个域内基准和 MemEye、MemLens 两个域外基准上，以 Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct 为答案模型时，MemPilot-Perf 在全部五个基准上取得最高 LLM-judge 分数（65.82、63.41、35.97、25.07、27.17），换用 Qwen3.5-9B 答案模型后同样全部最高（67.64、74.09、37.57、21.83、24.28）。MemPilot-Bal 在 Mem-Gallery 上 F1 为 57.26、成本 1.4e-2，MemPilot-Cost 把成本压到 8.2e-3 但 F1 降至 32.67。消融显示五个基准平均 judge 分从 37.40 分别跌至：去掉 LLM/VLM 委派 14.58、去掉边际效用 14.82、去掉目标优势解耦（GDPO）21.94、去掉检索—指令解耦 15.35。
article.why_it_matters: 它把记忆策展从「预先建好、查询时照用」改写成运行时的计算分配问题：同一套策略通过偏好向量在不同质量、成本、延迟的工作点上滑动，并与现成的查询无关记忆库保持兼容。对需要长程多模态交互的智能体部署来说，这提供了比单一性能最优点更贴近实际的配置方式。
article.limitations: 实验中的延迟并非实测墙钟时间，而是由固定开销加每 token 系数的仿射代理估计器给出，作者自己也承认需要稳定的系统级沙箱才能直接对真实延迟优化。此外，Curate 会把检索到的交互历史发给外部模型，存在隐私暴露风险；偏好系数仍需人工设定，且 Cost 偏好下质量下降明显（Mem-Gallery 上 F1 从 57.26 掉到 32.67），说明低成本工作点并不总能保住可用质量。
article.figure_caption_zh: MemPilot 总览：(a) 编排器迭代地在检索压缩记忆与把原始多模态历史委派给异构 LLM/VLM 之间选择，分解式控制覆盖证据检索、策展策略、视觉访问与模型选择；(b) 目标级优势解耦用于权衡质量、成本与延迟，前缀答案探测则估计每一步的边际效用。

page_papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
page_papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

article.headline: KronLSTM：更抗干扰的线性注意力更新规则
article.lede: 把 DeltaNet 的写入规则推广为 Kronecker Delta 形式，1.5B 模型在多针检索上领先，32k 扩
article.problem: 线性注意力把历史压进一个矩阵状态，上下文变长后需要记住的关联数量上升，彼此干扰成为瓶颈。DeltaNet 一类delta 规则每步写入集中在 d 维方向，而矩阵记忆有 d² 个方向可用，写入过于集中会加快旧关联被覆盖。作者用干扰分析论证：长上下文真正卡住的是能容纳多少条关联，而不是拟合单条关联的速度。
article.method: 论文提出 Kronecker Delta 更新规则，把写入分散到 d² 维矩阵记忆的各个方向，使每一步的写入在固定 β 下更平缓，并用门控机制稳定该更新，构成 KronLSTM 块。实验在 400M/40B 与 1.5B/100B 两个规模上，与 GDN-2、Mamba-3、KDA、mLSTM 等线性注意力及 SWA 混合模型对比，另将 1.5B 模型在 75B token 处分支、用 32k 序列长度继续训练 25B token 做上下文扩展。
article.results: 在 2k 上下文的真实召回测试集上，KronLSTM 平均准确率最高，在纯线性注意力模型和混合模型中各于六项任务里的三项取得最佳；使用 SWA 的混合模型整体可提升五到九个准确率点。NIAH 任务上，除 S1 外 KronLSTM 在所有序列长度上均为最佳或次佳，混合模型组中在每个任务的 16k 长度上准确率最高；4k 时在 S2 上领先 GDN-2 与 Mamba-3 达 15.2 个准确率点。MQ 任务上，随上下文从 4k 增至 16k，领先幅度从 2.4 扩大到 4.1 个准确率点；MV 任务上 4k 时落后最佳方法 GDN 3.5 点，但 8k 和 16k 分别领先 1.1 与 3.8 点。32k 扩展后两个模型的困惑度都改善约 4 点，KronLSTM 平均准确率更高、困惑度更低，并在六项召回任务中的五项更好。400M 规模上，相比其基础 mLSTM，KronLSTM 在六项任务中五项更优，平均提升 2.1 点，LAMBADA 困惑度从 43.40 降到 28.28。
article.why_it_matters: 结果提示长上下文的瓶颈可能不在位置外推，而在记忆更新规则的干扰累积，这为线性注意力与混合架构的状态设计提供了除门控和混合之外的另一条改进路径。
article.limitations: 优势并不全面：S1 任务上 GDN-2 始终更强，MV 在 4k 上下文时落后 3.5 点，32k 时两个模型的检索准确率都明显下降。正文只说明做了 parity、S3 置换与模运算的状态跟踪实验，未给出具体数字；写入更平缓也意味着拟合单条关联更慢，属于容量与速度的权衡。

page_papers.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
page_papers.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose

Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation

These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt

Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training

This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories
[
27
,
31
,
99
]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: MT Forcing 稳定多轮图像编辑
article.lede: MT Forcing 用单轮教师分布匹配和教师强制引导，缓解自回归扩散多轮图像编辑的视觉质量漂移与内容不一致。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑要求模型在上一轮输出上继续编辑，但训练时条件于参考历史、推理时条件于自身不完美历史，暴露偏差会使误差递归累积。现有方法在几轮后常出现视觉质量退化（伪影、细节丢失）和内容不一致（非编辑区域被改动、先前编辑未保留）。
article.method: MT Forcing 包含两个互补目标：Single-Turn DMD 将截至当前轮的所有指令重组为 bundled prompt，用单轮教师从源图直接执行累积编辑，并对学生自回归 rollout 做 DMD 分布匹配；Teacher-Forcing Guidance 在参考轨迹上用 flow matching 监督依赖历史的转移，先做 warmup，再以较低权重作为蒸馏正则。最终训练目标为 DMD 损失加上 λTF 倍教师强制损失。
article.results: 在 MTEdit-Bench step-wise 子集（100 个 session、每个 8 轮指令）上，SenseNova-U1.5 第 8 轮的 IF/CC 分别提升 4.65 和 4.46，SenseNova-U1 分别提升 7.45 和 6.82；SenseNova-U1.5 的 DRS 全程维持在 4.20–4.35，基线则从 4.09 降至 3.03；其八轮平均 Pixel 从 6.34 降至 0.74，降幅 88.4%。消融中完整方法取得 9.66 IF、8.40 CC、4.30 DRS 和 0.74 Pixel，均优于仅 DMD（9.02/7.64/4.12/2.51）和仅 TF 引导（9.10/7.83/3.92/2.74）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把自回归扩散中的自 rollout 训练与教师强制思路迁移到多轮图像编辑，为统一多模态模型提供了一种不依赖双向多轮教师、在训练中抑制长期漂移的方案。
article.limitations: 实验仅覆盖 SenseNova-U1/U1.5 两个模型和 MTEdit-Bench 的 100 个八轮 session，且主要与各自基座对比，未与其他专门多轮编辑方法横向比较；IF/CC 由 Qwen3.5-Plus 打分，λTF 取 1 或 0.5 时还出现明显模糊，说明一致性与清晰度之间存在权衡。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing 总览：单轮 DMD 将学生 rollout 边际分布对齐到单轮教师分布，教师强制引导在参考轨迹上监督历史相关转移，整体训练先 warmup 再联合 DMD 与教师强制正则。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

page_papers.title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
page_papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

Abstract
Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose
Interlock
, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects.
Interlock
compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00–4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20–6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89–4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.
1
Introduction
Long-horizon agents increasingly work with records, rules, resources, and partially completed artifacts. A short request can require reconciling conflicting evidence, determining which objects need attention, selecting a feasible plan, and updating several related results. The environment supplies the facts and constraints that determine this work. A decision can also activate further obligations: deferring an action may require an explanation and a handoff, while changing an allocation may require corresponding revisions to schedules and budgets. These obligations can outlive the interaction in which they are discovered: after many intervening reads, computations, and edits, the agent must still apply the earlier evidence and decisions to every affected result.
Local progress can coexist with an incomplete outcome (Figure
1
). A correct decision can leave necessary consequences unfulfilled, and mutually consistent outputs can share an unsupported assumption. These failures concern the relationships that connect evidence, decisions, and the requested outcome. They motivate our central question:
how can task synthesis preserve conditional obligations and turn their fulfillment into transferable training experience?
Figure 1:
From local correctness to task completion.
A correct flight booking can still leave schedule and budget updates
unfinished.
Interlock
preserves grounding, coupling, and realization
relations during task synthesis to connect evidence, decisions, and
required downstream effects.
We characterize this structure as a typed completion graph.
Grounding
connects environmental evidence and rules to the decisions they support.
Coupling
links components that must share a feasible choice or satisfy a joint constraint.
Realization
connects a decision to every downstream record, artifact, or state that must reflect it. Their interaction is especially demanding over long executions: an early finding can constrain work completed many interactions later, and a revised decision can require coordinated changes to several existing artifacts.
Task synthesis and environment generation provide a scalable basis for agent training. Prior work constructs verified tool-use data
(
Qin et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2024
)
, generates environments and task scenarios
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Song et al., 2026
)
, and composes extended tasks through tool dependencies and reusable workflows
(
Tu et al., 2026
;
Shi et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Common specifications can also align instructions, environments, and verifiers
(
Ivanov and Rana, 2026
)
. Our organizing unit is the complete set of conditional obligations for an outcome. It determines both the unresolved work placed in an environment and the evidence needed to accept the result.
We propose
Interlock
to make this graph an explicit synthesis constraint. Reusable domain descriptions and archetype contracts define evidence roles, task-specific decisions and shared states, joint conditions, and downstream consumers. Three generation roles compile the same graph into a workspace, task/contract, and rubric while leaving concrete associations and decisions to the agent. A source-coverage review traces every typed relation from the original graph through these artifacts; a public-input critic independently checks whether the resulting criteria are supported by solver-visible materials and assessable from execution artifacts. Completion-filtered training then selects executions that realize every applicable effect.
Our evaluation connects task structure, execution behavior, and training utility. Statistical analyses and case studies examine dependencies and completion failures. The training protocol uses Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B separately, retaining each model’s own accepted rollouts for SFT of that same model. Both backbones improve on AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB. Gains over the original checkpoints reach 4.00–4.50 percentage points in AutomationBench task pass rate, 3.20–6.64 points in JobBench weighted score, and 3.89–4.16 percentage points in Harvey LAB criterion pass rate. These results show that experience from complete synthetic executions transfers to independently authored tasks across different environments. Our contributions are threefold:
•
A typed representation of task completion.
We model long-horizon tasks as completion graphs whose grounding, coupling, and realization relations connect public evidence, consequential decisions, joint constraints, and required effects.
•
Graph-grounded synthesis and review.
We compile the same graph into the environment, task specification, deliverable contract, and outcome criteria, with complementary reviews for source coverage and public support.
•
Empirical validation of training utility.
We evaluate the generated experience through completion-filtered fine-tuning of two backbones and measure transfer across three external benchmarks.
2
Related Work
Task synthesis and environment generation provide a scalable source of agent experience.
ToolAlpaca
(
Tang et al., 2023
)
, ToolLLM
(
Qin et al., 2024
)
, and ToolACE
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
broaden tool coverage and interaction diversity, while APIGen
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
incorporates format, execution, and semantic verification.
Beyond tool-use data, AgentGen
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
, AutoForge
(
Cai et al., 2025
)
, and EnvScaler
(
Song et al., 2026
)
extend synthesis to environments and their associated planning tasks or executable scenarios.
Agent-World
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
further couples environment-task discovery with self-evolving training, and ClawGym
(
Bai et al., 2026
)
brings synthesis to persistent workspaces through persona-driven intents, skill-grounded operations, and hybrid verification.
To construct extended interactions, ToolFlow
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
plans coherent tool-use dialogues, while APIGen-MT
(
Prabhakar et al., 2026
)
turns verified action blueprints into multi-turn interactions.
BUTTON
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
, TaskCraft
(
Shi et al., 2026
)
, and AgentSynth
(
Xie et al., 2026
)
construct complex requests by composing or expanding smaller tasks.
Complementary approaches, including VOYAGER
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, OS-Genesis
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
, and Explorer
(
Pahuja et al., 2025
)
, obtain curricula or tasks through environmental state and exploration.
Alongside task complexity, another line of work addresses consistency among generated instructions, environments, and verifiers.
Endless Terminals
(
Gandhi et al., 2026
)
generates containerized tasks with completion tests, while RST
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
extends verified reference solutions and realigns instructions and verifiers with the resulting workflows.
CodeMidas
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
derives coding tasks from existing implementations, grounds synthesized tests in execution of the original code, and filters tasks through execution checks and agent rollouts.
Anchor
(
Ivanov and Rana, 2026
)
addresses artifact drift by deriving task artifacts and certified solutions from a common constraint program.
Graph-guided synthesis provides more explicit control over the dependencies underlying generated tasks.
ScaleEnv
(
Tu et al., 2026
)
constructs tasks from tested tool dependencies, EnvFactory
(
Xu et al., 2026b
)
uses topology-aware sampling to generate grounded queries, and SkillSynth
(
Fan et al., 2026
)
instantiates paths through a scenario-mediated skill graph.
These approaches organize generation around tool connectivity and skill relationships.
Interlock
instead uses task-completion relationships as synthesis constraints: its typed completion graph grounds decisions in evidence, imposes joint constraints, and specifies required downstream effects.

4.2
Main Results
Interlock-RFT achieves the highest score in every evaluation column for both backbones (Table
1
), outperforming the original checkpoints and ClawGym-SFT. Each backbone is trained on its own accepted trajectories, and the gains extend across coordinated API execution, professional deliverables, and legal work.
For Qwen3.6-27B,
Interlock
improves AutomationBench task pass rate by 4.00 percentage points, JobBench Main and Easy weighted scores by 4.35 and 6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rate by 3.89 percentage points over the original checkpoint. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the gains are 4.50 percentage points on AutomationBench, 3.20 and 4.31 score points on JobBench Main and Easy, and 4.16 percentage points on Harvey LAB. The improvements therefore cover task completion on AutomationBench, weighted rubric fulfillment on JobBench, and criterion satisfaction on Harvey LAB.

4.7
Case Studies of Task Completion
Figure
6
traces completion requirements
in two synthesized tasks using public inputs and recorded artifacts.
For each task, we compare two rollout attempts of Qwen3.6-27B on
identical public inputs.
Operating recovery.
A four-week recovery plan must reconcile supply, order commitments,
and financial effects. In attempt 1, Qwen3.6-27B allocates 970 HX units against
770 available; advancing an inbound shipment changes its arrival time,
not the total supply. Its 3,920-kit plan also exceeds 3,250 shared trays,
partially serves an unsplittable 230-unit order, and omits a selected
$6,800 expedite cost from contribution margin despite recording the
cash outflow. In attempt 2, the same model uses 760 HX units, caps kits at
3,250, excludes the whole unsplittable order, and deducts its own
selected action costs.
Training schedules.
The February 2026 training cycle links due employees, shift availability,
instructor credentials, and publication records. Attempt 1 of Qwen3.6-27B produces
matching schedule and publication rows but omits two of six due
trainees, schedules a 12:00–14:00 class outside an 08:00–11:30 release
window, and assigns an instructor on February 16 whose credential
expires on February 12. Attempt 2 of the same model retains all six
trainees, uses a shared 09:30–11:30 window, and schedules that
instructor on February 11. Appendix
F
extends the analysis to
field-trial protocols, charging networks, and payroll close.

5
Conclusion
Interlock
organizes long-horizon task synthesis around typed completion graphs. Grounding, coupling, and realization relations constrain how public evidence, consequential decisions, joint conditions, and required effects are compiled into task environments and outcome criteria. Dual-view review checks both graph preservation and public support, while completion-filtered RFT selects executions that realize every applicable graph effect. Training improves both Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B across AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB, supporting the value of complete synthetic execution experience for transfer across task environments.
AI use statement
We used generative AI tools to assist with prompt design and manuscript
preparation, including language polishing, bilingual editing, and the
preparation of figures and captions. As described in
Section
3
, AI agents are integral to the task synthesis and
training-data collection procedure: they generate initial workspaces,
task instructions, and outcome rubrics; review task requirements and
quality; execute tasks; and assess the resulting artifacts. The roles
and verification procedures for these agents are documented in the
methodology and experimental setup. We have manually reviewed all
AI-assisted work, including manuscript revisions, prompts, generated
task materials, and execution and evaluation records. We take
responsibility for the final content of this work, including its text,
analyses, claims, and artifacts produced with AI assistance.

F.1
Field-Trial Protocol: Decisions Must Remain Executable and Interpretable
The research lead needs a 2027 field-trial authorization protocol and
a consistent reviewer note. In attempt 1, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B reverses the public risk
condition: the confidence-interval branch flags risk when it excludes
a yield loss above two bushels per acre, whereas the rule flags risk
when it cannot exclude that loss. The plan also retains conditional
AP7 treatment at SD-L2 despite its conflict with the associated
May 9 pre-emerge constraint. This constraint applies to that operation
and AP7 feasibility. Seasonal workload totals do not supply the
required dated allocation of observations and staff. The protocol
further makes grower-paid resprays reimbursable, and its secondary
weed endpoint becomes primary in the reviewer note.
Attempt 2 of the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model uses four sites with AP5, preserves both
required environments, and meets the public minimum of two sites per
environment. It retains the risk condition, dated activities, payer
boundary, and endpoint roles. The saved Judge counts for attempts 1
and 2 are 15/22 and 22/22. The five focal failures in Figure
13
connect grounded interpretation to a jointly feasible design and to
the measurements and explanations that must realize it.

Benchmarks and evaluation.
We assess out-of-domain (OOD) generalization by transferring from the
Interlock
synthetic task distribution to three independently constructed benchmark distributions. We use the public releases of AutomationBench and Harvey LAB. The evaluated benchmark instances are excluded from
Interlock
’s synthesis inputs and RFT data. This setting tests whether experience acquired in generated task environments supports completion of externally specified tasks.
AutomationBench
contains 600 public benchmark tasks, with 100 tasks in each of six business domains. Agents coordinate actions across applications through APIs, and programmatic assertions evaluate the final application state. We report
pass rate
: the percentage of task executions satisfying every required assertion
(
Shepard and Salimans, 2026
)
.
JobBench
contains 130 tasks across 35 occupations, divided into
Main
and
Easy
sets of 65 tasks each. The tasks require agents to reconcile heterogeneous reference materials and produce professional deliverables. Main includes more demanding reasoning and source reconciliation; Easy uses self-contained reference workspaces without web search. We run JobBench with the
OpenCode
harness and use
GPT-5.5
to return an overall binary pass/fail judgment for each weighted rubric group
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
.
Harvey LAB
contains 1,251 tasks across 24 legal practice areas in the public release used in our evaluation. Tasks combine a client matter, supporting documents, and reviewable work products. We use
GPT-5.5
as the judge for its deliverable-specific binary criteria, which assess factual support, legal analysis, and required content
(
Harvey AI, 2026
)
.

a clean public-input critic report, a normally terminated real execution,
complete criterion judgments, and a sound package-quality assessment
with no outstanding confirmed or undetermined defects.
The two reviews establish source coverage and public support;
the post-execution judge separately assesses the resulting artifacts
and package quality.
Trajectory acceptance is recorded separately as
A
V
​
(
x
,
τ
)
=
1
A_{V}(x,\tau)=1
and is not required for task admission.
Confirmed defects in materials, the request, or the rubric return to
their responsible generation stage. Source-specification and graph
defects require offline correction and keep the candidate internal.
Revisions receive fresh reviews. The two review views share at most one
generation-time rubric recompilation; post-execution revision follows
the separately bounded quality-repair budget.
Appendix I
Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Agents
Long-horizon benchmarks provide concrete settings in which successful interaction must produce the requested outcome.
WebArena
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
and OSWorld
(
Xie et al., 2024
)
evaluate realistic web and desktop tasks with execution-based outcome checks.
AppWorld
(
Trivedi et al., 2024
)
tests stateful multi-application coding and unintended changes, and ToolSandbox
(
Lu et al., 2025
)
emphasizes implicit state dependencies and intermediate milestones.
These settings connect task success to environmental state and applicable rules, motivating our treatment of completion as a set of linked requirements.
WorkArena++
(
Boisvert et al., 2024
)
targets compositional planning and reasoning in knowledge work, while TheAgentCompany
(
Xu et al., 2026a
)
combines websites, code execution, and workplace communication.
Terminal-Bench
(
Merrill et al., 2026
)
couples challenging command-line tasks with dedicated environments and tests, and Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench
(
Li et al., 2026c
)
evaluates extended workflows with graded subtasks and partial credit.
Their emphasis on coordinated work and outcome evaluation complements
Interlock
’s focus on preserving completion requirements during task synthesis.
Our external evaluations span three forms of consequential work.
AutomationBench
(
Shepard and Salimans, 2026
)
brings together cross-application orchestration, autonomous API discovery, and layered policy compliance.
JobBench
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
evaluates expert-prioritized delegations in heterogeneous reference workspaces using fact-anchored chains of binary rubric criteria.
Harvey LAB
(
Harvey AI, 2026
)
evaluates legal work in document-rich matter workspaces through deliverable-specific binary criteria covering factual support, analysis, and required content.
Using each benchmark’s own evaluation protocol, these independently authored tasks assess the downstream value of the synthesized environments and data for agents facing new evidence, constraints, and required effects.

article.headline: 用类型化完成图合成智能体长程任务
article.lede: Interlock 把任务建模为类型化完成图，再用完成筛选的轨迹做拒绝采样微调；两套 Qwen3.6 在三个外部基准上都
article.problem: 长程智能体任务往往证据分散、状态只完成一半、资源与产物彼此依赖，模型容易出现「局部正确但整体没做完」：单个要求都满足，决策之间的联合约束和它应有的下游后果却被漏掉。论文认为这类失败源于环境证据、决策与必须产生的结果之间的关系没有被显式建模，而现有任务合成方法多以工具依赖或技能图为组织单位。
article.method: 作者把每个任务表示为一个类型化完成图：grounding 边把公开证据与规则连到决策，coupling 超边对多个决策或效果施加联合条件，realization 边把决策连到所有必须兑现的下游效果；效果还带有触发条件、适用对象范围与结果条件。三个生成角色把同一张图分别编译成可重置工作区、公开请求与私有评分细则，随后由「来源覆盖」审稿追溯原始要求是否被保留，由「公开输入」审稿只凭求解器可见材料检查细则是否可判定。任务通过审核后，用 agent-as-judge 实际查看工作区、必要时编写并运行校验脚本，只保留满足全部必需条件的轨迹，对同一基座做拒绝采样微调。
article.results: 语料保留 3,278 个任务，每个基座 5 次尝试共 32,780 次执行（32,370 次正常终止），每个基座各取 8,957 条自身被接受的轨迹、约 1.54 亿监督 token 做 SFT。相对原始 checkpoint，Qwen3.6-27B 在 AutomationBench 任务通过率提升 4.00 个百分点（14.33→18.33），JobBench Main/Easy 加权分提升 4.35 与 6.64 分（14.11→18.46、54.46→61.10），Harvey LAB 准则通过率提升 3.89 个百分点（73.96→77.85）；Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 的对应提升为 4.50 个百分点（9.00→13.50）、3.20 与 4.31 分（11.81→15.01、51.86→56.17）以及 4.16 个百分点（54.18→58.34）。在执行长度上，Interlock 轨迹平均 84,293 token、27.63 个助手轮次、42.10 次工具调用，而 ClawGym 轨迹为 14,940 token、11.92 轮、14.76 次。在固定轨迹数下把训练域从 16 扩到 128，四个指标均单调上升。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「任务是否真正完成」写成合成阶段可检查的图约束，并给出证据：在完全独立构造的基准上，用合成任务自采轨迹做 SFT 也能带来跨环境的稳定增益。这为长程智能体的数据生产提供了一条不同于堆工具调用规模、而以条件性义务为组织单位的路线。
article.limitations: 增益幅度有限，最好的 AutomationBench 通过率也只有 18.33%，而且只验证了两个 Qwen3.6 基座加 SFT 一种训练方式，未与强化学习、其他数据规模或更强基座对比；作为对照的 ClawGym-SFT 反而低于原始 checkpoint，基线偏弱使结论的普适性存疑。评测高度依赖 LLM 判分（JobBench 与 Harvey LAB 用 GPT-5.5 作裁判，训练数据筛选用的 agent-as-judge 也由模型驱动），论文自己的案例中判分给出 29/29 通过，独立文件审计却发现两次执行共有的 19.5% 税率错误。
article.figure_caption_zh: Interlock 总览：左侧把 grounding、coupling、realization 三类关系编译进工作区、公开请求与私有评分细则并经来源覆盖与公开支持两道审稿，右侧通过真实执行与 agent-as-judge 判定来准入任务、筛选轨迹，每个基座用自己的被接受轨迹微调。

page_papers.title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
page_papers.abstract: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.
page_papers.content:
RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Yu Li
Shenghe Hu
Yuhan Wang
Yaoxiang Pu
Haotong Zhang
Yuanpei Chen
Yaodong Yang
Abstract
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data.
Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation.
In this work, we propose
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that
RoboFFT
consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate
RoboFFT
into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website:
https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/
.
Figure 1:
We present
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policy with forward process. (a) Reverse finetuning formulates the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP, while forward finetuning aligns with the same objective as training by following the forward noising process.
(b) One framework across popular generative robot policy on simulation benchmarks.
(c) Real-world deployment with integration of real world RL.
(d) Improved performance in success rate, training stability and efficiency.

Keywords:
Diffusion RL, Generative Robot Policy, Robot Manipulation
1
Introduction
Generative robot policies, typically based on diffusion and flow-based models
[
43
,
42
,
15
,
29
]
, have become a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor skills from demonstrations by modeling complex and multi-modal action distributions
[
12
,
56
,
53
]
, which significantly improves robot action accuracy and robustness and yields substantial performance gains in complex manipulation tasks
[
12
,
53
]
. However, policies trained purely by imitation learning remain constrained by the quality and coverage of the demonstration data. Imperfect demonstrations, covariate shift, and insufficient exposure to deployment-time states can all limit the final task performance of behavior-cloned policies
[
13
,
40
]
. Online reinforcement learning (RL) naturally presents itself as a promising paradigm to further improve generative robot policies, as it empowers the policy to directly maximize task rewards by continuously interacting with and learning from the environment.
Applying policy gradient RL methods to generative robot policies is nevertheless nontrivial. Unlike autoregressive policies, whose token likelihoods are tractable, diffusion and flow-based models typically lack a tractable exact likelihood formulation. This makes popular policy gradient objectives, such as PPO, difficult to be applied directly. Existing approaches address this issue by formulating the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP embedded in the high-level environment MDP, and optimizing through this two-level decision making trajectory
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
(Fig.
1
(a), left). Despite its promising results, reverse-process finetuning introduces substantial computation and memory overhead, and may suffer from gradient instability due to long denoising chains, especially in high-dimensional and long-horizon manipulation tasks.
To address these issues, we propose
RoboFFT
, a simpler yet more effective framework for online RL finetuning of generative robot manipulation policies through the
forward
noising process, inspired by recent studies from other application domains such as image generation and simple locomotion
[
52
,
59
,
34
]
. Instead of assigning credit through the reverse denoising chain,
RoboFFT
approximates the exact log-likelihood with a more computationally stable and efficient form akin to the score / flow matching loss for pretraining, yielding a principled PPO-style objective that is aligned with the imitation-learning objective while avoiding complicated likelihood computation or backpropagation through the full reverse trajectory. For flow-based policies, we further adopt SDE sampling by injecting noise into the sampling process, enabling controllable exploration during online data collection. In practice, Monte Carlo estimation, ratio-temperature calibration and further adaptations make likelihood estimation and updates robust across different policy architectures and tasks.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks such as Robomimic
[
33
]
and LIBERO
[
30
]
, which pose difficulties like high-dimensional visual observation, long horizon planning and sparse reward for finetuning. Experimental results across different tasks demonstrate substantial and consistent performance improvements over pretrained diffusion and flow policies and achieve competitive or better performance compared with representative reverse and forward process finetuning baselines, while reducing optimization overhead. We further verify the applicability of our method on more complicated VLA and real world deployment settings, and study the key designs through ablations and visualizations. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework that performs policy gradient finetuning in the forward noising process for generative robot policies.
(2) We carry out practical implementation of
RoboFFT
for representative generative robot policies (flow, diffusion and VLA) on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks, showing that
RoboFFT
achieves superior performance and improved training stability and efficiency.
(3) We integrate
RoboFFT
into the real world reinforcement learning framework for practical deployment and demonstrate its effectiveness over real world tasks.
(4) We carry out a systematic ablation analysis of key design choices and conduct investigative experiments to provide empirical insights for the mechanism of
RoboFFT
.
2
Related Work
2.1
Policy Gradient for Robot Manipulation
Policy gradient and actor critic methods provide a standard framework for learning continuous-control policies from interaction data
[
50
,
45
,
28
,
41
]
. Due to the
training stability with high-dimensional action spaces, they have been widely applied to a range of robotic control problems, including dexterous manipulation, legged locomotion, and agile navigation
[
48
,
9
,
10
,
1
,
17
,
21
]
. For long-horizon manipulation, however, training from scratch remains highly exploration-intensive and is often impractical. A more practical paradigm is therefore to finetune policies initialized from demonstration data. Prior studies have shown that reinforcement learning can further improve such demonstration-initialized policies beyond behavior cloning while substantially reducing the exploration burden
[
38
,
46
,
37
]
. RoboFFT follows this finetuning paradigm, while focusing on diffusion- and flow-based robot policies whose action distributions are implicitly induced by generative sampling processes, making the likelihood ratio computation required by policy gradient methods nontrivial.
2.2
RL for Generative Models
Reinforcement learning has recently been widely applied to generative model finetuning in offline

,
35
,

,

,

54
,

,
52
,
59

[
5
,
39
,
57

Forward-process methods instead optimize policy via constructing surrogate likelihood objectives or contrastive learning, better aligning RL finetuning with generative pretraining
[

,
34
,
54
,
59
]
. DiffusionNFT and AWM

59
,
52
]
study this idea for text-to-image generation. FPO and FPO++
[
34
,
54
]
extend it to robotic control, but mainly focus on locomotion tasks. In comparison, RoboFFT studies forward-process finetuning in more challenging robotic manipulation, and covers more extensive settings including both diffusion and flow policies, VLA finetuning, and real world deployment with practical stabilization designs.

5.4
Evaluation on Real World
To evaluate the effectiveness of
RoboFFT
on real world robotic manipulation tasks, we integrate our method into a practical real-world RL framework
[
31
,
32
,
11
,

]
. However, directly applying PPO-style online optimization to real robots is challenging due to limited interaction budgets, slow data collection, and the absence of parallel environments. Inspired by RL100
[
26
]
, we therefore adapt
RoboFFT
to an offline-to-online formulation while retaining its core components including forward noising, the matching loss surrogate ratio, and PPO-style clipping. Specifically, we first pretrain a flow-based policy using human demonstrations collected via SpaceMouse teleoperation.
We then perform multiple offline RL iterations. In each offline iteration, we perform offline PPO-style optimization on the collected rollout data, where IQL
[
25
]
is used to estimate advantages from offline trajectories. After each offline RL update, we deploy the updated policy on the real robot to collect additional trajectories, which are added to the offline dataset for the next offline RL iteration. To stabilize policy improvement and avoid drifting away from reliable human behaviors, we combine the newly collected rollout data with the original teleoperation demonstrations and conduct imitation learning to update the base policy for the next iteration.
During the online RL phase, we continue PPO-style updates initialized from the offline actor and IQL critic. We use a sparse binary

6
Limitations
Although
RoboFFT
enables stable online finetuning of generative robot policies through the forward noising process, it still has several limitations. First, the weighted score/flow matching loss is only a surrogate for the true action log-likelihood, and its scale may vary across noise schedules, action dimensions, and policy architectures. Therefore, additional calibration such as temperature scaling is still needed to ensure stable PPO-style updates. Second, our current framework relies on on-policy PPO, which has limited data efficiency and cannot fully reuse historical trajectories. This makes real-world deployment challenging, especially when data collection is restricted to a single robot. Although offline-to-online paradigms such as RL100
[
26
]
can partially alleviate this issue, they usually require iterative data collection and offline retraining, which remains time-consuming in practice. Future work may explore more sample-efficient variants that better leverage historical trajectories and human intervention data for safer and faster real world robot learning.
7
Conclusion
We present
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies. By applying forward noising to sampled actions and using the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio,
RoboFFT
enables PPO-style policy optimization without requiring explicit likelihood estimation. Experiments on representative simulation benchmarks show that
RoboFFT
consistently improves popular generative robot policies on long-horizon and sparse-reward manipulation tasks, while achieving better training stability and efficiency. Further integration into a real world RL framework also demonstrates its effectiveness on real robot tasks.

B.1
Robomimic Benchmark
We use Robomimic
[
33
]
as the simulated manipulation benchmark throughout our main experiments. Robomimic provides sparse-reward robot manipulation tasks collected from human demonstrations, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating whether online finetuning can improve a behavior-cloned generative policy beyond its initial demonstration-trained performance. Following the data processing and environment conventions used in DPPO and ReinFlow
[
39
,
57
]
, we evaluate four Robomimic tasks: Lift, Can, Square, and Transport. The corresponding observation and action specifications are summarized in Table
1
.
The four tasks cover different manipulation difficulties. Lift requires the robot to grasp and lift an object, while Can is a pick-and-place task where the robot must manipulate a can into the target container. Square is a more precision-sensitive assembly task in which the robot must manipulate a square nut and place it onto a positioning peg. Transport is a long-horizon bimanual manipulation task that requires coordinated control of two robot arms to move an object across the workspace. Thus, the benchmark spans both short-horizon single-arm manipulation and longer-horizon bimanual manipulation.
We consider both state-input and pixel-input variants. In the state-input setting, the policy observes low-dimensional proprioceptive and object state features. In the pixel-input setting, the policy observes RGB image(s) at
96
×
96
96\times 96
resolution together with a compact proprioceptive state. Lift, Can, and Square use a single camera view, while Transport uses two camera views. For all tasks, the action is continuous. Lift, Can, and Square use a 7-dimensional action space, whereas Transport uses a 14-dimensional action space due to its bimanual control setup.
All Robomimic tasks use sparse rewards. We report success rate as the primary evaluation metric. The maximum episode length
T
max
T_{\max}
is task-dependent: 300 decision steps for Lift and Can, 400 for Square, and 800 for Transport. In online finetuning, the policy predicts action chunks and executes the first
H
exec

B.4
Baseline Methods and Configurations
We compare RoboFFT with representative online RL fine-tuning baselines for diffusion- and flow-based robot policies.
DPPO.
Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
[
39
]
is a representative reverse-process fine-tuning method for diffusion policies. It formulates the reverse denoising process together with the environment interaction process as a two-level MDP, and applies PPO to optimize the Gaussian likelihoods of denoising transitions. We use DPPO as the canonical diffusion-policy RL baseline for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
ReinFlow.
ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends the reverse-process policy-gradient paradigm to flow-based policies. It injects stochasticity into the deterministic flow trajectory, turns the sampler into a discrete-time Markov process with tractable Gaussian transition probabilities, and performs PPO-style optimization over the internal sampling trajectory. We use ReinFlow as the primary flow-policy baseline.
FPO.
Flow Policy Optimization
[
34
]
is a forward-process policy-gradient method that constructs a PPO-style surrogate ratio from conditional flow matching losses. We adapt FPO into our online fine-tuning codebase for Robomimic. To ensure fair comparison under the same tasks and pretrained policies, most environment and optimizer settings are shared with RoboFFT. The main algorithmic differences are that FPO does not use our SDE explorative sampling strategy and ratio-temperature calibration adopted in RoboFFT, while following the original FPO convention of using

DRWR.
DRWR is a lightweight diffusion reward-weighted regression baseline following the implementation convention in DPPO
[

. It performs forward-noise matching style updates weighted by rewards or returns, and serves as a simple forward-process reference that is architecturally close to our approach but does not use the PPO-style objective and the many critical designs introduced by our work.
For all baselines, we match the Robomimic environment wrappers, observation preprocessing, action chunking, base-policy training data, and evaluation protocol whenever applicable. The hyperparameters of DPPO, ReinFlow, and DRWR follow their original implementations unless a task-specific adaptation is necessary. Since the released ReinFlow manipulation implementation focuses on pixel-input Robomimic tasks, for state-input tasks we adapt secondary settings such as optimizer and update-batch configurations while keeping the core ReinFlow design unchanged. For fair comparison, the number of inference steps and finetuning steps are tuned on each task, so that each baseline achieves its nearly best performance. RoboFFT-F and RoboFFT-D are respectively implemented upon the ReinFlow

RoboFFT-F and RoboFFT-D share the same high-level forward-process policy-gradient principle: both apply forward noising to rollout actions and construct a PPO-style surrogate ratio from the corresponding score / flow matching loss. Appendix C
Additional Analyses for the Robomimic Experiments
C.1
Performance Analysis
This subsection provides additional discussion for the main Robomimic comparison in Sec.
5.1
, where the comprehensive performance of RoboFFT-F, RoboFFT-D and the baseline methods are evaluated under both state-input and pixel-input settings.
Across the easier
Lift
and
Can
tasks, RoboFFT-D and RoboFFT-F reach final success rates comparable to reverse-process baselines such as DPPO and ReinFlow. Their convergence can be slightly slower in some early-stage curves, but the final policy quality remains competitive. This suggests that the forward-process surrogate ratio preserves enough policy-gradient signal for improving already competent pretrained policies, while avoiding explicit likelihood computation through the reverse denoising chain.
The advantage of RoboFFT becomes more pronounced on the harder tasks. On
Square
and
Transport
, especially with pixel observations, RoboFFT shows a more sustained improvement trend and stronger final performance. Reverse-process methods can suffer from instability or later performance recession, likely because optimizing through a long internal sampling chain introduces a more complicated credit-assignment path and a heavier computation graph, making the gradients and parameter updates instable. In comparison, RoboFFT directly applies forward noising to the final rollout action and optimizes a matching-loss-based surrogate ratio, which keeps the optimization path closer to imitation pretraining.
The forward-process baselines, DRWR and FPO, are generally less competitive in the Robomimic manipulation setting. DRWR uses reward-weighted regression and does not include a PPO-style trust region, making it more sensitive to high-variance reward weights in sparse-reward tasks. FPO uses a forward-process PPO-style ratio, but in our implementation it lacks the manipulation-oriented stabilization designs used in RoboFFT, including controlled SDE exploration and ratio-temperature calibration. These differences help explain why simply applying a forward matching loss is not sufficient for robust online fine-tuning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.
