Appendix H
Extended Related Work
H.1
Generative Models for Robot Manipulation
Generative models have become an increasingly important policy class for robot manipulation, as they provide expressive distributions over complex and potentially multimodal action sequences. Early approaches
[
58
,
27
]
formulate imitation learning with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). More recently, diffusion-based policies have demonstrated substantially greater expressiveness for continuous control. Diffusion Policy
[
12
,
19
]
models the conditional action distribution through an iterative denoising process, enabling stable learning of high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions and motivating a broad family of diffusion-based manipulation policies. Flow-matching models provide an alternative generative formulation by learning continuous transport from a simple noise distribution to the action distribution. Methods such as ManiFlow
[
53
]
further improve sampling efficiency and policy expressiveness through consistency-based flow training, demonstrating strong performance on diverse manipulation tasks. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models have extended robot policies toward large-scale generalist control by leveraging pretrained vision-language representations and heterogeneous robot datasets. RT-2
[
6
]
and OpenVLA
[
22
]
generate discretized robot actions within large autoregressive vision-language models, while
π
0
\pi_{0}
[
4
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
18
]
combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation.
H.2
RL for Generative Robot Policy
Reinforcement learning has been increasingly explored to improve generative policies beyond behavior cloning. Early studies mainly focus on offline RL with fixed datasets. Diffusion Q Learning
[
49
]
parameterizes the actor as a diffusion model and combines diffusion regression with Q value maximization, while IDQL
[
14
]
uses an implicit Q-function to select actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy. This idea has also been extended to flow-based policies. Flow Q Learning (FQL)
[
36
]
learns a flow matching behavior policy together with a one-step RL policy, avoiding recursive differentiation through iterative flow generation. Although these methods exploit the expressiveness of generative policies, their improvement is constrained by the coverage of the offline dataset and the accuracy of learned value functions.
More recent work considers online or offline-to-online adaptation of pretrained generative robot policies. One direction keeps the base policy frozen and learns a lightweight steering or residual component. DSRL
[
47
]
performs RL in the latent-noise space of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy without modifying its parameters, while residual RL methods learn corrective actions on top of a frozen behavior cloning policy
[
2
,
44
,
20
]
. These approaches preserve pretrained behaviors and reduce the complexity of online optimization, but restrict policy improvement to the residual or latent space exposed by the frozen policy.
In contrast, full policy finetuning directly updates the generative model parameters. DPPO
[
39
]
formulates diffusion denoising as a multi-step MDP and applies PPO over reverse denoising transitions. ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends likelihood-based online optimization to flow policies by injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow trajectories. Forward process methods such as FPO
[
34
]
and its extensions
[
54
]
instead construct policy-gradient objectives from flow matching losses, avoiding explicit marginal likelihood computation. Reinforced finetuning has also been extended to VLA policies, with
[
11
,
51
]
combining offline value learning and online policy optimization for real-world manipulation. RoboFFT belongs to the full policy finetuning family, but performs PPO-style optimization through the forward noising process, providing a unified framework for diffusion, flow, and VLA policies.

article.headline: 用前向加噪给生成式机器人策略做在线RL微调
article.lede: RoboFFT 把前向加噪的匹配损失当作代理似然，让扩散与流式机器人策略无需精确似然即可做 PPO 式在线微调。
article.problem: 扩散、流匹配等生成式机器人策略靠模仿学习训练，受示范质量不高与部署时分布漂移的限制，继续提升往往需要更多专家数据。在线强化学习可直接最大化任务奖励，但这类策略的动作分布由迭代采样隐式给出，精确似然不可解，PPO 所需的策略比率难以直接计算。现有做法把反向去噪链视作多步马尔可夫决策过程来优化，计算与显存开销大，长去噪链还容易带来梯度不稳定，在高维、长程操作任务上尤为明显。
article.method: RoboFFT 不在反向去噪链上分配信用，而是对采样出的动作重新做前向加噪，复用预训练时的加权 score／流匹配损失，把它当作替代负对数似然来构造策略比率，再套用 PPO 的裁剪目标。对确定性采样的流策略，作者在采样过程中注入噪声，将其变为 Euler-Maruyama SDE 采样器以提供可控探索；训练中用蒙特卡洛多次采样估计匹配损失、并用比率温度系数重新标定比率的尺度。真机部署时改为离线到在线流程：先用 IQL 从离线轨迹估计优势做离线 PPO 式更新，再切换到在线微调。
article.results: 在 Robomimic 的 Lift、Can、Square、Transport 四个稀疏奖励任务（state 与 pixel 输入）上，RoboFFT 的最终成功率与反向过程基线相当或更好，在更难的任务上更稳；效率上 RoboFFT-F 相对 ReinFlow 平均训练时间加速 1.53×，RoboFFT-D 在四个 state 输入任务上相对 DPPO 平均加速 38.0×（其蒙特卡洛样本数 N_mc=16）。以 ReinFlow 式闭式比率为参考，每轮取 2048 个动作块比较，Spearman 秩相关仅约 0.2，但训练末期至少 90% 的动作块相对误差低于 5%。VLA 实验中把方法接到 3.3B 参数的 π0 上，在 LIBERO-Object 与 LIBERO-Spatial 上稳定优于预训练策略、与 πRL 大体相当。真机四个任务各 20 次试验的成功率从预训练到离线再到在线分别为：pick eggplant 12/20→18/20→20/20，peg insertion 10/20→19/20→20/20，pour 9/20→15/20→18/20，cabinet retrieval 5/20→14/20→17/20；同一数据预算下 pick eggplant 上 BC 聚合为 14/20、DRWR 为 12/20、离线 RoboFFT 为 18/20、在线为 20/20。
article.why_it_matters: 它把生成式策略的强化学习微调从「沿整条去噪链反传」改成「复用预训练损失」，在长程、稀疏奖励的操作任务上更省算力也更稳，并已验证可扩展到十亿参数级 VLA 与真实机器人。
article.limitations: 加权 score／流匹配损失只是真实动作似然的代理，其数值尺度会随噪声调度、动作维度和策略结构变化，仍必须靠温度标定等手段才能稳定 PPO 更新；论文自己也指出代理比率与参考比率的秩相关只有约 0.2。此外框架依赖 on-policy PPO，数据效率有限、无法充分利用历史轨迹，真机场景需借助离线到在线的反复采数据与重训，实际仍然耗时。
article.figure_caption_zh: RoboFFT 流程：先用遥操作数据与匹配损失预训练基座策略，再用 SDE 采样器生成动作并从环境获得奖励，最后对动作前向加噪、复用匹配损失作为替代似然完成 PPO 式更新。

figure.caption: Overview of {RoboFFT}. We first collect the offline data leveraging teleoperation and pretrain the base policy with the score / flow matching loss. The pretrained policy then generates actions using an SDE sampler and receives reward feedback from the environment. Finally, we apply forward noising and reuse the matching loss as a surrogate likelihood for PPO-style policy update.

page_papers.title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
page_papers.abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes. The source code is publicly available at https://mias.group/MaSS.
page_papers.content:
Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable
Mengtan Zhang   Yuchuan Cui   Yu Ma   Zizhan Guo   Wei Ye   Rui FanTongji University
Abstract
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation is appealing for its potential to scale with unlabeled data, yet existing methods often degrade when trained on diverse scenes. This study finds that, under self-supervision, models tend to encode dataset-specific structural biases rather than transferable scene geometry, leading to cross-domain optimization conflicts. To address this issue, this study proposes the MaSS framework, aiming to make self-supervised depth learning scalable to diverse data. MaSS introduces a dedicated structural representation pathway explicitly decoupled from contextual features, which is guided by a novel scene-structure discrimination objective to learn generalized, layout-aware structural representations for depth decoding. Trained and evaluated on four diverse datasets, both individually and jointly, MaSS substantially outperforms prior self-supervised methods and is the first to consistently benefit from mixed-domain training. Zero-shot evaluation on eight additional datasets further demonstrates its remarkable generalizability, particularly on those entirely out-of-distribution scenes.
The source code is publicly available at
https://mias.group/MaSS
.

1
Introduction
The fundamental advantage of self-supervised learning lies in its potential to leverage ubiquitous unlabeled data for scalable model training. However, most existing self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SSMDE) research
[
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
]
is predominantly confined to training models individually on single datasets or scenarios, leaving much of this potential unexplored. Recent efforts have attempted to directly train models with existing SSMDE methods on large-scale video sequences curated from online platforms
[
6
,
7
]
, as well as to incorporate vision foundation models (VFMs) as backbones
[
8
,
7
]
. Despite these advances, overall performance improvements remain limited. As demonstrated by our preliminary experiments (see Fig.
1
(b)), when existing methods are trained simultaneously on diverse monocular video data (
e.g.
, indoor, outdoor, dynamic, and adverse weather scenarios), they fail to benefit mutually from the increased diversity and do not exhibit improved generalization to out-of-distribution scenes. Instead, we observe a performance decline compared to models trained individually on a single dataset. This observation demonstrates that existing SSMDE methods have not yet achieved effective scalability to diverse data.
This study begins by investigating the challenges that arise when SSMDE is exposed to diverse data distributions during training. It is worth noting that the novel-view synthesis-based supervision inevitably introduces noisy and artifact-laden supervisory signals in scenarios involving occlusions, textureless regions, and illumination changes
[
9
,
10
]
. Even setting aside such noise, the gradients induced by self-supervised losses often fail to reflect depth errors faithfully
[
4
]
. As a result, the optimization process is inherently prone to local minima, leading to poor convergence stability
[
4
]
. Although these challenges frequently occur during self-supervised training, existing methods can still achieve reasonable accuracy on a single, homogeneous dataset
[
3
]
. This is largely because the network can exploit the structural bias inherent to that dataset, thereby compensating for weak supervision. The key evidence we find is that under the existing SSMDE framework, the coarsest, high-level feature of the depth encoder does not capture depth-related cues, such as the foreground–background relation and perspective geometry. Instead, it primarily reflects the dataset-specific structural biases. When training on diverse datasets, different data domains often require the model to learn inconsistent structural biases for their respective convergence, leading to the observed performance drop.
These findings motivate us to explicitly guide the network to learn a robust, generalized scene-structure representation for depth decoding. Based on this core idea, we develop the
MaSS
framework that
Ma
ke
S
elf-supervised depth learning
S
calable to diverse data. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM through a bidirectional interaction architecture, drawing inspiration from
[
11
]
. In this design, the depth encoder focuses on extracting geometric cues that are difficult to recover from VFM features
[
8
]
. The interacted VFM features are then fed into two feature projectors to reconstruct complementary, collapse-free representations under explicit constraints and learning objectives. Specifically, one projector is adapted to learn a contextual representation informative for depth estimation, such as object-level spatial relationships, while retaining generalized semantics with the original VFM features as anchors. The other projector is then constrained to be decoupled from the contextual one, thereby reserving its representational capacity for scene structure.
To explicitly define this representation, we introduce a scene-structure discrimination objective via contrastive learning. This objective organizes the feature space based on scene layout similarity, which is measured by the histogram distribution of predicted depth. Driven by this objective, the second projector learns transferable structural representations that capture global scene layout and perspective geometry, rather than dataset-specific biases. Together, these two complementary representations enable more reliable depth predictions while reducing their reliance on dataset-specific biases.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that MaSS outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SoTA) self-supervised methods by a large margin (as presented in Fig.
1
(a)) and achieves accuracy comparable to certain supervised depth foundation models. Moreover, MaSS represents the first self-supervised approach to achieve clear performance gains from increasing the diversity of training data (Fig.
1
(b)), resulting in notable generalizability improvements particularly on out-of-distribution scenes (Fig.
1
(c)).
2
Related Works
To alleviate the reliance on extensive ground-truth data in monocular depth estimation (MDE), SSMDE from monocular video, first introduced in the study
[
12
]
, has attracted growing attention. Within this paradigm, improvements have focused on enhancing photometric supervision
[
1
]
, addressing scale inconsistency
[
13
]
, and incorporating additional visual cues to handle occlusions and dynamic scenes
[
14
,
3
,
15
,
16
,
4
]
.
Though significant progress has been made, these SSMDE methods are typically trained on single domains with limited-scale datasets and rely on task-specific network architectures
[
17
,
18
,
19
,
20
]
. The study
[
21
]
first demonstrates the feasibility of self-supervised depth learning from heterogeneous in-the-wild videos by jointly estimating depth, camera motion, object motion, and camera intrinsics. With the rise of VFMs
[
22
,
23
]
, increasing efforts have been devoted to developing depth foundation models (DFMs)
[
24
,
25
,
26
]
trained on large-scale annotated data, achieving strong performance and generalization.
Building upon this trend, recent studies
[
6
,
7
]
have taken initial steps toward scaling SSMDE training, while the others
[
9
,
27
,
5
]
demonstrate that developing DFMs in a self-supervised fashion requires not only harnessing the large pretrained models’ capacity, but also addressing challenges unique to self-supervised learning. Among them, cross-domain learning conflicts under mixed-domain training pose a fundamental yet underexplored obstacle to scalability, which this work primarily aims to address.
Three lines of research inform our approach. The first draws on pretrained knowledge to improve depth representations. For example, the study
[
28
]
uses a pretrained semantic network to guide the learning of geometric features. The studies
[
29
,
30
]
further emphasize preserving transferable pretrained representations during adaptation. The second focuses on organizing depth representations. The prior arts
[
31
,
32
,
33
,
27
]
have introduced contrastive objectives that structure the feature space according to weather variations, color or geometric consistency, historical predictions, and relationships guided by language. The third conditions depth prediction distributions on scene characteristics to account for domain shifts. For example, the study
[
34
]
conditions these distributions on scene categories. Drawing on these insights, MaSS explicitly decouples contextual and structural representations, preserves contextual relationships derived from VFMs, and adaptively organizes structural features according to similarities in scene layout. Depth prediction is then conditioned on the resulting structural representations to reduce learning conflicts across domains.
Figure 2:
Feature activation map comparison among a conventional self-supervised depth model, DINOv2, and the two representations learned by MaSS. (a) The conventional depth model tends to encode dataset-specific biases, whereas (b) DINOv2 lacks sufficient geometric cues. In contrast, MaSS decouples features into contextual and structural representations: (c) contextual ones capture fine-grained object details and foreground–background relations; (d) structural ones encode global scene layouts that are transferable across diverse datasets.
3
Methodology
SSMDE models are prone to learning dataset-specific inductive biases and struggle to generalize across varying depth distributions during both training and inference. For example, Fig.
1
(c) presents depth predictions on out-of-distribution indoor and outdoor scenes from two representative self-supervised depth models
[
3
,
4
]
, trained on the NYUv2
[
35
]
and KITTI
[
36
]
datasets, respectively. It can be observed that the model trained on driving scenes tends to predict depth with a vanishing point, while the model trained on small rooms fails to capture the more uniform depth distributions in large halls. To find the source of such inductive biases, we investigate the internal feature representations. As shown in Fig.
2
(a), the DepthNet encoder
[
4
]
trained on driving data produces feature activation maps with a consistent low-activation region. This pattern closely resembles the biased depth predictions in Fig.
1
(c) and fails to reflect variations aligned with the actual scene geometry. These results indicate that the dataset-specific inductive biases are already embedded in the intermediate representations. The above findings inspire us with a possible solution to make self-supervised learning scalable: explicitly guide the network to learn robust, generalized structural representations that are discriminative of scene layout before decoding depth.
Figure 3:
The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework.
MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.
3.1
MaSS Model
The first restriction of existing approaches towards this goal is from the model architecture design.
Although the pretrained VFM (
e.g.
, DINOv2
[
22
]
) exhibits strong generalization and is widely adopted as initialization for supervised depth foundation models
[
24
,
37
,
38
]
, its adaptation is unreliable under self-supervision due to noisy training signals
[
9
]
. Direct fine-tuning may deteriorate the pretrained representations
[
39
]
, yet keeping the VFM frozen leaves its semantic features containing less sufficient geometric cues for structural modeling
[
8
]
(as seen in Fig.
2
(b)). This dilemma motivates a bidirectional interaction architecture between a trainable traditional depth encoder and a frozen VFM encoder, drawing on the ViT-Adapter design
[
11

Another key observation is that different viewpoints of the same scene, or different scenes containing similar objects, may appear contextually alike yet differ substantially in spatial structure. Conversely, visually distinct scenes can share similar structural layouts.
Such misalignment suggests that entangling contextual and structural features within a single representation pathway may lead to representational conflict and collapse.

Implementation details.
The MaSS model utilizes the pre-trained DINOv2 ViT-B/14 architecture

The proposed scene-structure discrimination objective operates on the depth predictions to formulate supervision for representation learning.

Mixed dataset training.
While our models achieve strong results when trained on individual datasets, such settings do not reflect the scalability challenges posed by large-scale and diverse training data, which constitute the primary focus of this work.
To this end, we further conduct comparative experiments in a mixed-dataset training setting. Specifically, each training batch is assembled by randomly sampling data from four datasets, thereby simulating a realistic, large-scale training scenario with substantial data diversity. To maintain a comparable number of training iterations to the individual-dataset setting, the number of training epochs is reduced to one-third. Under this setting, we reproduce several SoTA methods

4.4
Ablation Study
Efficacy of each innovative component.
To verify that the three key components of MaSS for learning generalizable structural representations are all indispensable, we conduct ablation studies in Table
4
(a).
Removing (a1) the contrastive learning objective eliminates explicit supervision for structural representation learning, leading to a significant performance drop, particularly on zero-shot datasets.
Removing (a2) the specialized structural pathway for representation decoupling prevents the model from preserving contextual information while learning structure, resulting in consistent degradation across all datasets.
Removing (a3) the interaction architecture forces the model to learn structural representations directly from DINOv2 features, which lack sufficient geometric cues, and thus causes a substantial performance decline.
Superiority over alternative designs.
MaSS builds upon well-established components such as DINOv2
[
22
]
and ViT-Adapter
[
11
]
, making it important to verify that the superior performance stems from our design rather than from simply adopting these components. To this end, we compare MaSS with several plausible alternative configurations in Table
4
(b):
(b1) directly fine-tuning a DPT
[
59
]
head with a frozen pretrained DINOv2 backbone,
(b2) fully fine-tuning the entire DINOv2–DPT architecture, and
(b3) incorporating ViT-Adapter while fine-tuning both the adapter and the DPT head.
Results show that MaSS outperforms all these alternative designs by a large margin. This confirms our analysis that effective scaling of self-supervised depth learning requires explicitly modeling scene structure, rather than relying solely on stronger pretrained backbones.
Effect of VFM backbone.
As demonstrated in Table
4
(c), replacing the VFM backbone with a stronger self-supervised pretrained model (DINOv3
[
30
]
) leads to only marginal performance changes. This result corroborates our earlier analysis that pretrained VFMs in our framework mainly provide generalizable semantic priors and are not directly responsible for depth decoding.
This naturally raises a follow-up question: since pretrained depth or geometry foundation models encode rich geometric priors, can MaSS benefit from them, or even further enhance such models?
We investigate this question in the

5
Conclusion
This study revisited self-supervised depth estimation from the perspective of large-scale, mix-domain training and prediction,
recognizing that the model’s tendency to capture dataset-specific structural bias is the key barrier.
MaSS addressed this by coupling a depth encoder with a pretrained VFM and explicitly decoupling the structural representations from the contextual ones to learn scene-generalized structural representations via contrastive learning.
MaSS achieved SoTA accuracy and remarkable out-of-distribution generalization, demonstrating improved scalability with larger and more diverse data.

Figure S1:
Quantitative analyses of the proposed scene-structure discrimination objective for structural representation learning.
A.1
Details of Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures
In the main paper, we define a structural discrepancy metric to determine positive and negative samples within a training batch, thereby formulating a scene-structure discrimination objective for learning structural representations. To illustrate how the metric functions and how the objective guides representation learning, we present several quantitative examples in Fig.
S1
.
The key observations from Fig.
S1
can be summarized as follows:
(1) Our method does not trivially treat each sample as the sole positive instance, nor does it degenerate into discriminating samples based on coarse scene categories (
e.g.
, indoor vs. outdoor).
As shown in Fig.
S1
(a), Sample ① is an outdoor scene but is not considered positive relative to other outdoor samples; this is because its structural layout—a narrow passage flanked by cars and buildings—differs from more open outdoor environments. Fig.
S1
(b) provides an inverse case, where a wide-open outdoor scene (Sample ①) is correctly distinguished from narrow outdoor passages. These observations are further supplemented by Sample ⑥ in Fig.
S1
(c).
Moreover, our method captures shared structural properties across scene categories. For instance, in Fig.
S1
(d), the outdoor scene in Sample ⑥ forms positive pairs with multiple indoor samples due to their similar structure. Similarly, in Fig.
S1
(e), the indoor library aisle (Sample ①) is identified as positive relative to outdoor samples ③, ⑤, and ⑥, which share the “narrow corridor” structure. Meanwhile, it remains negative to the room scene of Sample ②. These results demonstrate that our model prioritizes underlying structural similarity over nominal scene labels.
(2) The hyperparameters of the proposed structural discrepancy metric, together with the masking strategy, effectively identify meaningful contrastive relationships. As visualized in the Discrepancy Metric and Pos./Neg. Mask columns, the resulting similarity maps align well with the expected structural relationships described in the above analysis. Meanwhile, the threshold used in our implementation effectively determines the positive and negative sample pairs accordingly.
(3) Finally, within the MaSS framework, the specialized pathway effectively learns structural representations that are discriminative with respect to different scene structures. This is evidenced by the strong consistency between the feature similarities of the learned structural representations and the in-batch structural discrepancy relationships computed from the predicted depth maps.

Compared with commonly used indoor benchmarks, the indoor subset spans a larger depth range, while the outdoor subset also mainly consists of closer-range scenes rather than typical driving environments.
A.5

We provide a quantitative analysis of the data distributions across all datasets used in this work to better illustrate how our approach improves the scalability of self-supervised depth learning and enhances model generalizability.
As shown in Fig.

Notably, while nuScenes shares a relatively similar depth distribution with KITTI, its RGB distribution differs significantly.

Instead, the performance degradation is largely attributed to appearance shifts, revealing the limited robustness of conventional encoder architectures with restricted pretraining. In contrast, our method learns robust and transferable contextual and structural representations from diverse appearance distributions, substantially improving generalization in depth estimation.

B.3
Generalizability Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
While the previously discussed OOD datasets demonstrate the strong generalization capability of our model, their diversity and domain shift relative to the training data remain limited. To further evaluate robustness, we collect a set of in-the-wild images from online repositories and mobile photography, covering a wide range of real-world challenges.
As illustrated in Fig.
S4
, the first three rows (a–c) present unstructured natural scenes. Notably, (a) and (c) contain specular reflections on water surfaces, while (b) includes dense vegetation with high-frequency textures.
Rows (d–f) exhibit complex geometries and structures that differ significantly from standard urban or indoor benchmarks, such as the detailed roof tiles in (e) and the repetitive grid structure in (f).
Row (g) includes power lines to evaluate the model’s ability to estimate thin structures.
Rows (h–j) further evaluate model robustness under extreme lighting and motion blur conditions. In particular, row (j) presents a challenging case with strong visual ambiguity at a road junction caused by shadows and lighting effects.
Qualitative comparisons are conducted among SC-DepthV3
[
3
]
(trained on NYUv2), SC-DepthV3
†
, Jasmine
[
9
]
(trained on KITTI), and MaSS
†
. As shown in Fig.
S4
, SC-DepthV3 performs unsatisfactorily on complex and unseen structures and tends to interpret scenes with an indoor bias. When trained under the mixed-dataset setting, SC-DepthV3
†
further deteriorates, suffering from severe structural confusion caused by the diverse training data. Jasmine represents one of the strongest self-supervised generative depth models. Although it produces detailed predictions and exhibits improved generalization due to diffusion priors, extreme RGB domain shifts can cause the diffusion process to become unstable and produce depth predictions with significant errors. In contrast, our method remains robust across these challenging in-the-wild scenes, producing depth predictions with both fine-grained details and consistent structural layouts.
Figure S4:
Qualitative monocular depth estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
Figure S5:
Qualitative monocular reconstruction estimation results on in-the-wild, out-of-distribution data.
B.4
Geometric Fidelity Evaluation on In-the-Wild Data.
Since ground-truth depth is unavailable for these in-the-wild images, quantitative evaluation is infeasible. Instead, we assess the geometric correctness of the predicted depth through monocular 3D reconstruction.
We compare our method with two representative monocular reconstruction approaches, VGGT
[
38
]
and MoGe
[
62
]
. To evaluate geometric fidelity, we synthesize novel viewpoints with slight viewpoint changes relative to the original image. As shown in Fig.
S5
, VGGT produces relatively noisy depth maps on these in-the-wild scenes, leading to noticeable artifacts in the reconstructed geometry. MoGe represents one of the most robust monocular reconstruction foundation models, benefiting from strong geometric supervision during training, and achieves high-quality reconstructions in most cases, with only minor local inconsistencies observed in (b)-(d). Our method, benefiting from the inherent geometric constraints of self-supervised learning as well as effective scaling with diverse training data, achieves reconstruction results comparable to these prior approaches, with significantly less training data. These results highlight the potential of self-supervised methods for building versatile “DepthAnything”-style models from ubiquitous unlabeled data.
Appendix C
Discussion and Future Work
In addition to increasing the training data scale, as discussed in Sect.
4.5
, the scalability of SSMDE also depends on the availability of diverse and suitable training data.
Although self supervision enables learning from imagery collected in the wild, systematically curated datasets covering diverse scenes remain scarce. Existing methods therefore still rely heavily on commonly used datasets originally collected for supervised learning. Constraints imposed by data collection platforms (
e.g.
, vehicles, handheld devices, or UAVs), together with the high cost of sensor calibration and annotation, often limit these datasets to relatively homogeneous scenes, such as typical indoor rooms and common driving environments. This limited diversity may constrain the potential benefits of self-supervision. Such limited diversity may even reduce the potential advantages of self-supervised learning. Systematically curating large and diverse datasets from imagery collected in the wild is therefore a promising direction for advancing SSMDE and extending the benefits of self-supervision to other vision tasks.

article.headline: MaSS解耦场景结构，让自监督深度估计可扩展
article.lede: MaSS把深度特征解耦为上下文与结构两路，用场景结构判别的对比学习抑制数据集偏置，首次让混合域自监督训练不再掉点。
article.problem: 自监督单目深度估计理论上能随无标注数据规模扩张，但现有方法基本只在单一数据集上训练。作者发现，在自监督下模型倾向编码数据集特有的结构偏置而非可迁移的几何：在驾驶数据上训练的模型编码器会产出固定低激活区域，预测深度时带上消失点式的分布；在室内小房间上训练的模型则无法处理大厅更均匀的深度分布。把多个域的数据混在一起训练时，这些互相冲突的偏置导致性能反而不如各自单独训练。
article.method: MaSS用一个双向交互模块，把可训练的传统深度编码器与冻结的DINOv2 ViT-B/14连接起来，再把交互后的VFM特征送入一对「锚定—解耦」投影器，分别产出上下文与结构两路表示。作者用锚定项让上下文表示保留VFM跨样本的语义关系，用解耦项迫使结构支路只学互补的几何线索。结构支路的学习信号是一个场景结构判别目标：把预测深度图下采样8倍、用20个软分箱统计深度直方图，以对称KL散度衡量样本间的布局差异，相似度超过阈值0.95的样本构成正样本对，再做多正样本InfoNCE对比学习。
article.results: 在四个数据集上单独训练时，MaSS在KITTI取得Abs Rel 0.094、δ1 0.909，DDAD 0.128/0.845，NYUv2 0.109/0.868，nuScenes 0.139/0.851，均优于表中列出的此前自监督方法。在同一批次内随机混合四个数据集训练后，MaSS进一步降到KITTI 0.092/0.913、DDAD 0.125/0.862、NYUv2 0.104/0.890、nuScenes 0.134/0.852，而对比方法混合训练后普遍明显下降（如DCPI-Depth在NYUv2从0.151恶化到0.331）。八个额外数据集的零样本评测中，混合训练的MaSS在Waymo为0.123/0.867、Cityscapes 0.103/0.896、DIML 0.104/0.890，DIODE为0.289/0.736。消融显示去掉对比学习目标后Waymo Abs Rel从0.123升到0.163，去掉交互结构后升到0.190。模型93.2M参数、81.6G FLOPs、150K训练样本，单张RTX 4090、批大小6约需2.5天。再加入50K TartanAir样本（150K→200K）后，DIML与DIODE等更难分布外域上Abs Rel与δ1平均改善+4.3%和+3.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「混合域训练反而更差」这一自监督深度的 scalability 障碍明确归因到结构表示的缺失，并给出一个可复现的解法：不换更强的骨干、不堆标注，而是显式约束特征的解耦与判别。对想用海量无标注视频训练深度模型的团队，这是一条比直接微调VFM更可行的路线。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认，可扩展性证据仍是初步的：训练规模只到200K样本，与Depth Anything、MoGe等监督基础模型使用的百万级数据相差很远，更大数据量下是否仍成立尚未验证。此外MaSS在标准室内数据集上仍落后于监督深度基础模型，场景结构判别目标还需要额外一个epoch的初始化才能启用；而且论文中与KBR系列等方法的数值对比受Median与逆深度域LSQ对齐方式差异影响，跨方法比较并非完全等价。
article.figure_caption_zh: MaSS框架总览：通过双向交互模块把传统深度编码器与冻结的预训练VFM相连，交互后的特征经一对锚定—解耦投影器生成不塌缩的上下文与结构表示，结构支路靠判别场景结构学到可泛化的表示。

figure.caption: The overall architecture of the proposed MaSS framework. MaSS bridges a conventional depth encoder with a frozen pretrained VFM via a bidirectional interaction module. The interacted VFM features are fed into a pair of anchored–decoupled feature projectors, producing collapse-free contextual and structural representations. The structural projectors learn generalized representations from discriminating scene structures, making the self-supervised depth learning scalable.

page_papers.title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
page_papers.abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
page_papers.content:
SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
Efthymios Tsaprazlis  Bowen Yi   Tiantian Feng
Email:
tsaprazl@usc.edu
Junghwan Kim   David Jurgens   Shrikanth Narayanan
University of Southern California   University of Michigan
Abstract
Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce
SPARC
(Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
1
1
1
Our code and data are available at
https://huggingface.co/datasets/timtsapras23/SPARC
and
https://github.com/bowenyi-pierre/SPARC
.
1
Introduction
Conversational language is one of the most abundant forms of personal data. People speak to voice assistants, dictate messages, attend recorded meetings, and publish podcasts; even much social-media text approaches the register of speech. Regulatory frameworks have responded to the acoustic side of this reality: under the GDPR
Regulation (2016)
, voice recordings constitute biometric personal data, and voiceprint-based speaker recognition is treated as a well-understood re-identification risk
(
Nautsch et al., 2019
;
Tigunova et al., 2020
)
. Far less attention has been paid to what lies beyond acoustic signals, to the words and phrases themselves, and how language is being used.
Transcription is often understood as separating
what
was said from
how
it sounded, and this distinction carries privacy weight: once pitch, timbre, and other acoustic characteristics are removed, conventional speaker-recognition systems no longer apply. Yet a transcript preserves word choice, syntax, discourse markers, and conversational habits, and these linguistic traces may suffice to link an anonymous transcript to a known speaker or to infer sensitive characteristics of that speaker
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
)
. Prior work shows that speakers can be distinguished in human-transcribed conversations and that attribution survives ASR errors
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
;
Aggazzotti et al., 2025
)
, but reports that performance declines under conversational topic controls. Whether this pattern holds against modern LLM adversaries, and whether
demographic attribute labels
can be verified alongside identity, remain open questions.
To answer them, we introduce
SPARC
(Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a transcript-privacy benchmark built from two large-scale podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent. SPARC pairs speaker- and attribute-verification trials under a unified protocol, using episode- and metadata-based topic proxies to assess speaker-linked information in transcripts.
Our comprehensive benchmark results show that transcribed speech
retains speaker-linked information.
Overall, embedding-based attackers degrade in the within-episode condition (0.350 to 0.460 EER, approaching the 0.5 chance rate), but LLM adversaries retain speaker-verification signal in the same setting (0.322–0.345 EER) and reach 0.253–0.285 EER in the cross-episode condition on both corpora. Moreover, LLMs detect agreement on inferred sex and accent labels more reliably than the embedding models, while age-label agreement stays near chance. We further trace how leakage scales with the adversary’s resources. Shortening the exposed probe text degrades the strongest attackers the most. Even an adversary with extensive reference material is bottlenecked by the probe. Limiting the amount of released text is thus a partial mitigation, although it attenuates rather than eliminates leakage. Finally, we show that average-case metrics could misstate the threat. Specifically, at a 1% false-positive rate, two LLMs with nearly identical AUC and EER differ by more than
2
×
2\times
in the fraction of positive trials they accept, so the models that matter most for privacy are not captured by AUC or EER alone.
Our contributions are: (i) SPARC, a large-scale benchmark dataset for pairwise speaker and attribute-label verification in transcribed natural speech, with standardized trials across probe-length and enrollment budgets; (ii) a systematic evaluation of embedding-based and LLM adversaries showing that LLMs retain speaker-verification signal under episode-context controls; (iii) evidence that attribute-label agreement remains difficult to verify, though LLMs detect a coarse sex- and accent-label signal; (iv) ablations showing that limiting exposed text degrades LLM attackers even under extensive enrollment, offering a practical but partial mitigation; and (v) a low-FPR analysis demonstrating that average-case metrics mischaracterize trial-level linkage risk, with implications for how transcript privacy should be evaluated.
2
Related Work
2.1
Text-Based Authorship Attribution and Verification
Recent authorship attribution and verification systems learn author representations that transfer across documents and domains. LUAR, for instance, learns general-purpose author embeddings for open-set verification
(
Rivera-Soto et al., 2021
)
. A persistent concern is that such representations may encode what an author discusses rather than how they use language, motivating content-independent style representations, topic-regularized training, and probing studies that separate stylistic from topical information
(
Wegmann et al., 2022
;
Sawatphol et al., 2022
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
. Most recently, LLMs have been applied to zero-shot, end-to-end verification and, beyond pairwise verification, to identity linking, extracting identity-relevant cues from unstructured profiles to retrieve candidate users across platforms
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Lermen et al., 2026
)
.
A parallel line of work provides datasets and benchmarks for authorship analysis. VALLA standardizes datasets, splits, and metrics to compare attribution and verification methods
(
Tyo et al., 2023
)
, and RAVEN tests whether verification models exploit topic-dependent shortcuts
(
Sawatphol et al., 2024
)
. Closer to our setting, HANSEN aggregates 17 human speech-transcript datasets, along with AI-generated spoken text, for attribution, verification, and human–AI detection
(
Tripto et al., 2023
)
. Most directly,
Aggazzotti et al. (2024)
construct speaker-verification trials from human-transcribed conversations and find that performance declines once conversational topic is controlled; follow-up work examines how ASR errors affect transcript-based attribution
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2025
)
. Text-only verification on VoicePrivacy data also reveals speaker-linked cues, partly through semantic keyword overlap
(
Gaznepoglu et al., 2025
)
. SPARC complements these resources with large-scale, naturally occurring podcast transcripts, episode- and metadata-based controls, and a single protocol to evaluate speaker verification and attribute-label agreement.
2.2
Personal Attribute Inference from Text
Early efforts in author profiling focused on developing feature-based and neural classifiers for age and gender prediction, such as in the PAN author-profiling shared tasks
(
Rangel et al., 2013
)
.
Recent work reframes this capability as a privacy risk:
Staab et al. (2024)
show on PersonalReddit, a manually annotated dataset of 520 real Reddit profiles with eight attributes, that pretrained LLMs can infer personal information from text without relying on verbatim training-data memorization. Because the underlying profiles are sensitive, the dataset is not publicly released, making dataset construction a central challenge in this area. RedDust labels more than 300,000 Reddit users with profession, hobby, family status, age, and gender using high-precision self-disclosure patterns
(
Tigunova et al., 2020
)
, while SynthPAI uses LLM agents seeded with synthetic profiles to generate over 7,800 Reddit-like comments annotated with personal attributes, yielding a public, privacy-preserving benchmark whose conclusions are validated against real data
(
Yukhymenko et al., 2024
)
. These resources offer either broad scale or wide attribute inventories, but all concern authored social-media text, leaving attribute leakage in transcribed speech unexplored.
2.3
Speech and Text Anonymization
VoicePrivacy studies acoustic anonymization while preserving linguistic content
(
Tomashenko et al., 2024
)
. Text-anonymization work evaluates authorship obfuscation and privacy–utility trade-offs
(
Loiseau et al., 2025a
;
Loiseau et al., 2025b
;
Loiseau et al., 2026
;
Aggazzotti et al., 2026
)
. SPARC evaluates existing transcripts rather than transforming them.
3
Dataset
3.1
Source Corpora
The SPARC dataset is drawn from two publicly available large-scale English podcast datasets.
NaturalVoices
(
Du et al., 2025
)
is a dataset of 5,049 hours of spontaneous podcast speech sourced from MSP-Podcast recordings, including meta-information at the utterance level with speaker identity, sex, speech quality, and transcripts. In total, the dataset has over 2,670 speakers across 6,790 episodes. We use only single-speaker speech segments from episodes released with a CC-BY 4.0 license, and we adopt the age and sex labels provided in the original metadata.
SPoRC
(
Litterer et al., 2025
)
consists of over 1.1 million English podcast episodes collected from public RSS feeds between May and June 2020. Furthermore, it has a machine-diarized subset of over 220,000 hours that identifies 386,000 hosts and 535,000 guests. Because SPoRC does not provide utterance-level speaker metadata, we use its provided single-speaker episode subset. To control speech volume variation, we retain only the middle 50% of episodes by transcript word count. We derive all demographic labels through automatic inference using speech data (Section
3.3
). Together, NaturalVoices offers richer utterance-level annotations, and the retained SPoRC subset broadens speaker and episode coverage.

3.3
Speaker Attribute Inference
For NaturalVoices, we take the age and sex labels from the dataset, which are inferred by a pretrained model
Burkhardt et al. (2023)
. For SPoRC, we infer age and sex using Vox-Profile
Feng et al. (2025b)
, a speech foundation-model benchmark that provides state-of-the-art classifiers for speaker traits. Accent labels in NaturalVoices and SPoRC are inferred with Voxlect
Feng et al. (2025a)
, a benchmark for dialect classification including English. Utterance-level accent is predicted by a Whisper-large-v3 model over 16 English dialect classes. On the other hand, age and sex are predicted jointly by a WavLM-large model.
We aggregate to the speaker level by averaging the predicted probability vectors across all retained utterances from the same speaker and selecting the highest-scoring class for accent and sex; age is averaged directly. Dataset statistics of SPARC are reported in Table
1
. We find that there are slightly more male speakers in both sub-datasets. Moreover, most speakers are inferred to age between 30 to 60, whereas SPoRC contains a notably larger proportion of younger speakers (<30: 36.3% vs. 15.7%). On the other hand, North American accent accounts for roughly 77–78% of speakers in both datasets, but the remaining speakers span 15 other English dialect categories with none exceeding 6%. As a result, we binarize accent classes to North American vs. Other.
Three independent annotators judged 50 recordings per attribute, sampled to balance the attribute categories. Model–majority agreement was 98% for sex, 88% for accent, and 64% for age (Appendix
A.5
).

4
Evaluation
4.1
Problem Setup
We aim to investigate whether spoken language can provide information to characterize an individual’s identity or personal attributes. To this end, we formulate our problem similarly to established approaches in the Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV), adapting two evaluation tasks from VoxGuard
Tsaprazlis et al. (2026)
(measuring
User Privacy
and
Attribute Privacy
). Concretely, we consider an adversarial setting in which the goal is to determine whether two sets of utterances originate from the same speaker, or whether they are produced by speakers sharing a specific inferred attribute label (e.g. sex). The adversary is provided with an
enrollment
set, used to construct reference representations and a
probe
utterance whose underlying identity or attribute membership is unknown. These are pairwise verification tasks, not identification from a population.
4.2
Trial Generation
We construct verification trials from NaturalVoices and SPoRC for four verification tasks:
speaker identity
,
sex
,
age group
, and
accent
. Throughout, a
podcast series
contains multiple
episodes
; we use
podcast
to refer to a single episode. For each (speaker/attribute, podcast) pair, we form a probe by traversing the transcript from the beginning and accumulating complete utterances until its length falls within
±
5
\pm 5
words of the target probe length
P
P
. For same-podcast trials, enrollment has the final
L
L
non-probe utterances from the same podcast; for cross-podcast trials, it comprises the first
L
L
utterances from another eligible podcast appearance.
L
L
controls the amount of enrollment text. This construction defines four base conditions:
Easy Positives
pair the same speaker within the same podcast,
Hard Positives
pair the same speaker across podcasts,
Easy Negatives
pair different speakers across podcasts, and
Hard Negatives
pair different speakers within the same podcast. In NaturalVoices, the single-speaker constraint applies to segments rather than episodes: episodes may contain multiple speakers, enabling all four trial conditions. The retained SPoRC episodes contain only one speaker and therefore support only
Hard Positives
and
Easy Negatives
. For attribute tasks, positive and negative labels analogously indicate whether the two speakers share the evaluated attribute label. For reporting, we call within-episode trials
same-topic
and cross-episode trials
different-topic
. These are episode-based proxies because NaturalVoices lacks topic annotations or descriptions, and within-episode texts are expected to share more context. Comparing the conditions tests whether performance persists after controlling for episode co-membership.
This design serves two purposes. First, it allows us to measure model performance separately under easy and hard conditions and identify where models struggle. More importantly, it provides a diagnostic for spurious topical correlations: when probe and enrollment texts come from the same podcast, a model may perform well by exploiting shared content rather than speaker-specific linguistic style.
Across all SPoRC verification tasks, we control for topic by limiting episode-title/description similarity and matching positive and negative trials by this similarity and podcast category overlap. Speaker-verification negatives are additionally matched on sex, age group, and accent group. Full details and trial counts are provided in Appendix
A.1
.
4.3
Model Scoring
We evaluate eight models grouped by scoring approach. Five are representation-based baselines: four pretrained neural encoders—SentenceBERT
(
Reimers and Gurevych, 2019
)
, PCM
(
Kim et al., 2025
)
, CISR
(
Wegmann et al., 2022
)
, and LUAR
(
Rivera-Soto et al., 2021
)
—and a lexical TF–IDF
(
Sparck Jones, 1972
)
baseline. These methods construct representations of the probe and enrollment texts and score each trial using cosine similarity. The remaining three models are prompted LLMs: GPT-5-mini, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-9B. For each trial, we provide the probe and enrollment utterances and ask the model to return a score from 0 to 100 indicating the likelihood that the speakers share the same identity or evaluated attribute. Exact prompt templates and scoring details are provided in Appendix
A.2
.
4.4
Evaluation Metrics
We report three complementary metrics that probe different regions of the ROC curve. Our primary metric is the
Equal Error Rate (EER)
: the error rate at the operating point where the false acceptance and false rejection rates coincide (lower is better; chance corresponds to 0.5). EER characterizes a concrete operating point rather than an average over thresholds, and it is not inflated by skewed positive-to-negative trial ratios, a property we rely on for the imbalanced accent trials. We additionally report
AUC
, the probability that a randomly chosen positive pair receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative pair, as a complementary rank-based summary of overall separability. Because neither metric reflects the stringent operating points at which re-identification becomes consequential, we follow
Tsaprazlis et al. (2026)
and report
TPR@FPR
at 1% and 0.1% false-positive rates, the fraction of positive trials accepted at thresholds with the stated false-positive rates.

Particularly, the different-topic condition most closely reflects real-world usage. In practice, samples of the same speaker will mostly come from different conversations and contexts, so verification must succeed across topical variation.
Overall, the finding in the different-topic condition is consistent across both corpora: LLMs including GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B attain EERs of 0.285 and 0.281 on NaturalVoices and 0.253 and 0.262 on SPoRC, far below the random chance baseline and well below SentenceBERT (0.351 and 0.350). The AUC results show the same ranking, with 0.77–0.80 for the LLMs versus 0.70 for SentenceBERT.
On the other hand, the same-topic condition serves as a diagnostic: episode co-membership is shared by positive and negative trials, though other contextual cues may remain. Here SentenceBERT degrades sharply, from 0.350 EER in the combined setting to 0.460, approaching chance, and the remaining embedding baselines show a similar collapse (LUAR: 0.378 to 0.452; PCM: 0.386 to 0.462; CISR to 0.492, effectively chance), consistent with reliance on episode context. This reflects a long-standing limitation of authorship attribution where models tend to conflate what is being said with who is saying it. The two strongest LLMs are far more robust. Llama-3.3-70B retains a 0.322 EER and GPT-5-mini 0.345 (both at 0.721 AUC). Still, the increase from the combined setting (0.284 and 0.277) shows that the LLMs are not fully immune to episode context. TF-IDF is a notable exception among the baselines where its EER rises only mildly in the within-episode condition (0.362 to 0.409), and it is the strongest non-LLM model on SPoRC (0.318 EER, 0.740 AUC), suggesting that surface word-choice statistics carry some speaker-linked signal, although it remains behind GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B in every condition.

5.2
Attribute Verification
We next ask whether transcripts support inferred demographic-label verification, evaluating sex, age, and accent under the same three conditions. As before, we focus on SentenceBERT as the representative embedding-based model and on GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B. We report results on NaturalVoices here; on the SPoRC attribute trials models show similar behavior, and that analysis, together with full results for all systems, is provided in Appendix
A.3
.
5.2.1
Sex-Label Verification
Verification on sex reveals a sharp divide between model families. Embedding-based models operate near chance across all conditions, with SentenceBERT EERs of 0.468–0.508, indicating little separation on this label-verification task.
Instead, GPT-5-mini and Llama-3.3-70B reach 0.377 and 0.420 EER in the realistic different-topic setting. Moreover, they retain this advantage under the same-topic control (0.437 and 0.422 EER). Their performance in the within-episode comparison suggests a modest label-agreement signal, although the responsible linguistic cues remain unclear.
5.2.2
Age Group
The benchmark results show that age-group agreement is the most difficult attribute task, where performance remains near chance in all three main conditions. The best EERs are only 0.447 in the different-topic and 0.440 in the same-topic condition, both from PCM (Table
11
); among the main-text models, GPT-5-mini reaches 0.459 in the different-topic setting. Embedding-model AUCs in the different-topic setting range from 0.517 to 0.556, and Llama-3.3-70B falls below chance in the combined condition (0.546 EER, 0.433 AUC), suggesting a systematic bias in its age judgments rather than useful sensitivity. Given these small and inconsistent effects, we find no reliable evidence that the tested systems can verify age-group agreement from transcripts.
5.2.3
Accent/Dialect
Accent yields the clearest two-tier separation of all attributes. Embedding-based models sit at chance in the different-topic setting (0.494 EER for SentenceBERT; 0.494–0.534 AUC across the embedding baselines) and gain little in the within-episode condition. LLMs, by contrast, extract a markedly stronger signal. For example, GPT-5-mini achieves a 0.268 EER (0.771 AUC) in the different-topic setting and 0.350 under the same-topic control; Llama-3.3-70B reaches 0.320 and 0.332 EER, the best same-topic result. These results show agreement on accent labels, but do not identify which linguistic cues the LLMs use. Because the task uses an imbalanced North American vs. non–North-American distinction, these results do not establish performance on individual dialects but only on this binary coarse distinction.

Probe length is the binding constraint for verification.
Shortening the probe to 50 words degrades every model, with larger losses for the two strongest LLMs than for SentenceBERT. GPT-5-mini’s EER rises by 0.065 in the different-topic setting (0.285 to 0.350), against 0.047 for Llama-3.3-70B and 0.038 for SentenceBERT.

Two further observations sharpen the picture. First, the average-case ordering does not survive. SentenceBERT, despite a clearly worse EER (0.351 vs. 0.281), matches Llama-3.3-70B at
1
%
1\%
FPR (0.143 vs 0.133), so conclusions drawn from average-case metrics alone would misrank low-FPR performance. Second, the gap is partly mechanistic. Prompted LLMs emit coarsely quantized scores, and a model whose confidences concentrate on a few round values yields a step-like ROC whose resolution at low FPR is limited by score granularity rather than by the underlying signal; GPT-5-mini’s smoother, better-separated high-confidence tail may contribute to its stronger low-FPR performance.
6
Conclusion
We introduced SPARC, a large-scale benchmark for pairwise speaker and attribute verification from speech transcripts and evaluated five attribution models and three LLMs across four verification tasks. Our results show that speaker-linked information persists under the evaluated episode and metadata controls. Removing the acoustic signal therefore does not completely remove the speaker information and speech privacy evaluations should consider linguistic content as well as voice. Moreover, attribute agreement remains challenging to verify, with a modest signal for biological sex and accent labels, while age-group agreement is near chance for every system. Shorter transcripts reduce speaker-verification performance, especially for the strongest models, but do not eliminate it. Moreover, similar EER and AUC scores can conceal large differences in trial-level TPR at low false-positive rates.
We hope SPARC supports the development and evaluation of transcript-level privacy defenses.
Limitations
Data Scope
SPARC contains only English podcast speech and retains relatively clean, single-speaker segments through SNR, music, and dual-ASR-agreement filters. The findings may therefore not generalize to noisier or overlapping speech, other conversational domains, or multilingual and code-switched settings.
Attribute Labels and Accent Evaluation
SPARC’s sex, age, and accent labels are model-derived rather than independently verified demographics. The category-balanced, 50-recording audit measures perceptual consistency on a small selected sample, not corpus-wide accuracy; agreement is weakest for age. Attribute results therefore measure agreement with proxy labels. Approximately 77–78% of speakers are assigned a North American accent, and no other individual dialect exceeds 6%, motivating the North American/Other grouping. This imbalanced binary task cannot support conclusions about fine-grained accent verification, especially for lower-resourced dialects
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
. Negative pairs also constitute only 19% of the combined NaturalVoices accent trials, reducing statistical precision. A more balanced corpus is needed for individual-dialect evaluation.
Model and Score Scope
We evaluate three LLMs using a single zero-shot scoring prompt. Because of inference cost, we obtain one response per LLM-trial pair and therefore do not quantify variability across repeated generations. In addition, we notice that LLMs’ uncalibrated 0–100 scores often cluster at a few rounded values, limiting ROC resolution at low FPR. The findings are therefore specific to the evaluated model–prompt configurations; calibrated or likelihood-based scoring could produce different rankings.
Linguistic Cue Attribution
We do not attribute individual decisions to lexical, syntactic, discourse, stylistic, or ASR-derived cues. Such analysis is needed to separate speaker habits from residual context, particularly for the coarse accent-label result.
Scope of Topic Control
For NaturalVoices, episode membership is only a proxy for topical overlap: one episode may span multiple topics, while different episodes may discuss similar subjects. The within- and cross-episode conditions therefore control episode context rather than semantic topic identity. For SPoRC, title/description filtering and category matching provide additional metadata-based proxies but cannot eliminate residual topical overlap. In the original SPoRC speaker protocol, 81.4% of positive trials are within-series whereas all negatives cross series; the additional cross-series control reduces this imbalance and yields higher EERs. Neither analysis isolates speaker style from correlated textual cues, including personal facts and speaker-relevant ASR errors
(
Aggazzotti et al., 2024
)
.
Ethical Considerations
SPARC is intended to audit privacy leakage from speech transcripts, but the capabilities it evaluates are inherently dual use. The recordings were collected from publicly available podcast feeds; for NaturalVoices, we retain only episodes released under CC-BY 4.0. Nevertheless, public availability does not imply that speakers anticipated automated linkage or demographic profiling. We therefore position SPARC as a resource for privacy research and discourage its use in forensic, law-enforcement, employment, eligibility, or other high-stakes decisions.
Because SPoRC does not provide verified age, sex, or accent labels, we use Vox-Profile and Voxlect as reproducible proxies
(
Feng et al., 2025b
;
Feng et al., 2025a
)
. Vox-Profile’s strongest models report 98.0% accuracy for binary speaker-sex classification and 69.5% for three-way age-group classification, while the Voxlect Whisper-Large model used in our study reports 83.0% accuracy for English dialect classification. We reduce utterance-level noise by averaging predictions across each speaker’s retained utterances and report a small perceptual audit in Appendix
A.5
. These labels nevertheless remain model-inferred, and source-benchmark performance or agreement on a selected audit sample may not transfer fully to SPARC. The binary sex and coarse age and accent categories should therefore not be interpreted as verified demographic identities. We use them only for trial construction and aggregate analysis, not for downstream profiling or individual-level decisions. Any reuse should preserve their inferred provenance and comply with the source licenses, Voxlect’s Responsible AI License, and applicable privacy requirements.

A.1.1
NaturalVoices
NaturalVoices episodes may contain multiple speakers and therefore support all four trial types: Easy Positives, Hard Positives, Easy Negatives, and Hard Negatives. Speaker trials are labeled according to whether the probe and enrollment texts belong to the same speaker. For the demographic tasks, trials are labeled according to whether the speakers share the evaluated sex, age-group, or accent label. For each eligible probe speaker-episode pair, enrollment partners requiring a different episode or speaker are randomly sampled from the corresponding eligible pool using a fixed seed; positive and negative trials are not matched one-to-one by episode or topic. Demographic trials are then retained according to attribute agreement without artificially balancing the classes, so their counts reflect the resulting attribute distributions. For the NaturalVoices speaker ablation, trials are fixed when varying
L

A.1.2
SPoRC
The retained SPoRC episodes are single-speaker. Therefore, different-speaker, same-episode trials cannot be constructed, and all negative trials span different podcast series (characterized by different RSS feeds). Positive speaker trials pair the same speaker across distinct episodes, which may originate from the same or different podcast series. Negative speaker trials pair different speakers from different podcast series and require the speakers to share the same sex, age-group, and accent labels, reducing the possibility that broad demographic differences distinguish the trial classes.
We use two metadata-based topic proxies. First, we concatenate each episode’s title and description and represent the resulting text using L2-normalized TF–IDF features over unigrams and bigrams. Candidate episode pairs with cosine similarity greater than 0.10 are excluded. Second, we represent each podcast series’ non-empty category labels as a set and compute the Jaccard similarity between the two category sets. After the TF–IDF filter, candidate pairs are stratified jointly by TF–IDF similarity and category overlap. For each positive trial, we sample one eligible negative trial from the same stratum, producing balanced trial classes with closely matched distributions of the two metadata-topic measures. We additionally exclude pairs containing exact utterance overlap and screen positive speaker trials for explicit speaker-name leakage.

A.2
Model Scoring and Inference Details
A.2.1
Embedding-based Models
We evaluate pretrained embedding model baselines without task-specific supervised training: sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 (SentenceBERT), AnnaWegmann/Style-Embedding (CISR), Blablablab/multilingual-style-representation (PCM), and rrivera1849/LUAR-CRUD (LUAR). All models are imported from the Sentence Transformers library and run on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU. For SentenceBERT, CISR, and PCM, we average L2-normalized utterance embeddings within each side and compute cosine similarity. TF–IDF uses word unigram and bigram representations fitted without labels to the unique utterances in each task and input configuration. LUAR receives 16 utterances per side: longer sets are truncated, while shorter sets are padded by repeating the final utterance; each utterance is limited to 32 tokens. Probe and enrollment representations are compared using cosine similarity.
A.2.2
LLM Scoring
We query gpt-5-mini through the OpenAI API and meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo and Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B through the Together API. Each trial is presented as a single zero-shot user message. GPT-5-mini uses low reasoning effort and low response verbosity, while Llama uses the provider’s default decoding settings; no temperature is explicitly supplied to either model. For Qwen, we disable reasoning and use temperature (1.0),
top_p
=0.95,
top_k
=20,
min_p
=0, presence penalty (1.5), and repetition penalty (1.0), following the model card’s recommended non-thinking configuration for reasoning tasks. These settings were not tuned on the evaluation labels. We extract the first numeric value from each response and constrain it to the requested 0–100 range.
All three LLMs receive the same prompt structure. The identity-verification prompt is:
You are a speaker verification judge.
Estimate how likely it is that the probe and enrollment utterances came from the SAME SPEAKER. Focus on stylistic and linguistic cues, not topic similarity. Output one number from 0 to 100: 0 = definitely different speaker 100 = definitely same speaker

NaturalVoices
Tables
9
–
12
report EER and AUC for all eight systems on NaturalVoices, covering the combined, easy, hard, same-topic, and different-topic conditions, with
Δ
\Delta
columns giving the change from the base configuration under each reduced input budget.
The easy/hard split, omitted from the main text for space, shows the effect of episode co-membership. On easy trials, probe and enrollment share an episode only on positive pairs, and SentenceBERT reaches 0.168 EER on identity. On hard trials, episode co-membership points toward the wrong label, and the embedding baselines have EERs of 0.546–0.621 on identity, consistent with reliance on episode context. The LLMs also degrade (GPT-5-mini: 0.542 EER; Llama-3.3-70B: 0.556). The same pattern appears for demographic-label agreement, where hard-condition EERs for the embedding models reach 0.62–0.80.
The ablation columns extend the analysis of Section
5.3
to all systems and conditions. The probe-length effect is consistent across model families. In the cross-episode condition, reducing enrollment from

Qwen3.5-9B tracks the embedding baselines throughout (0.418 EER on cross-episode identity, chance-level attribute performance), indicating that the LLM advantage observed in the main text is not shared by every LLM. Finally, the age-label results for Llama-3.3-70B (0.546 combined EER) improve under reduced information, consistent with response bias rather than a reliable age signal.
A.4
Cross-Series SPoRC Speaker Verification
The original SPoRC speaker protocol includes 1,594 cross-series positive trials across the four input settings, while every negative trial crosses series (Appendix
A.1
). Restricting both classes to cross-series pairs removes series co-membership as a direct class cue. Table
7
reports EER for the two strongest LLMs. At the base configuration, EER rises from 0.253 to 0.402 for GPT-5-mini and from 0.262 to 0.391 for Llama-3.3-70B, but remains below the 0.5 chance value. Under this control, EER varies by at most 0.011 (GPT-5-mini) and 0.015 (Llama-3.3-70B) across the four input settings, so the probe-length effect of Section
5.3
is not visible in this stricter protocol. This control does not eliminate all differences in semantic topic or speaker-specific context.

article.headline: SPARC 基准：语音转录仍能关联说话人
article.lede: 研究团队用两个播客语料库构建 SPARC，检验纯文本能否指认说话人及性别、年龄、口音。
article.problem: 语音匿名化长期聚焦声学信号，但转录把「说了什么」和「听起来怎样」分开后，词选择、句法和话语习惯仍然保留，可能足以把匿名文本关联回已知说话人。已有工作显示转录文本确实携带说话人信息，但在话题控制下性能会下降，而现代 LLM 对手以及性别、年龄、口音这类人口统计标签能否同样被验证，仍是开放问题。
article.method: 作者构建 SPARC（Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus），从 NaturalVoices 和 SPoRC 两个播客语料中抽取超过 12,500 名说话人、约 150 万条经质量过滤的语句，并附带来源元数据或模型推断的性别、年龄、口音标签。基准在统一协议下生成说话人身份、性别、年龄组和口音四类配对验证 trial，以集内/跨集和 SPoRC 的标题、分类元数据作为话题代理，评测 5 个表征式归因模型和 3 个 LLM，并系统改变 probe 长度（200 词 / 50 词）与注册语句数（20 条 / 5 条）。
article.results: 在 200 词 probe、20 条注册语句的基线下，跨话题说话人验证中 GPT-5-mini 与 Llama-3.3-70B 在 NaturalVoices 上 EER 为 0.285 和 0.281、在 SPoRC 上为 0.253 和 0.262，低于随机水平 0.5，也低于 SentenceBERT 的 0.351 和 0.350；LLM 的 AUC 为 0.77–0.80，SentenceBERT 为 0.70。改为同话题条件后嵌入模型明显退化（SentenceBERT 的 EER 从 0.350 升到 0.460，LUAR 从 0.378 升到 0.452，PCM 从 0.386 升到 0.462，CISR 达 0.492），LLM 仍保持 0.322（Llama）和 0.345（GPT-5-mini）。属性验证出现分化：跨话题性别验证 GPT-5-mini 与 Llama 的 EER 为 0.377 和 0.420，嵌入模型在 0.468–0.508 徘徊；口音验证 GPT-5-mini 达 0.268 EER（AUC 0.771）、Llama 为 0.320；年龄任务最好 EER 仅 0.447（PCM），Llama 在合并条件下甚至低于随机（0.546 EER、0.433 AUC）。把 probe 缩到 50 词使 GPT-5-mini 的 EER 上升 0.065（0.285 到 0.350）、Llama 上升 0.047、SentenceBERT 上升 0.038；注册语句从 20 条减到 5 条影响更小（GPT-5-mini 上升 0.041），两者同时缩减时 GPT-5-mini 上升 0.076、Llama 上升 0.064，但 LLM 跨话题 EER 仍有 0.35–0.36。在 1% 假阳性率下，GPT-5-mini 的 TPR 为 0.277，Llama-3.3-70B 仅 0.133，而两者的 AUC（0.790 对 0.789）与 EER（0.285 对 0.281）几乎相同。
article.why_it_matters: 结果表明，去掉声学信号并不能消除说话人关联风险，语音隐私评估需要同时考虑语言内容，而 SPARC 为转录层面的隐私防线提供了可复现的评测基准。此外，AUC 与 EER 相近的模型在低假阳性率下可能相差两倍以上，提示平均指标会误判真实链接风险。
article.limitations: 语料仅覆盖英语播客，且经信噪比、背景音乐和双 ASR 一致性过滤后只保留较干净的单说话人片段，难以外推到噪声、重叠语音或多语种场景；性别、年龄、口音标签均为模型推断而非独立核实，口音被简化为北美/其他二分，年龄标签的人工审计一致率仅 64%。三个 LLM 只用单一零样本提示、每个 trial 仅采样一次，0–100 分数在整数附近聚集，限制了低假阳性率下的 ROC 分辨率，结论也只适用于所评测的模型—提示配置。
article.figure_caption_zh: SPARC 构建流程：从 NaturalVoices 和 SPoRC 中筛出信噪比达标、无背景音乐的单说话人语音，两个 ASR 模型一致率不低于 90% 时保留，并用来源元数据或模型预测标注年龄、性别与口音。

figure.caption: Overview of the SPARC construction pipeline. Eligible single-speaker speech from NaturalVoices and SPoRC is filtered for SNR and background music, retained when two ASR models agree by at least 90\%, and annotated with age, sex, and accent labels from source metadata or model predictions.

page_papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
page_papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

Abstract
Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters.
To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone’s causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost.
This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge.

Introduction
Human brain encoding models predict neural responses to stimuli, providing computational insights into how the brain processes information.
State-of-the-art (SoTA) encoding models mostly follow a goal-driven paradigm
(
Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016
)
: a large model pretrained on behavioral tasks is used as a
frozen
feature extractor, and only a readout is learned from neural data
(
Adeli et al., 2025
;
Hwang et al., 2025
;
Gokce et al., 2026a
;
d’Ascoli et al., 2026
)
. This approach leverages strong pretrained priors, but misses the opportunity to exploit the backbone’s expressiveness to specialize for brain encoding.
Adapting large pretrained backbones with neural data promises to scale models to the complexity required to capture human brain computation, and to best combine neural information and behavioral task training. In practice, however, such adaptation is difficult, because neural data are costly and scarce relative to the size of contemporary models. Methods that do let neural data shape the representation have had mixed success. Training smaller models from scratch
(
St-Yves et al., 2023
;
Khosla and Wehbe, 2026
)
has not reached SoTA performance on whole-brain human benchmarks, and full fine-tuning of a pretrained backbone has been reported to underperform freezing it
(
Yang et al., 2023
)
.
Low-rank adaptation won Algonauts 2023
(
Yang et al., 2023
)
, but only with a relatively small ViT, and it has not been tested on large multimodal models.

On the same backbone
Qwen3-Omni
as the prior SoTA
(

Moreover, we show the adapted multimodal model remains interpretable. Prior work often identifies a region’s preferred modality by determining which unimodal encoder its readout relies on. With multimodal backbones, we instead use feature attribution to identify modality contribution, which recovers the canonical topography: early visual cortex is driven by video, and auditory and lateral temporal cortex by audio. Comparison with the frozen backbone shows that adaptation reweights the contributions of the three modalities, particularly increasing the contribution of the audio inputs, and increases cross-modal mixing within the backbone (§
5.4
).
Finally, to scale the number of adapted models, we develop a batched multi-LoRA kernel that trains many LoRAs jointly on one shared backbone, significantly reducing training time. This enables 200+ independently adapted models, whose ensemble ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard, surpassing unpublished entries as well. We additionally show that the ensemble performance is jointly governed by ensemble size, individual model quality, and model diversity (§
5.5
).
Together, our results suggest three complementary scaling directions for future brain encoding models under the PEFT paradigm:

We use the mean Pearson correlation across the four subjects as the primary fMRI prediction metric. The seed-to-seed variability is small: methods whose mean correlations differ by less than 0.00077 cannot be reliably separated (LoRA+linear with 15 seeds; App.
