5.1

Discussion
Three axes for scaling PEFT for brain encoding.
Together, our results suggest three complementary scaling directions for future brain encoding models:
1) Scale up
the pretrained prior by leveraging increasingly capable backbones;
2) Scale down
the adaptation by updating only a small number of parameters; and
3) Scale out
by training a large number of lightweight adapters to shared backbones with various inductive biases
(
Mind Lab et al., 2026
)
. Together, PEFT turns a single powerful pretrained model into a family of specialized encoding models without training each backbone from scratch.
Toward a brain foundation model.
Our experiments do not constitute a brain foundation model, but scaling along the three directions discussed above could lead to one. A large pretrained backbone could use a single shared adapter trained on neural data spanning tasks, datasets, subjects, and even species. In this work, we only scale out the number of adapters for ensemble. However, future work could train a separate adapter for each task, dataset, subject, or even ROI with a hierarchical structure or with meta-learning.
Together, this hierarchical approach and the three scaling directions we discuss above can create a brain foundation model with efficient specializations for different downstream tasks.
Limitations.
Our models are trained on one benchmark with four subjects, all watching audiovisual narrative. The adapters transfer to a held-out subject (App.
19
) and to a second dataset (App.
20
), but neither test leaves the domain of narrative film. We leave the joint training on multiple datasets and modalities to future work.

article.headline: 用LoRA适配104B主干做大脑编码
article.lede: 用LoRA适配104B多模态主干做脑编码，同主干上超过此前SoTA，200多个适配器的集成登顶公开榜单。
article.problem: 脑编码模型的主流做法是把预训练大模型冻结，只用神经数据训练读出层，这样虽然能利用强大的预训练先验，却没有机会让主干专门适配大脑编码任务。而从零训练大模型或对任务预训练后的模型做全量微调，在神经数据上效果都不理想，因为神经数据昂贵且规模有限。此前的低秩适配虽曾在Algonauts 2023获奖，但只用在较小的ViT上，尚未在大型多模态模型上验证。
article.method: 作者在大规模多模态主干上插入rank-16的LoRA，例如在Qwen3-Omni上改到第32层注意力模块并在此截断解码器，只引入8.91M可训练参数，再配线性或交叉注意力读出层映射到1,000个脑区。为降低计算开销，方法利用主干的因果结构一次前向预测多个时间点，替代滑窗式特征提取，避免重复计算。训练先用SGD联合优化适配器与读出层，再用分脑区岭回归以闭式解重新拟合线性读出；另实现批量多LoRA内核，可在共享主干的多个LoRA上并行训练。
article.results: 在CNeuroMod/Algonauts 2025的fMRI数据（1,000个脑区、四名被试观看七季《老友记》）上，用相同训练配置测试九个多模态主干，LoRA均带来提升；在与此前SoTA相同的Qwen3-Omni主干上，该方法在已发表方法中取得新的SoTA。作者报告所用最大主干达104B参数，称其为迄今适配脑编码的最大模型；主配置的可训练参数为8.91M（适配器）加52.3M（读出层）。种子间波动为0.00077，平均相关系数差异小于该值不可区分。批量多LoRA内核使200多个独立适配模型的集成在Algonauts赛后公开榜单上排名第一，超过未发表条目；特征归因还显示适配后音频模态贡献上升、主干内部跨模态混合增强。
article.why_it_matters: 它把脑编码从“冻结主干加读出层”推进到“轻量适配主干”，并给出扩大主干、缩小可训练参数、增加适配器数量三条可组合的扩展路线，同时让多模态主干的模态贡献仍可解释。
article.limitations: 实验只在一个基准、四名被试上进行，刺激全部是有声叙事影片；适配器虽能迁移到留出被试和第二个数据集，但两者都没有跳出叙事电影这一领域。此外，摘要与正文给出的正文片段未给出与基线相比的具体相关系数提升数值，论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: 示意图对比冻结主干的传统范式与PEFT适配范式，并列出扩大主干、缩小适配器、扩充适配器数量这三条扩展方向。

figure.caption: {From frozen backbones to PEFT, and three directions to scale PEFT for brain encoding.} {(a)}~The dominant paradigm: a frozen pretrained backbone with readouts trained for brain encoding. The backbone prior is strong, but it is not specialized for brain encoding. {(b)}~We advocate using PEFT to adapt strong pretrained backbones, retaining the powerful prior while allowing flexible neural adaptation. This suggests three complementary scaling directions: {Scale up} to stronger priors leveraging more capable backbones; {Scale down} the size of trainable adapters for brain encoding with limited data; and {Scale out} the number of adapters with different specializations.

page_papers.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
page_papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.

article.headline: 两个分解引导扩散草稿模型提吞吐
article.lede: DScout 将训练损失与推理吞吐各拆为若干因子，Qwen3-4B/8B 上平均加速 3.84× 与 4.14×。
article.problem: 投机解码用草稿模型并行提议、目标模型并行验证来加速大模型推理，扩散草稿器还能进一步并行生成提议。但提议能力更强或平均接受长度（MAT）更高，并不必然带来更高吞吐：验证只接受连续前缀，早期拒绝会让后面本可正确的预测失效，MAT 收益被限制；而每轮延迟一旦上升，更高的 MAT 也可能换不来吞吐。
article.method: 训练侧，DScout 把逐位置损失分解为包含项、加权项与预测损失，据此设计并组合混合视野训练、块内解掩码和接受度加权损失，使监督信号与前缀接受机制对齐。推理侧，它把吞吐分解为 MAT 与每轮延迟之比，用这一形式指导目标条件深度、草稿器深度和推理块大小的选择，为每种负载找高吞吐配置。
article.results: 在六个基准上，DScout 在 Qwen3-4B 和 Qwen3-8B 上相对自回归解码的平均加速分别为 3.84× 和 4.14×，相比当前最优基线的平均加速再提升 9.1% 和 7.1%。跨模型与不同并发设置，其推理配置策略比 DScout 的固定配置最多再带来 9.75% 的平均加速。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明扩散草稿器的收益瓶颈不只在接受长度，还在“接受长度除以每轮延迟”这一整体比值，为训练目标与推理配置的联合设计提供了可操作的分解框架。
article.limitations: 实验集中在 Qwen3-4B/8B 两个模型，是否适用于更大模型和其他草稿架构尚不清楚；论文给出的是相对加速比，未给出绝对吞吐、每轮延迟和配置搜索开销的具体数字；且训练侧三项技巧各自的独立贡献也缺少消融数据。

page_papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
page_papers.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.

Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. The methods also differ in how they use experience and supervision after initialization. RLT performs online residual reinforcement learning on a single robot, while our RECAP implementation performs one round of offline policy improvement on multi-robot data. Both use additional human corrective actions during subsequent policy learning. FERT instead learns from successful autonomous executions, using binary task outcomes and failure-guided retrieval to prioritize training experience without additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. It also avoids learning a value function for advantage estimation. Together, these results show that, under the evaluated task and training configurations, FERT uses fleet-generated actions and task-outcome feedback to improve task success beyond the shared expert-supervised initialization without collecting further expert demonstrations or corrective actions.

For (M)HG-DAgger, single-robot training on the relatively challenging Phone Charging, Stool Assembly and Phone Packaging tasks can yield lower success rates than the SFT initialization. This may reflect overfitting to the environment of an individual robot and the behaviour of a single operator, limiting generalization to other robots. Performance improves as the fleet expands, but further increases in robot numbers lead to saturation on Phone Charging and Phone Packaging and a decline on Stool Assembly. This pattern motivates examining learning with less demanding action supervision as fleets grow. Limited human monitoring and intervention capacity is a possible explanation for the observed saturation, alongside changes in the collected data.
For FERT, success rates generally increase with fleet size across all five tasks.
On Phone Packaging, expanding the training fleet from 16 to 96 robots raises success from 86.7% to 98.3%, a gain of 11.6 percentage points. At smaller fleet sizes, FERT can still perform below its initialization. For example, training with eight robots reduces success rates relative to the initial policies on both Stool Assembly and Phone Packaging. One possible explanation is that successful experience collected by smaller fleets is insufficiently rich to cover the different failure contexts encountered by the policy, limiting the effectiveness of failure-guided retrieval and subsequent policy updates.
Together, these results show more consistent performance gains for FERT as fleet size and total collected experience increase across the evaluated tasks and scales. These findings support using experience generated during deployment to improve a shared policy as more robots contribute data. FERT collects this experience with binary task-outcome labels, without requiring additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions.

Conclusion
We studied how robots can use experience generated during deployment to improve policy reliability without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. As the fleet grows, keeping teleoperators available to monitor execution and provide corrections becomes difficult; the fleet’s own experience offers an alternative source of actions for learning. Collective experience learning (CEL) organizes this experience into a shared learning loop after expert-supervised initialization. We realized CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses successful robot actions as training targets and failed executions to guide experience selection. The fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) connects robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization while accommodating local interruptions. FERT supplies the learning mechanism, and FATS sustains the distributed process through which the fleet contributes and uses experience.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieved success rates of 93.3-99.2% on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provided more experience and generally improved FERT performance across the evaluated sizes. On Phone Packaging, training with 96 robots raised success from 79.2% at initialization to 98.3%. Ablations supported the contribution of failure-guided retrieval, and system measurements characterized collection and communication during fleet operation. These findings support policy improvement from collective experience beyond expert-supervised initialization, including transfer to other robot instances of the same platform.
The current study evaluates task-specific policies on five tasks using a single robot platform. Broader task distributions, heterogeneous robot platforms and adaptation to changes over longer periods of operation are directions for future work. More broadly, CEL connects the expansion of robot deployment with a growing source of experience for shared learning. Through a common policy, experience generated by individual robots can contribute to capabilities available across the fleet. This points towards a model of robot deployment in which fleets contribute not only task execution, but also the experience from which their capabilities can improve, without requiring expert action supervision to scale in proportion.

Human-intervention frames are always labeled positive, overriding both the threshold and indicator dropout. We replace the original natural-language advantage indicators with dedicated positive, negative, and null tokens. Non-intervention samples use indicator dropout with probability 0.3. The policy is fine-tuned with the conditional flow-matching objective and evaluated with the positive indicator at guidance scale 1.

article.headline: 机器人集群共享经验，成功率最高99.2%
article.lede: 机器人集群把部署中的失败作为线索，检索共享的成功轨迹来微调策略，无需额外人类纠正，五个真实操作任务成功率93.3%–99
article.problem: 机器人基础模型能提供初始操作能力，但物体属性、接触条件和个体差异会让策略在实际部署中失效，多阶段任务中误差还会累积。现有做法依赖遥操作员持续监控并在失败时接管纠正，随着集群规模扩大，这种人力监督难以同步扩展。论文要回答的是：能否让部署中的机器人仅靠自身执行经验互相学习，而不必持续采集专家示范或纠正动作。
article.method: 作者提出集体经验学习（CEL）范式，让已部署机器人共享执行经验以改进一个公共策略，具体实现为失败引导的经验检索微调（FERT）。FERT 用视觉与本体的特征编码观测，以失败上下文从集群共享的成功轨迹中检索相关片段，并提高这些片段的采样优先级，用其中的动作作为监督信号，训练时只使用二元任务成败标签。配套的容错异步训练系统 FATS 基于 RLinf 实现，负责协调经验收集、策略优化与策略分发，并容忍集群内的局部中断。
article.results: 在五个真实操作任务上，所得策略在未参与训练数据收集的机器人上达到93.3%–99.2%的成功率，每个任务评估120次试验。在固定每个机器人采集时间的前提下，FERT 的成功率总体上随集群规模增大而上升；多阶段手机包装任务中，训练机器人数从16增至96时成功率由86.7%升至98.3%，提升11.6个百分点，而以初始化策略为起点则从79.2%升到98.3%。不过小集群并不总有效：用8台机器人训练时，凳子装配和手机包装上的成功率反而低于初始策略。
article.why_it_matters: 它把部署本身变成训练数据来源，让集群规模直接转化为经验量与策略可靠性，而不必按机器人数线性扩充遥操作人力。这为「机器人边干活边变强」的部署模式提供了一个可运行的工程闭环。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖单一机器人平台上的五个任务专用策略，作者也承认更广的任务分布、异构平台以及长时间运行中的适应仍未验证。此外小集群下 FERT 可能不如初始策略，说明失败引导检索需要足够丰富的成功经验才成立。
article.figure_caption_zh: 失败引导的经验检索微调流程：机器人异步采集带二元成败标签的自主经验，用失败上下文从成功轨迹中检索相关片段并提高其采样优先级，更新后的策略再回到集群继续产生经验。

figure.caption: {Failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning.} Robots asynchronously collect autonomous experience with binary task-outcome labels. Observations are encoded using visual and proprioceptive features. Failure contexts retrieve related segments from successful trajectories, and these segments receive increased sampling priority during policy fine-tuning. Updated policies return to the fleet to generate further experience.

page_papers.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
page_papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.

Abstract
Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
The code will be released soon.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs)
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2025
;
Bai et al., 2026
)
have advanced rapidly in language understanding, generation, and reasoning. Their growing capabilities support knowledge-intensive applications, but reliable answers require facts that can be missing, poorly retained, or outdated in pretrained parameters
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
. Knowledge injection addresses this gap by incorporating information from an external corpus. A central challenge is to incorporate this knowledge effectively while preserving existing capabilities and keeping knowledge acquisition and inference costs manageable.
Existing approaches face different trade-offs in addressing this challenge. Continued pretraining (CPT)
(
Gururangan et al., 2020
)
learns from an additional corpus through language modeling, while LoRA
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
offers a parameter-efficient way to adapt the model. These approaches keep inference self-contained, but adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities
(
Biderman et al., 2024
)
. Non-parametric retrieval instead provides external evidence during generation. RAG
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
conditions on retrieved passages, and RETRO
(
Borgeaud et al., 2022
)
incorporates retrieved chunks within the decoder. These methods provide access to corpus knowledge without first learning it in model parameters, but datastore search and evidence processing can add substantial inference latency
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
.
Parametric memory learns from retrieved knowledge offline, enabling inference without explicit retrieval. MLP Memory
(
Wei et al., 2026a
)
and Memory Decoder
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
learn to predict retrieval-derived next-token distributions. However, this inference advantage comes with substantial offline costs. Constructing token-level training targets requires retrieval at individual token positions across the corpus, resulting in substantial data construction costs
(
Wei et al., 2026b
)
. Training memory modules on these targets further incurs significant computational cost. Moreover, these methods rely on shallow fusion through output-probability interpolation, without incorporating memory into the decoder’s hidden states. Intuitively, integrating memory into intermediate hidden states allows subsequent layers to further process and combine it with the evolving context. The broader challenge is to enable language models to acquire external knowledge efficiently and use it effectively.
In this work, we introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that combines efficient knowledge acquisition with deep fusion within the decoder (Figure
1
). At a high level, DFM shares memory supervision across multiple token predictions while allowing each token to use the learned memory according to its context. We jointly train a memory predictor and a memory fusion module, using retrieved target memory to supervise the predictor and the standard language modeling objective to train both modules. In this way, external knowledge is not only stored in the predictor’s parameters, but also injected into intermediate hidden states through the fusion module, allowing subsequent decoder layers to utilize the memory during generation. The LLM backbone remains frozen throughout, and memory prediction is performed at the chunk level.
Our experiments demonstrate improvements in both efficiency and downstream performance. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches that construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. DFM achieves the highest average score across six QA tasks on both backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, adaptation across code, mathematics, and law yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively. Ablations further highlight the importance of fusion placement and gate initialization, while showing comparatively small changes in average QA performance across the tested chunk sizes and numbers of memory slots.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce
DFM, a parametric memory architecture with deep fusion
, which integrates learned corpus knowledge into intermediate hidden states so that subsequent decoder layers can process memory together with the evolving context. Inference requires no explicit retrieval.
•
We reduce
the overhead of supervision construction and memory training
through chunk-level supervision and end-to-end training with a frozen backbone. For training data construction, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items than existing parametric memory approaches based on token-level targets.
•
We demonstrate
improved QA performance and domain adaptation
. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Across code, mathematics, and law, average gains over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base reach 6.51 and 4.38 points, respectively.
2
Related Work
Model Adaptation.
Continued pretraining adapts language models to additional corpora through further language modeling
(
Gururangan et al., 2020
)
, while LoRA
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
offers a parameter-efficient way to adapt the model.
Such adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities
(
Biderman et al., 2024
)
.
Deep Fusion Memory keeps the backbone frozen and learns an added memory module from retrieval-derived targets, jointly training memory prediction and fusion.
Retrieval-Augmented Language Models.
Non-parametric memory exposes corpus information through several interfaces.
k
k
NN-LM retrieves context–token pairs and interpolates a neighbor-derived next-token distribution with the language model output
(
Khandelwal et al., 2019
)
, whereas RAG conditions generation on retrieved passages
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
.
RETRO combines chunk retrieval with cross-attention inside the Transformer
(
Borgeaud et al., 2022
)
.
xRAG projects a retrieved document embedding into a single token representation prepended to the query, reducing the context passed to the generator
(
Cheng et al., 2024
)
.
These methods retain an external retrieval dependency at inference.
Deep Fusion Memory predicts continuous memory parametrically and uses it inside the decoder without online search.
Parametric Memory.
MLP Memory trains an MLP to predict
k
k
NN token distributions from language model representations
(
Wei et al., 2026a
)
.
Memory Decoder learns a similar distributional target with a standalone decoder
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
.
Memory Decoder at Scale extends this approach to large-scale general and domain memory pretraining
(
Wei et al., 2026b
)
.
MemSFT specializes frozen backbones through a domain memory and a learned token-wise router over the backbone and memory output distributions
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches avoid explicit retrieval at inference, but token-level retrieval incurs substantial data construction costs, and output-probability interpolation provides only shallow fusion.
Deep Fusion Memory reduces the cost of supervision construction by sharing target memory across tokens within each chunk and fuses predicted memory into hidden states through gated cross-attention.

At inference, the language model uses the same predictor and fusion modules without constructing target memory. 4.2
Question Answering Performance
Overall Performance.
Table
1
compares DFM with non-parametric and parametric methods across six QA benchmarks. DFM achieves the highest average on both backbones without online retrieval. On Mistral, it raises the six-task mean from xRAG’s 24.14 to 27.21, a
12.71% relative improvement
over the strongest baseline. On Qwen3-8B-Base, it improves from MLP Memory’s 23.80 to 26.46, a
11.19% relative improvement
. These correspond to absolute gains of 3.07 and 2.66 points, showing comparable relative benefits across the two backbone families. Relative to Base, DFM gains 13.59 and 3.75 points, improving all six tasks on Mistral and five on Qwen3. It also outperforms CPT and LoRA on every Mistral task and five Qwen3 tasks.
Single-Hop Question Answering.
On Mistral, DFM reaches 33.57 on NQ and 42.47 on WebQA, improving over Base by 13.27 and 13.19 points. These scores exceed the strongest baseline on each task by 6.18 and 2.26 points, showing gains beyond those obtained through either explicit retrieval or parameter adaptation alone. On Qwen3, NQ improves from 17.60 to 27.46, exceeding RAG by 3.04 points. WebQA instead decreases from 41.78 to 39.47, while MLP Memory achieves 43.26. The contrasting WebQA outcomes show that memory adaptation is not uniformly beneficial across backbones, even when the original weights remain frozen.
Multi-Hop Question Answering.
DFM improves over Base on all four multi-hop benchmarks for both backbones. On Mistral, it leads on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, with Bamboogle increasing from 3.91 to 22.65. Its 2Wiki score rises from 5.87 to 25.00, although RAG remains stronger at 31.02. On Qwen3, DFM achieves the best results on 2Wiki, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, including a 7.55-point gain over Base on 2Wiki. It also improves HotpotQA to 26.46, below xRAG’s 27.74. These results indicate that predicted memory can support tasks requiring multiple pieces of evidence, while explicit retrieval retains an advantage on some benchmarks.

Conclusion
We presented Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that combines efficient supervision construction with deep fusion within the decoder. Sharing target memory across tokens in each chunk reduces retrieval work, while gated cross-attention allows subsequent decoder layers to process predicted memory together with the evolving context. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. DFM improves the six-task QA average over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, DFM improves performance over the base models across code, mathematics, and law. These results demonstrate that shared supervision and learned internal fusion can support efficient knowledge acquisition and effective memory use.

Appendix A
Experimental Details
A.1
Question Answering
Data construction.
We use section and infobox text from Wikipedia December 2018. Records are grouped by normalized article titles and assigned to training, validation, and test splits in proportions of 99.8/0.1/0.1% using seed 42. We remove exact text duplicates across splits, append EOS to each record, and pack records within each split into 2,048-token sequences. Incomplete final sequences are discarded. Tokenization yields 4.70B, 4.29B, and 4.08B training tokens for Mistral, Qwen3, and OLMo3, respectively. Each sequence is divided into non-overlapping 32-token chunks. We encode training chunks with the frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder, using last-token pooling and L2 normalization to obtain 1,024-dimensional representations. A FAISS IVF-PQ index supports offline neighbor retrieval. Following Section
3.1
, each preceding chunk retrieves target memory for the next chunk. We retain the top-16 full chunk embeddings in retrieval-rank order, including the nearest neighbor, and mask the first chunk from memory supervision. The datastore contains training chunks only.
Training.

The predictor has 28 layers, hidden width 1,024, FFN width 3,072, 16 query heads, and eight KV heads. Its 16 output heads predict the continuous memory slots. Evaluation.
Table
4
summarizes the six QA benchmarks. DFM uses zero-shot greedy decoding without online retrieval, gold documents, or chain-of-thought demonstrations. Questions are formatted with task-specific question–answer templates. Generation stops at a newline or the token limit, with period and comma as additional stop strings for WebQA. Evaluation batches contain one example per GPU, except WebQA, which uses four. For QA, each memory query is formed from the current visible prompt chunk rather than the preceding chunk used during training. The queries and predicted memory remain fixed during generation. For newly added chunk positions, the adapter pads queries and query-validity masks with zeros, so these positions receive no direct memory update. Generated answer chunks do not refresh the queries, and incremental predictor caching is not used in the reported implementation. F1 measures normalized token overlap and takes the maximum over accepted answers. Substring match checks whether a normalized reference answer occurs in the generated response. Scores are reported on a 0–100 scale, and Avg. is the unweighted mean across the six tasks.

We use the default DFM configuration for Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, with the backbone frozen and the same memory predictor, shared projector, fusion layers, and gate initialization as in the QA experiments. DFM uses learning rate

Sequence length is 8K for Code training on Qwen3-4B-Base and 2K for all other backbone–domain pairs. CPT and LoRA use the same data and sequence length as DFM. Both use learning rate

RAG.
RAG uses the frozen Base backbone without additional training. It retrieves the top-1 document from the corresponding domain’s training corpus using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Retrieved Code is prefixed as comments, while Math and Law use a background prefix. The original task prompt is preserved in full; only retrieved background is truncated when the input budget is exceeded. Few-shot examples, sample counts, generation settings, and scorers are identical to Base.
Evaluation.
HumanEval uses three demonstrations and four samples per problem, while HumanEval+ uses zero demonstrations and one sample. Code reports sample-average execution correctness, estimating pass@1. GSM8K uses eight demonstrations and one sample. LawBench evaluates 500 examples for each of its 20 tasks in the zero-shot setting. All methods use a common

article.headline: 分块参数化记忆 DFM：检索查询降 32 倍
article.lede: 上海交大 LUMIA 实验室提出 DFM，把分块级参数化记忆经门控交叉注意力注入解码器隐状态，推理时无需检索。
article.problem: 大模型要可靠回答需要外部知识，但继续预训练会带来灾难性遗忘，推理时检索又增加延迟。已有的参数化记忆（MLP Memory、Memory Decoder 等）依赖 token 级检索目标，离线构建代价高，而且只在输出概率层面做浅层插值融合。
article.method: DFM 把训练序列切成互不重叠的 32-token chunk，只用前一个 chunk 做一次检索，取回 top-16 的 chunk 嵌入作为目标记忆，再由一个因果 Transformer 预测器从池化的 chunk 嵌入回归这组记忆向量。预测记忆经共享投影器映射到解码器隐空间，在选定层通过与自注意力并行的、逐头 sigmoid 门控的交叉注意力写入隐状态。主干全程冻结，记忆预测与融合以语言建模损失加目标记忆 MSE 端到端训练，推理不需要检索或外部编码器。
article.results: 六个 QA 任务上，DFM 在 Mistral-7B-v0.3 上平均 27.21，比最强基线 xRAG 的 24.14 高 12.71%（绝对 +3.07）；在 Qwen3-8B-Base 上平均 26.46，比 MLP Memory 的 23.80 高 11.19%。领域适配上，Qwen3-4B-Base 与 Qwen3-8B-Base 的平均分为 64.69 和 67.52，分别比 Base 提升 6.51 与 4.38 分。构建目标记忆时，检索查询从 4B 降到 125M（减少 96.88%），检索条目从 4.096T 降到 2B（减少 99.95%），即论文所述的 32× 与 2048× 缩减；新增 0.75B 参数（约为 1.5B 配置 MLP Memory 的一半），训练时间由约 64 小时降至 24 小时（减少 62.5%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一条不靠在线检索、也不靠输出概率插值的知识注入路径：chunk 级监督把外部知识写进解码器中间层，让后续层与上下文一起处理，离线构建和训练开销都明显下降。
article.limitations: 提升并不一致：Qwen3-8B-Base 上 WebQA 从 41.78 降到 39.47，2Wiki 上 RAG 的 31.02 仍高于 DFM 的 25.00，Qwen3-4B-Base 的 LawBench 也比 CPT 低 1.25 分。消融均为单次运行且只在 Mistral 上做，QA 推理时用当前提示 chunk 而非训练时的前一个 chunk 构造记忆查询，效率对比也基于特定的 1.5B MLP Memory 配置。
article.figure_caption_zh: DFM 总览：(a) 记忆预测器由池化 chunk 嵌入预测目标记忆；(b) 选定解码器层接入记忆做下一 token 预测；(c) 由前文预测的记忆经逐头门控交叉注意力融合进下一 chunk 的 token 隐状态，推理不需要检索。

figure.caption: Overview of {}. {(a) Memory Prediction.} The memory predictor maps pooled chunk embeddings to predicted memory, supervised by offline target memory. A shared projector maps predicted memory to the decoder's hidden space. {(b) LLM Backbone.} Selected decoder layers incorporate memory for next-token prediction. {(c) Memory Fusion.} Memory predicted from the preceding context supports token predictions in the next chunk. Per-head gates control the memory cross-attention contribution alongside self-attention. Inference requires no retrieval.

page_papers.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
page_papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
page_papers.content:
Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
Woobin Park
Jaeyeon Kim
Yilun Du
Sitan Chen
Bohyung Han
Affiliation:

Abstract
Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference.
This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce
Priming Models
, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a
fixed
noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training.
Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training.
Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at
256
×
256
256\times 256
resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of
1.19
1.19
among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at
https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming
.
Figure 1:
Priming Models
dramatically improve the training compute vs. FID trade-off on ImageNet (
left
). Simple reconstruction pretraining provides an effective initialization that makes subsequent distributional post-training substantially more efficient (
right
).
1
Introduction
A central goal of generative modeling is to achieve high sample quality with efficient training and inference. Diffusion and flow-based models
(
Song et al., 2020
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Lipman et al., 2022
;
Albergo et al., 2025
)
have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities and now serve as backbones for several domains
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Abramson et al., 2024
;
Chi et al., 2025
)
, but they rely on iterative sampling with multiple network evaluations.
This has motivated considerable effort toward one- and few-step generation
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Much of this progress builds on diffusion and flow formulations, including consistency-based modeling
(
Song et al., 2023
;
Lu and Song, 2025
)
, flow-map learning
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
)
, and distributional distillation
(
Luo et al., 2023
;
Yin et al., 2024a
;
Yin et al., 2024b
)
. While promising, these approaches require a considerable amount of extra machinery to work, like specialized stabilization strategies, Jacobian–vector products, classifier-free guidance, a teacher to distill from, etc.
A complementary approach is to train a generator by directly matching its output distribution to the data distribution. This naturally supports generation in a single network evaluation and has a long history in GANs
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
and maximum mean discrepancy-based generators
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
. Translating these objectives into effective training, however, requires significant engineering effort
(
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
.
This latter approach has seen a recent resurgence of interest, with Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
demonstrating that direct distributional learning can produce high-quality one-step generators at scale. Their training recipes nevertheless rely on longer training-time schedules and subtle tricks like style-conditioning
(
Karras et al., 2019
)
. Thus, the simplicity of one-step inference still comes at the cost of substantial complexity in getting these models to train.
In this work, we therefore ask:
Does training a one-step generator need to be this complicated?
We introduce
Priming Models
, a drastically more straightforward framework for one-step generative modeling with just two basic components:
[Stage 1] Reconstruction pretraining:
We pretrain the network with a simple reconstruction objective – in fact, even denoising at a
fixed
corruption level suffices.
[Stage 2] Distributional post-training:
We use the pretrained network directly as a one-step
generator that maps Gaussian noise to samples, then
refine it by matching generated and real distributions
in feature space, e.g., using an optimal transport loss.
Empirically,
Priming Models
achieve strong performance with substantially reduced training compute across three visual domains:
•
ImageNet
: Priming Models achieve state-of-the-art FID (
1.19
)
1

1

(

4.2

(

•

1.9
.
•
World models
: Priming Models outperform the Drifting baseline
(
Lu et al., 2026a
)
with approximately half the training compute, while also achieving performance comparable to the (multi-step) flow matching baseline.
A key factor behind our strong empirical results is that
reconstruction pretraining substantially accelerates distributional post-training
(Figure
1
, right). Without the former, even when the distributional objective provides useful correction directions, the network’s Jacobian may hinder how effectively the parameters update to realize these improvements. Through controlled experiments, we demonstrate that reconstruction pretraining ameliorates this by aligning the Jacobian and shaping how readily the model’s outputs can be refined.
Together, our findings suggest a surprisingly minimal design principle for generative modeling: use reconstruction pretraining to
prepare
a generator for distributional post-training. Priming Models realize this principle, enabling high-quality one-step generators to be efficiently trained from scratch.

One-step samples from Priming Models across three visual domains.
2
Priming Models
We first present our motivation behind
Priming Models
. Distributional objectives, such as Sinkhorn divergence or Wasserstein distance, offer a natural approach to one-step generative modeling by directly matching generated and real distributions. The central challenge, however, lies in translating these objectives into effective training procedures, a difficulty that helped motivate interest in alternatives such as diffusion models
(
Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021
)
. Indeed, early maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based generators were demonstrated on relatively small datasets
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
;
Genevay et al., 2018
)
, while GANs have achieved high-quality generation at scale
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
;
Arjovsky et al., 2017
;
Brock et al., 2018
;
Karras et al., 2019
;
Sauer et al., 2022
)
but remain sensitive to optimization
(
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
.

Our intuition is that distributional training is challenging from scratch because at the start, the network has no information about the structure of natural images. first stage
toward learning the full noise-to-image mapping.

Comparison with other prior work.
Mainstream approaches to one-step generation build on diffusion or flow-matching trajectories
(
Liu et al., 2023a
;
Song et al., 2023
;
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Salimans and Ho, 2022
;
Yin et al., 2024b
)
. In contrast, Priming Models require neither prescribed trajectories nor a pretrained diffusion or flow model.
Recent work
(
Feng et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
uses distributional losses to improve already strong one-step generators. In Priming Models, reconstruction pretraining produces poor initial one-step samples (Figure
1
, right), and distributional post-training enables high-quality generation.
As noted at the beginning of Section
2
, Drifting
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
and W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
train models from scratch using distributional losses. Priming is more efficient than these methods and does not rely on additional modeling components such as classifier-free guidance or style embeddings; refer to Section
3
.
Most closely related to our work, D2O
(
Zheng and Yang, 2025
)
and
Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3)
demonstrate the conversion of multi-step diffusion models into one-step generators. Priming Models build on this perspective, but our results show that starting from a multi-step model is unnecessary: even denoising at a single fixed noise level without time conditioning, as well as alternative pretraining objectives (Section
4.1
), can provide an effective initialization for distributional post-training. Appendix
A
provides further discussion.

Fréchet distance
(
Dowson and Landau, 1982

is widely used to evaluate generative models, but directly optimizing it was believed to be challenging, as reliable estimation typically requires tens of thousands of samples. FD-loss

5
Conclusion
In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generative models end-to-end. Reconstruction pretraining prepares the generator for efficient distributional post-training, enabling strong empirical performance across multiple visual domains.
That said, our work leaves several open questions. Priming Models rely on pretrained feature encoders. Although we demonstrate our method with multiple sets of feature encoders, this dependence raises the question of whether it can be eliminated. The relationship between reconstruction pretraining and Jacobian alignment also warrants deeper investigation. Finally, closing the remaining performance gap with multi-step diffusion and flow models remains an important challenge.
Outlook.
More broadly, our results suggest that we may be overthinking the problem: the specialized formulations and elaborate training machinery used in prior work are not the only path to train one-step generators. We hope our work opens the door to simpler and more scalable approaches to one-step generative modeling.

Appendix A
Related Work
In this section, we review prior work on one- and few-step generative modeling, organized by their methodological category.
Category 1: Trajectory straightening and flow-map learning.
These lines of work obtain few-step generative models by learning from a diffusion or probability-flow trajectory. Progressive distillation repeatedly compresses a teacher sampler into fewer steps
(
Salimans and Ho, 2022
)
. Consistency Models instead enforce agreement among predictions made at different points along the same trajectory
(
Song et al., 2023
)
, while subsequent work improves their stability and scaling or extends consistency to trajectory segments
(
Geng et al., 2025
;
Song and Dhariwal, 2024
;
Lu and Song, 2025
;
Kim et al., 2024
)
. Rectified Flow and reflow
(
Liu et al., 2023a
;
Liu et al., 2023b
)
seek straighter transport paths that are easier to integrate in few steps. These straightening methods modify the coupling and resulting trajectory so that coarse numerical integration can accurately reach its endpoint.
A related but distinct family learns the finite-time transition across an interval of a flow-matching trajectory, such as a flow map or average velocity. This includes Flow Map Matching, Shortcut Models, MeanFlow, Improved MeanFlow, and Inductive Moment Matching
(
Boffi et al., 2024
;
Frans et al., 2025
;
Geng et al., 2026a
;
Geng et al., 2026b
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
. These methods differ in their targets and training estimators, but generally supervise a particular time-dependent transport or consistency relation.
Priming:
Priming Models do not attempt to recover a prescribed trajectory or flow map: reconstruction pretraining provides an initialization for the network, which we then directly use as a one-step generator.
Category 2: Teacher-guided distillation.
Another line of work distills a pretrained diffusion teacher into a one-step student, with much of the focus on designing effective distillation objectives. Diff-Instruct
(
Luo et al., 2023
)
uses score-based distributional objectives derived from a diffusion teacher, while DMD and DMD2
(
Yin et al., 2024b
;
Yin et al., 2024a
)
optimize the student using the difference between teacher and student score estimates. Score Identity Distillation
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
provides a related score-based formulation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation combines score distillation with an adversarial objective to improve fidelity in the low-step regime
(
Sauer et al., 2024
)
.
Priming:
These approaches inherit the cost and machinery required to obtain and query that teacher. In contrast, Priming Models are trained from scratch and therefore do not require a pretrained teacher.
Category 3:Distributional loss (from scratch).
Directly matching a generator distribution to the data distribution has a long history. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn a one-pass generator through an adversarially trained discriminator
(
Goodfellow et al., 2014
)
, with Wasserstein objectives and regularization improving the geometry and stability of training
(
Arjovsky et al., 2017
;
Gulrajani et al., 2017
;
Mescheder et al., 2018
)
. Generative Moment Matching Networks use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in place of adversarial discrimination, while MMD-GANs further learn the MMD kernel adversarially
(
Li et al., 2015
;
Li et al., 2017
)
.
Genevay et al. (2018)
trains implicit generative models directly using a Sinkhorn divergence. These works, however, are limited in empirical scope and, more importantly, differ from Priming Models in that we apply the distributional objective after a reconstruction pretraining stage.
Recent works revisit direct one-step learning at a more practical scale. YOSO
(
Luo et al., 2024
)
stabilizes adversarial one-step training through a self-cooperative diffusion GAN, while Adversarial Flow
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
trains with an adversarial objective but constrains the generator to learn the deterministic transport map associated with flow matching.
Priming:
Priming Models share the goal of direct distribution matching, but do not optimize it from random initialization: reconstruction pretraining first teaches the generator to correct corrupted inputs toward clean images, after which a distributional objective refines it into a one-step generator.
Category 3-1: Drifting Models.
Drifting Models
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
construct an attraction-repulsion field using a normalized Laplacian kernel and train the generator to match stop-gradient targets obtained by displacing its generated features along this field. W-Flow
(
Han et al., 2026
)
derives a training-time velocity field from the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Sinkhorn divergence, using barycentric projections computed from entropic optimal transport plans.
Van Assel et al. (2026)
additionally examine how the choice of frozen feature space affects transport stability in distribution matching.
Priming:
Priming Models introduce reconstruction pretraining before distributional optimization, and this stage is key to our strong compute vs. quality trade-off.
Our implementation also seeks to dispense with the additional engineering machinery used in these works. Both reported ImageNet architectures include learned random style embeddings, and both frameworks support classifier-free guidance; Drifting additionally normalizes its constructed drift field. Priming does not use these additional mechanisms and instead optimizes an OT-based distributional surrogate. All four models reported in Section
3
share exactly the same post-training configuration, further illustrating the simplicity of our approach.
This suggests that reconstruction pretraining can make distributional optimization more efficient while supporting a simpler training recipe. We hypothesize that this initialization reduces the need for additional training mechanisms, although our experiments do not isolate their individual contributions.
Category 4: Distributional loss (fine-tuning).
Distributional objectives have also been used to adapt pretrained generative models. MMD-DDM
(
Aiello et al., 2023
)
fine-tunes pretrained diffusion models with MMD to improve quality under a restricted sampling-step budget. DiffRatio
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
estimates the density ratio between noisy real and generated distributions to train a one-step model without a teacher score. FD-loss
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
makes feature-space Fréchet distance practical as a training objective by maintaining population-level feature statistics, and applies it to pretrained one- and multi-step generators. More recently, iRDM
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
scales MMD-based post-training across multiple pretrained representation spaces.
Most closely related to our work, D2O
(
Zheng and Yang, 2025
)
shows that adversarial fine-tuning alone can convert a pretrained diffusion model into a one-step generator, while
Yang et al. (2026, Section 4.3)
show that FD-loss can convert JiT, a multi-step diffusion model, into a competitive one-step generator.
Priming:
Priming Models build on the perspective that pretraining can prepare a network for subsequent distributional optimization. We investigate how simple this pretraining task can be, showing that reconstruction—even denoising at a single fixed noise level without noise-level conditioning—can provide an effective initialization for our distributional training, despite poor initial one-step samples (Figure
1
, right). We further examine alternative pretraining tasks (Section
4.1
) within the same framework.
Finally, viewing reconstruction pretraining and distributional post-training as a complete training procedure also enables comparisons with prior methods based on total training compute across both stages, measured in EFLOPs.

article.headline: 一步生成不必这么复杂：先重建再匹配分布
article.lede: 研究者提出 Priming Models：先在固定噪声水平做去噪重建预训练，再做特征空间分布后训练，ImageNet 一
article.problem: 扩散与流匹配模型推理时需要多次网络评估，一步生成因此成为热门方向，但现有方法大多依赖一致性蒸馏、流映射或带有教师模型的分布蒸馏，需要稳定化技巧、雅可比向量积、无分类器引导等大量额外机制。直接匹配分布的路线（GAN、MMD、Drifting、W-Flow）虽支持单步采样，却要靠长训练计划和风格条件等技巧才能训起来，训练成本依然高昂。作者因此追问：训练一步生成器真的需要这么复杂吗？
article.method: 论文把训练拆成两个阶段，且两个阶段优化同一个网络。第一阶段是重建预训练：在固定噪声水平 s=0.8 下做像素空间去噪重建（可加 LPIPS、ConvNeXt 感知损失），论文称即使把噪声水平取为单点分布也足够。第二阶段把该网络直接当作从高斯噪声到图像的一步生成器，用冻结特征编码器在特征空间做分布匹配，目标为 Sinkhorn/最优传输损失的 stop-gradient 代理，也可换成 MMD 或更简单的平均成对距离。
article.results: 在 ImageNet 256×256 上，Priming-L（预训练 160 epoch）取得一步生成器中最低的 FID 1.19 与 FDr5 7.10，总训练成本 238.95 EFLOPs，论文称约为 Drifting 的十分之一算力。文本到图像方面，logit-normal 噪声调度的版本在 GenEval 得 0.818、DPG-Bench 得 82.16，优于一步 MeanFlow；固定 s=0.8 的版本训练算力 293.53 EFLOPs，相对 MeanFlow 基线减少 1.86 倍。世界模型上，RT-1 的 FID 为 3.16（DriftWorld 为 8.99），训练算力比 DriftWorld 少 59.7%（12.37 对 30.71 EFLOPs），Bridge-V2 少 74.4%（9.50 对 37.05 EFLOPs）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把一步生成的门槛从“复杂蒸馏流水线”降到“一次简单重建预训练加一次分布后训练”，在三个视觉域上同时推进了训练算力与生成质量的帕累托前沿，并给出雅可比对齐这一可检验的机制解释。
article.limitations: 方法仍依赖冻结的预训练特征编码器（ResNet-MAE、ConvNeXt、SigLIP 等），作者自己把“能否去掉这一依赖”列为开放问题；雅可比对齐的证据主要来自 ImageNet 上的受控实验，且 ConvNeXt 全局均值特征并未跟随 FID 排序，说明该解释并不普遍成立；与多步扩散/流模型之间仍存在性能差距，且原文注明 FD-loss 报告的 FID 0.72 被排除在比较之外。

page_papers.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose RSIFlow, a Recursive Self-Improvement framework that integrates adaptive workflow orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose
RSIFlow
, a
R
ecursive
S
elf-
I
mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work
flow
orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
Figure 1:
Motivation of RSIFlow.
(A) Two coupled challenges in RSI.
(B) The execution loop of RSIFlow.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle complex tasks in coding, tool use, and multi-hop question answering
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2023
)
. To continuously enhance the development of agents’ capabilities in task domains, existing methods have adopted complementary approaches, including evolving execution harnesses
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, optimizing model parameters
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
, and refining executable artifacts
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
. These routes can be organized into self-improvement workflows that propose and evaluate changes using task feedback. Beyond executing such workflows, recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to strengthen not only task-solving capabilities but also the mechanisms that generate subsequent improvements
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Duan et al., 2026
)
.
Research on agent self-improvement spans three increasingly broad scopes of optimization. Component-level approaches optimize a predefined part of the system, such as the model or the harness (execution workflows)
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. System-level approaches coordinate updates across components, including joint model–harness optimization and feedback-driven selection of update targets
(
Chen et al., 2026d
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
. Meta-level approaches make improvement procedures editable through operator scheduling, program modification, and recursive skill evolution
(
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. These developments expand both what can be modified and how modifications are organized. However, broader editability alone does not establish how effectively a workflow addresses the agent’s current bottlenecks, or whether the ability to organize that workflow improves with experience. This motivates a central question:
how can RSI systems adapt self-improvement workflows to evolving bottlenecks while learning to organize these workflows more effectively?
We formulate this challenge as
dynamic workflow adaptation
in RSI, where adapting bottlenecks and evolving workflow orchestration must be considered together. As illustrated in Fig.
1
, self-improvement workflows must adapt to bottlenecks that vary with task requirements and the agent’s capability state. Even within a fixed domain, successful updates can reshape these bottlenecks and alter the effectiveness of subsequent workflow orchestration. Meanwhile, workflow orchestration is itself a capability that can improve through experience. Feedback from workflow execution supports the accumulation and refinement of reusable knowledge for diagnosis, workflow selection, and execution. These processes form a feedback loop: task-level updates reshape improvement requirements, while workflow experience refines the orchestration capability that guides subsequent updates.
To address this challenge, we propose
RSIFlow
, a framework that couples
adaptive workflow orchestration
with
meta-agent capability evolution
. We instantiate three self-improvement workflows targeting the
Harness
,
Model
, and
Artifacts
. A meta-agent uses execution trajectories and environmental feedback to diagnose the task agent’s bottlenecks, select a workflow, and orchestrate candidate generation and validation. It then distills orchestration outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles to revise its own harness, including execution procedures and skill invocation. This experience-driven self-revision closes a recursive feedback loop in which workflow orchestration outcomes refine the orchestration mechanism that guides subsequent improvements.
Our main contributions are:
•
We formulate
dynamic workflow adaptation
as a key challenge in RSI, highlighting the coupling between evolving performance bottlenecks and continual refinement of workflow orchestration.
•
We propose
RSIFlow
, which adaptively organizes self-improvement workflows and uses their observed outcomes to evolve the meta-agent’s own harness, including its execution procedures and reusable skills.
•
We evaluate
RSIFlow
across six benchmarks and two backbones, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of the 12 benchmark–backbone settings. Ablations support the benefits of both adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.
2
Related Work
Component-Specific Self-Improvement.
Many approaches to agent self-improvement optimize a single predefined component. STaR
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
)
improves model parameters by repeatedly fine-tuning on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers. AFlow
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
searches code-represented workflows, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
refines prompt-level harness specifications using pairwise feedback over revision histories. Related approaches include DSPy
(
Khattab et al., 2024
)
for language-model pipeline optimization, GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
for reflective prompt evolution, and ADAS
(
Hu et al., 2025
)
for meta-agent-guided search over agent programs. In contrast, AlphaEvolve
(
Novikov et al., 2025
)
evolves candidate programs through execution-based evaluation, targeting task artifacts rather than the agent’s improvement procedure. Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
iteratively revises outputs using self-feedback, while Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
retains verbal reflections to guide subsequent attempts and Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
accumulates reusable executable skills. Co-Harness
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
and HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
connect external structure and internal capability by alternating harness refinement with model optimization. Their coupled updates address model–harness compatibility, but the prescribed update order leaves open how to adapt workflow orchestration targets to evolving bottlenecks.
Figure 2:
Overview of RSIFlow.
(A)
Definition of task domains and agent workflows.
(B)
The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback.
(C)
The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows.
(D)
Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness.
The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.
Adaptive and Recursive Self-Improvement.
Beyond prescribed alternation, SIA
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
uses trajectory and performance feedback to choose between harness and weight updates, while its selection policy relies on a frozen language-model prior. HASE
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
integrates task solving and harness editing into one action space and trains the policy with GRPO. A complementary direction makes the improver itself editable: Hyperagents
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
co-evolves task-agent and meta-agent programs and demonstrates transferable improvement strategies, whereas MetaSkill-Evolve
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
recursively updates task skills and their improvement procedures on different timescales. Building on these complementary directions, RSIFlow couples bottleneck-aware workflow orchestration with feedback-driven Meta-Harness evolution.

Ablation Study
Table

evaluates adaptive workflow orchestration and Meta-Agent evolution over five rounds. Compared with Vanilla, RSIFlow improves Code, Tool Use, and SearchQA by 19.04%, 3.92%, and 18.20% , respectively, increasing the three-domain average by 13.72 %. While fixed-component workflows exhibit domain-specific strengths, adaptive orchestration achieves the highest scores across all three domains, outperforming the fixed workflow by 4.13% - 8.81% on average. Overall, RSIFlow exceeds the average of all four ablated variants by 6.17 %. Disabling Meta-Agent evolution reduces average performance by 5.74 % , highlighting the importance of distilling historical feedback into reusable skills and principles. These results demonstrate that adaptive component orchestration enables balanced cross-domain improvements, while experience-driven Meta-Harness evolution further strengthens workflow effectiveness.

Rollout-budget and performance efficiency.
Fig.
3
compares performance under varying rollout budgets on all six benchmarks. RSIFlow generally lies on or near the empirical
Pareto frontier and achieves the highest observed score on each
benchmark. This advantage is consistent with its adaptive component
selection and Task–Meta co-evolution: RSIFlow reuses rollout
evidence to guide targeted updates to the Task-Agent’s Model,
Harness, or Artifacts, rather than relying solely on additional
exploration under a fixed harness. The co-evolving Meta-Agent
further distills workflow outcomes into reusable skills and
refines its improvement procedure, allowing accumulated experience
to guide subsequent updates. Together, these mechanisms help
concentrate the rollout budget on informed workflow orchestration. Overall, RSIFlow offers a stronger performance–budget trade-off than the evaluated baselines.
Meta-agent backbone sensitivity.
We evaluate RSIFlow with three Meta-Agent backbones over five evolution rounds on HumanEval+. As shown in Fig.
4
, all three models achieve overall performance improvements, with gains of 11.48%, 5.09%, and 24.41% for Claude-Sonnet-5, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-5.6-Sol, respectively. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest final performance of 68.29%, albeit with greater API token consumption. From Round 3 to Round 5, it improves by 13.08%, compared with 6.15% and 4.17% for the other two backbones, suggesting that stronger Meta-Agents may better leverage accumulated intervention feedback. These results demonstrate that RSIFlow supports different Meta-Agent backbones, while the Meta-Agent’s underlying capabilities influence the cumulative effectiveness of recursive self-improvement.
Meta-evolution necessity analysis.
Table 3 compares different Meta versions improving the same initial Task-Agent, with scores averaged over two benchmarks per domain. Meta0 improves SearchQA by 10.10%, reaching 44.62% through harness updates. Although Meta4 also selects the harness, it further outperforms Meta0 by 20.56% and 9.51% on Code and SearchQA, respectively. Meta3 achieves the highest Tool Use score of 31.83% through artifact updates. These results indicate that the evolution of meta-agent capabilities not only enables better adaptive workflow orchestration but also enhances the performance of workflow orchestration across different task domains. 5
Conclusion
We presented
RSIFlow
, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling adaptive workflow orchestration with Meta-Agent evolution. Using accumulated execution feedback, the Meta-Agent identifies Task-Agent bottlenecks and selects Model, Harness, or Artifacts workflows. It distills successful and unsuccessful outcomes into reusable skills and principles to evolve its Meta-Harness. Across six benchmarks and two backbones, RSIFlow outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in 11 of 12 settings. Ablations validate both mechanisms, while budget analyses show a favorable performance–budget trade-off. These results demonstrate that continual Meta-Agent evolution enhances system effectiveness alongside adaptive workflow orchestration.
Limitations
RSIFlow is primarily evaluated using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as Task-Agent backbones. This setting is particularly relevant to resource-constrained agent deployments, where adaptive workflow orchestration enables targeted modifications to identified bottleneck components, while Meta-Agent evolution further improves bottleneck diagnosis and orchestration capabilities. However, whether these benefits remain significant with larger backbone models and at cluster scale remains unexplored. Future work will extend the evaluation to larger-scale settings to assess the scalability of RSIFlow.
RSIFlow couples the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent, evolving the Meta-Harness through reusable skills and general principles to improve workflow orchestration without updating the Meta-Agent’s model parameters. However, this process introduces additional computational overhead, while adopting a lower-cost Meta-Agent may compromise evolution gains. Moreover, the stability of experience-driven Meta-Harness updates remains to be fully investigated. Future work will explore counterfactual analysis to identify Meta-Agent deficiencies, apply targeted local modifications, and investigate Meta-Agent parameter optimization to improve evolution efficiency and stability.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
We evaluate self-improvement across code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. This section describes the six benchmarks, the update mechanisms of the baselines, and the experimental configurations. Appendix
B
gives the algorithms for the three intervention routes.
A.1
Training and Reporting Data
Our evolution pool contains 3,000 distinct training tasks,
partitioned into five task-disjoint batches of 600 tasks each.
Each round uses 200 code-generation tasks, 200 tool-use tasks,
and 200 multi-hop questions. The fixed reporting set contains
744 tasks. Table
4
gives the
dataset-level allocation.
Code generation.
TACO
Li et al. (2023)
contains algorithmic programming problems that
require implementing a program from a natural-language
specification and satisfying its input/output contract.
We use 1,000 training problems from the TACO portion of the
DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset
.
The selected tasks include standard-input/output and
function-based interfaces, with correctness assessed by
executing the submitted program against task-specific tests.
They provide execution trajectories and feedback for
improving program construction, interface handling, and
algorithmic reasoning. The allocation contributes 200 tasks
per evolution round; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are reserved for
reporting evaluation.
Tool use.
EnvScaler
Song et al. (2026)
provides executable, stateful environments
in which agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls.
Each task specifies a user goal and an initial environment
state; the agent must choose tools, construct arguments, and
adapt its actions to returned observations. Task-specific
validation checks assess whether the resulting state satisfies
the goal.
We allocate 1,000 scenarios to training, comprising 824 from
the source dataset’s
train
split and 176 from its
heldout
split. Both source partitions are assigned to
the training role in our study; tool-use reporting uses
BFCL-v3 and ACEBench. Each evolution round contains 200
EnvScaler scenarios. Different training tasks may share an
environment, so the round-disjoint allocation refers to task
instances rather than environment families.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
contains
questions that require combining evidence across Wikipedia
passages, including bridge and comparison questions.
2WikiMultiHopQA
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
requires following multi-hop relations across entities and
combining the retrieved facts into an answer. We select 500
questions from the official training split of each dataset.
The Task-Agent retrieves evidence through the search interface
and produces an answer, providing trajectories for improving
evidence retrieval and multi-step reasoning. Each round uses
100 HotpotQA and 100 2WikiMultiHopQA training questions.
Reporting uses a separate fixed set of 100 questions from
each dataset’s official development split.

A.2
Benchmark Descriptions
The reporting set contains 744 tasks: 342 code-generation tasks, 202 tool-use tasks, and 200 multi-hop questions. Each method is evaluated on the same task IDs with the same benchmark-specific scorer. Table
5
summarizes the task counts and reported metrics.
Code generation.
HumanEval+
asks the agent to implement a Python function from its signature and natural-language specification. Its 164 tasks test functional correctness, including edge cases exposed by the augmented EvalPlus tests
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
MBPP+
asks for short Python programs from natural-language descriptions and illustrative tests, covering basic algorithms, data structures, and program construction. We use a frozen 178-task subset of MBPP+ v0.2.0.
For both benchmarks, a task succeeds when the final submitted program passes the base and augmented test suites. We report system pass@1: one final submission per task after the allowed agent execution. HumanEval+ uses v0.1.10, and both benchmarks use EvalPlus revision
26d6d00
with the recorded parser and process-isolation adapters.
Tool use.
BFCL-v3
evaluates function selection and argument construction in single-call, multiple-call, parallel-call, relevance, and multi-turn settings
(
Patil et al., 2025
)
. These settings cover complementary aspects of tool use: selecting an appropriate function, supplying the required arguments, coordinating multiple calls, and determining whether an available tool is relevant to the request. The multi-turn tasks also test whether the agent maintains context across stateful tool interactions, connecting individual call decisions to the evolving interaction history. Our subset contains 152 tasks across 17 categories; native category-specific checks determine correctness, and the aggregate is weighted by the number of tasks. This weighting reflects the composition of the evaluated subset, with categories containing more tasks contributing proportionally more to the reported aggregate.
ACEBench
evaluates API use under Normal, Special, and Agent settings, including ordinary function calls, incomplete or ambiguous instructions, and multi-step interactions
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Together, these settings examine how agents translate user requests into API actions under different instruction and interaction conditions. We use 50 English tasks, which produce 57 native scoring records. We report the native weighted score and separately retain complete-task success; these quantities use different denominators. The distinction matters because one task can contribute more than one native scoring record. Record-level scoring describes the evaluator’s individual scoring units, whereas complete-task success summarizes outcomes at the original task level. We therefore specify both task and scoring-record counts when describing this evaluation.
Multi-hop question answering.
HotpotQA
requires combining evidence from multiple Wikipedia passages to answer bridge or comparison questions
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
. We use 100 development questions with the v1 fullwiki protocol.
2WikiMultiHopQA
requires composing facts about multiple entities along multi-hop reasoning chains
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
; we use 100 development questions and the original v1 evaluator.
These tasks test whether agents can connect dispersed evidence and resolve questions requiring relational reasoning.
For both benchmarks, the agent retrieves evidence through the search interface and submits an answer. The main metric is normalized answer-token F1, with exact match (EM) retained separately. The evaluator revisions are
3635853
for HotpotQA and
13800e5
for 2WikiMultiHopQA.

A.3
Training–Evaluation Separation
We separate training-time evolution from evaluation on the
744-task reporting set. For each evaluated evolution horizon
n
n
, we first complete
n
n
rounds on training tasks and then
evaluate the resulting system on the reporting set. Reporting
tasks are excluded from Task-model fine-tuning. Reporting-set
scores and item-level evaluation feedback are never used for
workflow selection, candidate acceptance, skill maintenance,
Meta-Harness revision, or manual selection of system versions.
Evaluations at different horizons measure the corresponding
training-derived states; their results are not fed back into
subsequent evolution.
The gain-based acceptance
rule in the evolution algorithm applies only to training-time
batches. The batch-level Artifacts procedure, including its
two-attempt allowance and fallback to the parent, is not run on
the reporting set. During reporting, the skill library and
Meta-Harness remain fixed across tasks. Permitted environment
feedback includes execution-interface signals such as
context-length limit errors and output-length or format
violations; it does not provide access to the reporting
evaluator for optimization or output selection. Reference
answers and hidden-test correctness signals are likewise
excluded from generation and output selection. All compared
methods receive the same environment feedback, tool permissions,
and per-task execution budgets.
We additionally checked the frozen training and reporting
manifests for overlap in task identifiers, recorded normalized
prompt hashes, and recorded task-group identifiers, finding no
matches between the two sets. This check establishes separation
under these matching criteria; it does not assess semantic
paraphrases or contamination in the backbone models’
pretraining data. Equal per-task execution budgets likewise do
not imply equal total evolution cost.
