A.4
Baseline Configurations
We compare seven baselines using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Within each backbone scale, the comparison protocol uses a common initial checkpoint and Task-Harness, task IDs, and evaluators. Table
6
summarizes editable Task components, weight training, Harness updates, adaptive component selection, and Meta-Agent evolution. These dimensions distinguish how each baseline allocates adaptation across model parameters, task components, and orchestration.
Model updates.
SFT
trains on successful Task-Agent trajectories while keeping the Harness fixed.
GRPO
samples groups of trajectories, scores their task outcomes, and updates the model using group-relative rewards
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
. Both methods improve the Task model without a component-selection mechanism.
Harness and joint updates.
AFlow
searches executable agent workflows through iterative proposal and evaluation
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
MermaidFlow
represents workflows as graphs and searches their structure
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
. These are the Harness-only configurations used in the main comparison.
HarnessForge
combines feedback-guided Harness modification with model training in a prescribed co-adaptation procedure
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
.
SIA
uses execution feedback to choose between Harness and model updates
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
)
.
Meta-Agent evolution.
HyperAgents
makes both the Task-Agent and Meta-Agent programs editable, allowing the improvement procedure itself to evolve
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. Its code-editing mechanism differs from parameter training.
RSIFlow
selects among Model, Harness, and Artifacts interventions and updates its Meta-Harness through accumulated intervention skills. The comparison therefore separates access to multiple Task-update routes from the ability to revise the Meta-Agent that chooses and implements them.
A.5
Hyperparameter Settings
The main configuration uses Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B as the Task model and GPT-5.6 Sol as the Meta model. Each of the five evolution rounds permits at most two candidate attempts. Candidates share the same parent, training batch, and evaluator; the first valid candidate with positive paired gain is accepted. Meta model parameters remain fixed throughout evolution.

The loop has two coupled outputs: an accepted Task state and an updated improvement mechanism. Every candidate starts from the same round parent, so rejected edits do not accumulate. Failed implementation attempts and non-improving evaluations still enter the experience record. On a new task batch, task-bound outputs are generated anew; reusable knowledge is carried by the Meta-Harness and accepted changes to the Task model or Harness.
B.2
Workflow Orchestration
The Meta workflow connects six operations: evidence collection, diagnosis, skill retrieval, component intervention, paired evaluation, and skill integration. Diagnosis returns a bottleneck hypothesis with trajectory references; retrieval returns applicable procedures and counterexamples; intervention returns a candidate and its change record; evaluation returns paired outcomes; integration returns the next active skill set and the Action changes needed to use it.
A decision record binds the selected component to its expected behavioral effect and preservation constraints before construction. The Model branch receives eligible trajectories and a training configuration; the Harness branch receives a localized modification brief and interface contract; the Artifacts branch receives the Task’s own output and permitted feedback. Evaluation determines Task acceptance, while the entire record informs Meta evolution. An accepted Task change and a revised Meta procedure are thus separate decisions within the same loop.

B.4
Harness Updates
Harness intervention changes how the agent executes tasks. Meta localizes a recurring execution defect, refines a modification brief, generates a complete implementation, and validates it. The functional components are Action, Skill, and Planning; concrete modules may implement context organization, action handling, memory retrieval, or verification. Localization identifies the mechanism to change, rather than merely listing files. Executable checks establish that a candidate can run. Acceptance additionally requires a positive paired task gain. An output-contract check can ensure that a coding task receives source code, whereas a receipt-grounded completion check can ensure that a tool operation has actually succeeded. These are changes to reusable execution behavior.

A general principle abstracts a shared decision criterion from component-specific cases. For example, completion requiring task-appropriate evidence connects a source-code contract check with a tool-receipt check, while their implementations remain separate. D.3
Component-Specific Skills and a General Principle
The cards in Appendix
F.3
present three component-specific procedures
and one general selection principle. The Harness and Model cards
summarize stored procedures and their observed feedback.
The Artifacts card formulates feedback-guided revision of the
Task-Agent’s own output under a limited budget. The final card
synthesizes how failure scope and intervention cost guide
component selection.
Applicability conditions determine when a procedure can be reused.
On a new task, Meta retrieves relevant revision guidance and
uses it to guide the Task-Agent in revising that task’s own output from its feedback.
The Artifacts procedure and general principle express
methodological guidance rather than additional measured
intervention outcomes.
Harness skills: repair a reusable execution rule.
The submission-contract skill applies when the required deliverable is source code but the agent returns prose or execution output. Its reusable content is the condition under which a complete-source check should be invoked and the execution behavior that enforces it. Reuse therefore changes how subsequent tasks are handled by the Harness. A valid submission can still contain an algorithmic error, so satisfying the output contract resolves an interface failure without establishing semantic correctness. This distinction explains why later feedback can motivate a different intervention route.
Model skills: construct an eligible learning signal.
The replay skill describes how verified successful Task-Agent calls become training examples. Checkpoint provenance, task identity, native success, and target validity determine whether a call provides suitable evidence for the update. Reusing this skill means applying the same data-selection and training procedure to the current parent and available trajectories. R4 supplements M1 because it provides another observed response to that procedure. The added evidence informs when replay is useful; it does not imply that increasing replay volume always improves every task domain.
Artifacts skills: revise the current deliverable.
The output-revision skill targets a defect that permitted feedback localizes within the Task-Agent’s current submission. Its steps operate through the existing interface: inspect the feedback, edit the relevant output, test the revision, and resubmit within budget. The reusable element is this conditional repair procedure, including the circumstances in which further retries are unlikely to help. A later task supplies its own program or answer and its own feedback. Thus, the skill can guide a new revision without transferring the earlier answer or changing the Task-Harness.
General principles: connect diagnosis to intervention scope.
A general principle connects these procedures through a shared decision criterion. The same failed coding task may require a submission check, learning from successful trajectories, or a local program edit. The relevant distinction is where the failure occurs and which available intervention can address it under the remaining budget. A bounded output repair is appropriate when the feedback identifies an actionable defect; a recurring execution problem motivates a Harness change, while a persistent capability gap with eligible training data motivates a Model update. The principle guides this comparison while component-specific skills supply the concrete procedure.

HHMMA illustrates knowledge development: H1 supplies a contract-checking criterion for H2 at R2; M1 accumulates training response evidence at R4; and R5 formulates a bounded output-repair procedure for local code defects. From a retrieved record to an executable intervention.
Retrieval provides Meta with a procedure; integration guides its use in the next attempt. Applicability informs diagnosis, procedures inform modification briefs, and preservation requirements constrain construction and validation. For example, a receipt-grounded skill links an unsupported completion claim to the evidence needed for assessment. The Harness change implements this check; paired evaluation determines whether it improves task outcomes. This chain connects the stored lesson to an intervention whose effects can be examined.

Appendix E
Extended Related Work
Agent System Design and Adaptation.
Recent work on LLM agents explores approaches to adapting execution structures, maintaining persistent memory, and coordinating information acquisition. HarnessForge
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
jointly evolves execution harnesses and reasoning policies through failure-guided harness modification and harness-conditioned policy alignment. For persistent memory, All-Mem
(
Lv et al., 2026a
)
separates online retrieval from offline topology consolidation, preserving evidence while supporting retrieval under bounded computational budgets. Typed links enable budgeted expansion from anchors to archived evidence. For breadth-oriented information gathering, moreover, A-MapReduce
(
Chen et al., 2026c
)
decomposes wide-search objectives into parallel retrieval tasks and aggregates results, using experiential memory to refine task allocation and recomposition. These approaches improve how agents organize execution and retain or acquire information, with emphases on system compatibility, memory maintenance, and scalability.
Structured Supervision and Credit Assignment.
A complementary line of research studies the structure and granularity of supervision for agent learning and language model post-training. GEAR
(
Lv et al., 2026b
)
models prerequisite and activation dependencies among rubric criteria with a probabilistic graphical framework, suppressing unsupported criterion contributions when constructing scalar rewards. The resulting reward captures criterion dependencies at the response level. For long-horizon agent distillation, AlignOPSD
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
aligns privileged supervision with functionally corresponding decisions and distributes outcome-based credit across variable-duration decision spans and their constituent turns. TRCA
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
derives step-level supervision from action-induced state transitions using Evidence, Execution, and Invalidity rubrics. Its foundational reward evaluates local transition quality, while its breakthrough reward recognizes newly satisfied task conditions, providing fine-grained learning signals without requiring successful reference trajectories or learned process evaluators, even when terminal success feedback is sparse.

article.headline: 元智能体自我进化，RSIFlow 六基准平均居首
article.lede: RSIFlow 让元智能体诊断任务智能体的瓶颈、自适应选择改进工作流，并把执行经验蒸馏为可复用技能，六个基准平均分均领先
article.problem: 现有自我改进方法多针对预设组件做优化：模型参数、执行框架 harness 或可执行产物；递归自我改进进一步把改进机制本身也变成可编辑对象。但该修哪里取决于任务需求与智能体能力状态共同塑造的瓶颈，而瓶颈会随成功更新而迁移；同时，如何编排工作流本身也是一种可以靠经验变强的能力，这两件事此前没有被放进同一个反馈回路。
article.method: RSIFlow 把任务智能体与元智能体定义为联合状态：元智能体依据执行轨迹与环境反馈诊断瓶颈，在 Model、Harness、Artifacts 三条组件级改进工作流中选择一条执行，候选必须在同一训练批次上取得正增益才会被接受，否则沿用父代状态。每轮结束后，元智能体对齐父代与候选轨迹，蒸馏出组件级技能与跨组件原则，经添加、补充、修订、合并四种证据驱动操作维护技能库，并据此改写自身的 Meta-Harness（动作接口、检索调用、执行指令），而其基座模型参数始终保持冻结。
article.results: 在 HumanEval+/MBPP+、BFCL-v3/ACEBench、HotpotQA/2Wiki 六个基准与 Qwen3-4B、Qwen3-8B 两个主干上，RSIFlow 在 12 个基准-主干组合中的 11 个取得最佳，总体得分 51.21%（4B）与 59.86%（8B），分别比最强基线高 6.06% 与 3.86%，逐指标平均提升 3.11%；HumanEval+ 上 4B 的 pass@1 提升 14.02%。消融显示，相对 Vanilla，Code、Tool Use、SearchQA 分别提升 19.04%、3.92%、18.20%，三域平均提升 13.72%；关闭元智能体进化使平均性能下降 5.74%。五轮案例（Harness–Harness–Model–Model–Artifacts）的分数轨迹为 32.23→38.04→45.46→47.11→51.21。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「改哪个组件」与「如何学会更好地改」放进同一个闭环，说明编排能力本身可以通过执行反馈递归积累，而不必更新元智能体的参数。
article.limitations: 作者自陈的局限包括：仅在 Qwen3-4B/8B 两个较小主干上评测，更大模型与集群规模下收益是否成立仍属未知；技能与 Meta-Harness 的更新带来额外算力开销，换用更便宜的元智能体可能削弱进化收益，且经验驱动更新的稳定性尚未充分研究。此外元智能体固定使用 GPT-5.6 Sol，案例研究只展示单条演化路径，单个技能的因果贡献并未被单独隔离。
article.figure_caption_zh: RSIFlow 总览：任务智能体执行任务并采集轨迹与反馈，元智能体检索技能自适应编排 Model/Harness/Artifacts 改进工作流，再把结果蒸馏为技能、原则与更新后的 Meta-Harness，从而闭合递归自我改进回路。

figure.caption: {Overview of RSIFlow.} {(A)} Definition of task domains and agent workflows. {(B)} The Task-Agent executes tasks to collect trajectories and feedback. {(C)} The Meta-Agent retrieves skills to adaptively orchestrate workflows. {(D)} Workflow results are distilled into skills, principles and Meta-Harness. The updated Meta-Harness guides subsequent orchestration, closing the recursive self-improvement loop.

page_papers.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
page_papers.abstract: Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose CoPE, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, CoPE trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, τ^2-bench, and AppWorld), CoPE (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to 1.9times and 2.0times higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead. The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.

Key challenges
. Both existing prediction targets are difficult to construct effectively in complex agentic environments.
(1)
Value targets are derived from only the shared outcome. A trajectory records only its final outcome, not the success probability of each step, so every step is labeled with this same outcome, whose randomness comes mostly from later actions and observations rather than from the step itself. Distinguishing between steps requires step-level annotations, additional rollouts from intermediate states, or exact recurrence of states across rollouts.
(2)
Observation targets are noisy and reach only one step ahead. In web navigation or agentic coding, most tokens of the next observation (e.g., HTML DOM trees or verbose terminal logs) are irrelevant to the decision (Fig.
1
a), so the prediction loss is dominated by reproducing them. The target also covers only single-step transition; reaching later steps requires chaining predictions, where errors compound.

Related Works
Sample-efficient agentic RL
. Methods for sample-efficient agentic RL follow two main directions. The first makes better use of outcome rewards, either by refining credit assignment within trajectories
(
Feng et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Luo et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Kong et al., 2026
)
or by converting completed interactions into extra policy supervision via hindsight rewriting or on-policy distillation
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026
;
Zheng et al., 2026
)
. These methods change how sparse outcomes are assigned or reused, without necessarily introducing a predictive objective. The second learns from the environment feedback available at every step, typically by adding auxiliary prediction of future states or observations to policy training
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Shrivastava et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. Such objectives provide dense token-level supervision but generally focus on a single environment transition.
CoPE
combines elements of both directions: success filtering reuses outcome rewards, while multi-horizon prediction learns from how trajectories unfold in action space rather than reconstructing observations.
Multi-horizon prediction
.
CoPE
is closely related to several forms of multi-horizon and outcome-conditioned prediction. Multi-token prediction trains language models to predict several future tokens
(
Gloeckle et al., 2024
)
, while robotic policies such as ACT and Diffusion Policy predict sequences of future actions
(
Zhao et al., 2023
;
Chi et al., 2023
)
. Multi-token prediction is closest architecturally because multiple offsets are learned by one backbone, whereas action chunking is closest in the structure of its targets. Outcome-conditioned sequence modeling conditions policies on desired returns, while self-imitation emphasizes high-return trajectories
(
Chen et al., 2021
;
Oh et al., 2018
)
; both connect policy learning to trajectory-level outcomes. Accordingly, the

CoPE

Q3: Why must action forecasting loss be conditioned on success, and what does it learn?
Fundamentally, the action forecasting loss must align with the primary RL objective. Without success conditioning, the model is forced to imitate average or failed trajectories, creating a severe objective conflict and leading to zero reward after the first few steps of training. With it, the forecaster learns how the agent behaves in episodes that eventually succeed. Because success depends on the task as well as on the agent’s choices, these episodes may over-represent easy tasks, a known limitation of outcome-conditioned imitation
(
Paster et al., 2022
;
Eysenbach et al., 2022
)
.

The reward checks state-based assertions on the final database, and 38% of Airline tasks expect the database to stay unchanged, against 4.4% in Retail. On these tasks, refusing the request is fully rewarded, and they are by far the easiest since the policy does not need to do anything: early in training they succeed 52% of the time, against 8.9% for tasks that require changing the database, so most successful episodes, the only ones the forecasting loss learns from, are refusals. Yet a refusal task and an action task differ only in details: a request to cancel a booking must instead be refused once the customer demands a refund above 50%. A rewarded refusal and an unrewarded one thus share nearly the same history, and the forecaster, trained only on the rewarded copies, carries refusals over to tasks that require action. These tasks then succeed even less often, which skews the targets further toward refusal.

Ethics Statement
This work introduces
CoPE
, a training algorithm for improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning for LLM-based agents; it is a methodological contribution rather than a deployed system, and its societal impact is largely mediated by how downstream practitioners apply it. All experiments are conducted on standard agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop,
τ
2
\tau^{2}
-bench, and AppWorld) using open-weight or proprietary models strictly for research evaluation; the work does not involve human subjects, crowdsourcing, or the collection of new personal data. By coupling action forecasting and policy optimization within a single backbone,
CoPE
can reduce environment-interaction costs without training or serving a separate world model, lowering the barrier for resource-constrained groups to study long-horizon LLM agents. We also note that, like other advances in sample-efficient agentic RL, more capable autonomous agents could in principle be misused for tasks such as automated misinformation or unauthorized web automation; practitioners building on
CoPE
in higher-stakes domains should pair it with appropriate safety evaluation, deployment-time monitoring, and human oversight.
AI Use Statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with method development and proof writing; to provide feedback on experimental design, including the separated-forecaster and implicit-ensembling analysis in Sec.
8
; to help interpret experimental results; and to implement parts of the training and evaluation code. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets, clean or reformat datasets, perform translation, or conduct qualitative data analysis. We also used generative AI tools to draft and edit text for clarity, suggest section organization, search for and summarize related literature, and format references. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted derivations, code, reported results, and citations and take responsibility for the final content.

Appendix B
Experimental Details
B.1
Baseline Methods
We compare our method with prompting and training baselines spanning verbal self-reflection, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, online reinforcement learning, and observation-space predictive supervision.
Reflexion.
Reflexion is a prompting baseline that asks the agent to verbally reflect on a failed trial and uses the resulting reflection to guide a subsequent attempt, without updating model parameters. We apply Reflexion to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld.
RFT.
Rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) samples trajectories, retains those that succeed, and fine-tunes the policy by maximum likelihood on their action tokens. Unlike GRPO, it treats the retained trajectories as supervised targets rather than optimizing a group-relative policy-gradient objective. We evaluate RFT on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld.
GRPO.
GRPO is an online reinforcement learning baseline.
For each training query, the actor samples a group of trajectories from the current policy and optimizes the policy using group-relative advantages.
Different from critic-based PPO, GRPO estimates advantages within each sampled group and therefore avoids training an additional value model.
In our experiments, GRPO is applied to ALFWorld, WebShop, SciWorld,
τ
2
\tau^{2}
-Bench, and AppWorld.

RWML.
RWML is a two-stage world-model-based baseline.
In the first stage, the backbone is trained on pre-collected
(

from matching the predicted and actual states. In the second stage, the
resulting model is optimized with standard online GRPO on the task reward.
Unlike ECHO and

, its world-model objective is applied only
before policy optimization rather than alongside it.
ECHO.
ECHO is a world-model-augmented reinforcement learning baseline that combines the GRPO loss on action tokens with an auxiliary cross-entropy loss on environment-observation tokens. It reuses the same rollouts, model backbone, and forward-pass logits as policy optimization, thereby providing dense predictive supervision without additional environment interactions or a separately pretrained world model. Unlike RWML, which learns its world model from offline trajectory data before policy optimization, ECHO couples observation-space world modeling directly with online policy updates. We use the same GRPO hyperparameters for ECHO and set the environment-prediction coefficient to
0.01
0.01
on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld.
EMPG.
EMPG is an entropy-modulated policy gradient baseline that re-calibrates the learning signal based on step-wise predictive uncertainty. Unlike standard policy gradients, where update magnitude is implicitly coupled with action entropy, EMPG amplifies updates for confident correct actions, penalizes confident errors, and attenuates updates from uncertain steps. An additional future-clarity bonus encourages the agent toward lower-entropy next states.
In our experiments, we apply EMPG on top of GRPO and evaluate it on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld.

Score.
The score measures the average environment reward or normalized task score. Different from purely binary task completion, some benchmarks provide graded feedback that reflects partial progress during task execution. For example, an agent may receive non-zero reward for completing intermediate steps even if the final task is not fully solved. Therefore, we report the average score to capture such process-level progress.
Success rate.
The success rate measures the fraction of tasks that are fully completed. A task is counted as successful only when the environment evaluator determines that the final goal has been achieved. This metric directly reflects end-to-end task completion ability.
For benchmarks with subcategories, we compute the same metrics within each group. Except for

τ
2
\tau^{2}
-Bench, we instead report the unweighted arithmetic mean of the retail, airline, and telecom domain-level results.

article.headline: 让语言智能体边行动边预测自身未来动作
article.lede: CoPE 在 GRPO 之外加入多步动作预测辅助目标，与策略共享骨干、联合训练，推理零额外开销。
article.problem: 训练长程语言智能体的瓶颈是 rollout 成本高，而标准 agentic RL 只从终端标量奖励学习，中间步骤的监督被大量浪费。已有的两类辅助目标都难做好：价值目标对轨迹中每一步都打上同一个最终结果标签，无法区分步与步；观测目标（网页 DOM、终端日志）冗长嘈杂、损失被无关 token 主导，且只覆盖一步转移。
article.method: CoPE 提出第三类目标——多步动作目标：在成功的 on-policy 轨迹上，让策略骨干从当前历史直接预测其后实际执行的 K 个动作，把中间观测边缘化掉，无需建模环境动态；论文默认 K=2。预测器与行动策略共享同一个 LLM 骨干（预测时附加一条规划指令，因此两者是不同分布），预测损失在每组内按成功轨迹数归一化后，与 GRPO 损失加权联合优化，λ=10⁻²。推理时仍按 π_θ 一步一个动作、不加预测指令，因此不增加推理成本。
article.results: 在五个基准上，CoPE 相对 GRPO 的总体指标均有提升：ALFWorld 提升 5.0 点，WebShop 成功率提升 12.5 点至 77.0%，ScienceWorld 提升 8.0 点至 72.5%；在 τ²-bench 上总体成功率从 27.5% 升至 28.7%（Retail 由 17.5% 升至 29.4%，Airline 由 26.2% 降至 16.2%）；AppWorld 常规 split 由 41.67% 升至 55.36%，challenge split 由 18.71% 升至 22.54%。样本效率上，ScienceWorld 上比 ECHO 和 GRPO 分别高至多 1.9× 和 2.0×，AppWorld 上比 GRPO 高 1.6×。开销方面，ScienceWorld 上预测前向平均每训练步只增加 11% 时间，而更短的 rollout 使实测端到端每步时间反而下降 9%。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明除了价值目标和观测预测之外，成功轨迹上的多步动作序列本身就是一种廉价、决策相关且无需额外模型的稠密监督，且能与 GRPO 在单一骨干内互相促进。对算力有限、又想做长程 agentic RL 的团队来说，这是一条几乎零推理代价的增益路径。
article.limitations: 成功过滤会让预测目标偏向容易的任务：τ²-bench 的 Airline 域中 38% 的任务期望数据库保持不变（Retail 仅 4.4%），这些“拒绝即得分”的样本主导了成功轨迹，预测器把拒绝行为带到需要实际操作的任务上，导致该域明显下滑。此外 AppWorld 上已发表基线使用不同的任务子集与协议（72/105 任务、50 步训练），作者也承认这并非受控对比，跨方法数字不宜直接比较。
article.figure_caption_zh: CoPE 总览：(i) 行动与预测共享同一个 LLM 骨干联合训练，L_AF 拟合成功轨迹上的动作块；(ii) 行动通过轨迹收集支撑预测，预测通过隐式时间集成反哺行动。

page_papers.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience
page_papers.abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

Introduction
Egocentric video offers a natural perspective on how humans and embodied agents perceive and interact with the world, requiring only a wearable camera without external camera setups.
By capturing the wearer’s movement and close-range interactions, it provides visual cues for recovering camera pose, scene depth, hands, and objects.
However, existing methods
[

Combining outputs from different methods often requires reconciling inconsistent scales and coordinate frames, complicating their use in downstream embodied AI applications.
This motivates a unified feed-forward framework that jointly recovers the camera, scene, hands, and objects within a single model.
Training such a unified model, however, requires large-scale egocentric data with joint annotations of the camera, scene, hands, and objects.
Although egocentric video is easy to record, obtaining reliable joint annotations is considerably more difficult due to frequent hand-object occlusions, rapid head motion, and motion blur.
Existing datasets

have made progress toward this goal, often using calibrated multi-camera or motion-capture systems to support reliable annotations.
However, these systems require substantial setup and calibration, making collection difficult to scale across diverse real-world environments.
Scaling jointly annotated egocentric data therefore calls for a collection and annotation pipeline that reduces reliance on such specialized infrastructure.
To address these challenges, we present
EgoXperience
, a full-stack paradigm for egocentric 3D reconstruction, encompassing data collection, annotation, modeling, and benchmarking.
Central to its annotation pipeline is
EgoX
-Engine
, which tracks target objects across video frames and uses pre-scanned object models and observed depth to estimate and verify their 3D poses.
SLAM-estimated camera poses place these object trajectories in a shared world coordinate system alongside scene geometry and hand annotations, providing geometrically aligned supervision.
Applying this engine to 50 hours of task-driven recordings spanning workspace manipulation, cross-room interactions, and outdoor loco-manipulation yields
EgoX

To translate this joint supervision into joint reconstruction, we introduce
EgoX

Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks,
EgoX
jointly reconstructs the camera, scene depth, hands, and objects at metric scale in a shared world coordinate system, all in a single forward pass.
During training, we supervise each component and additionally use the predicted camera poses to transform object and hand predictions into normalized world coordinates, where we supervise their positions and orientations.
This ties camera, hand, and object estimation together, encouraging geometrically consistent reconstruction.
Evaluated on four benchmarks,
EgoX

It ranks first in depth, hand, and object metrics across all four benchmarks and achieves the best camera accuracy on HOI4D. 3.1
EgoX
-Engine
Learning to jointly reconstruct egocentric activity requires annotations that describe the camera, scene, hands, and objects in relation to one another.
Obtaining these annotations is challenging because the observer and the interacting entities move simultaneously:
a change in image position may arise from camera motion, entity motion, or both.
EgoX
-Engine addresses this ambiguity by using stereo depth to recover geometry at metric scale and SLAM-estimated camera poses to align different annotations throughout each recording.
This allows hand-object motion to be expressed relative to the surrounding scene as the observer moves.
Fig.
3
summarizes the overall pipeline.
Capture and geometric reference.
We record with the HOMIE Gen2 head-mounted rig
[
51
]
, using its associated processing pipeline to estimate metric depth from the synchronized, calibrated front stereo pair and recover
camera trajectories via SLAM from its four calibrated fisheye cameras.
For each recording, we use the SLAM coordinate system as a fixed session frame and transform camera-relative scene, hand, and object estimates into this frame.
Figure 2:
Overview of EgoX-Data-6M.
Examples and statistics summarize capture settings,
task coverage, and aligned multimodal annotations.
Object geometry and motion.
Object annotation requires both a geometric reference for each instance and its changing pose during interaction.
We construct metric object meshes from 31 synchronized cameras mounted on a calibrated dome.
SAM 3
[
11
]
then extracts object masks from the captured views, which are used for mesh reconstruction with MV-SAM3D
[
33
]
.
To recover the object’s physical dimensions, we put an AprilTag
[
42
]
board inside the dome to provide the scale reference.
Given these metric object references, the engine recovers each object’s motion in the egocentric recording.
Specifically,
we first identify the target object using a first-frame mask and then specify the interaction interval over which to track it.
Using the masked RGB image and its corresponding stereo depth, we estimate the initial pose of the pre-scanned object model in the camera frame.
From this initial pose, we apply FoundationPose
[
62
]
to track the object throughout the specified interval, producing a camera-relative pose sequence.
We verify this sequence by checking whether the object model placed at the estimated pose agrees with the observed depth.
Sequences that pass verification are transformed through the SLAM-estimated camera poses into the session frame, aligning object motion with the scene and hand annotations.
Scene and hand annotations.
The scene and hand annotations used in this alignment are derived from the same calibrated stereo observations.
Specifically, we reconstruct scene geometry by back-projecting stereo depth and recover 3D hand keypoints through cross-view triangulation.
We use these keypoints to constrain MANO fitting, with additional reprojection, depth, and temporal terms to refine the estimated hand geometry and motion.
Hand shape parameters are shared across frames within each recording, while hand pose, position, and orientation are estimated independently for each frame.
Finally, we transform the fitted hands and scene points through the camera trajectory into the session frame, placing them in the same metric coordinate system as the tracked objects.

Given

-Engine, we apply it to annotate task-driven egocentric captures, constructing
EgoX
-Data-6M, which comprises 50 hours of video, 101 rigid objects, and 270 task scripts.
The recordings cover activities ranging from manipulation within a single workspace to interactions across rooms and loco-manipulation in outdoor environments.
The engine provides geometrically aligned camera, scene, hand, and object annotations across these settings, supporting joint reconstruction under both local manipulation and extended movement.

We organize data collection around task scripts, each specifying a manipulation goal, target objects, and

Specifically, workspace scripts focus on local object manipulation, whereas cross-room and outdoor scripts incorporate movement between interaction locations.
Annotation coverage.
We provide geometric annotations in a session-fixed metric frame, allowing camera motion, scene structure, and hand-object interactions to be related throughout each recording.
Additionally, we include second-level task captions to describe the ongoing activity.

To evaluate all reconstruction components on the same recordings, we reserve a quality-controlled, one-hour subset spanning the three activity settings as

This subset is used exclusively for joint evaluation of camera, scene, hand, and object reconstruction.
To broaden the training data beyond our own recordings, we incorporate additional public datasets.
Using these datasets together requires accounting for differences in both geometric conventions and available annotations.
We therefore convert their geometric labels to a common coordinate and scale convention and supervise the model using the labels available in each dataset.
This allows recordings with partial annotations to contribute to training without requiring every dataset to provide camera, scene, hand, and object labels.
We also clean erroneous annotations and align depth with hand and object geometry to reduce conflicting supervision (Appendix

Experiments
We evaluate camera, depth, hand, and object reconstruction on HOT3D,
EgoX-Bench, H2O, and HOI4D using identical 150-observation clips
across methods. Evaluation sequences are excluded from EgoX training.
EgoX uses RGB and first-frame object masks; object baselines may
additionally require estimated depth, intrinsics, per-frame masks,
or metric CAD assets. World-space hand metrics use estimated cameras;
object poses are evaluated in camera coordinates. No method receives
GT camera poses or scale in the main comparisons.

C
details the evaluation protocols.

Ablation studies
Metric scale prediction.
We remove ScaleHead and use oracle scale (G) to convert the ablated model’s predictions to metric units. Despite this advantage, W-MPJPE increases from 38.89

(Table
6

reconstruction beyond final rescaling.
Dense-depth prediction.
We remove DepthHead while retaining the remaining architecture and
predicted scale. W-MPJPE increases to 67.53 mm and AUC-S
50
decreases to 41.09 (Table
6
), showing that explicit depth prediction improves
hand and object reconstruction through the shared representation.

Conclusion
We present EgoXperience, a unified approach to learning
world-grounded egocentric representations through task-driven
capture, geometrically aligned annotation, and joint reconstruction.
EgoX-Engine provides aligned multimodal annotations for
the 50-hour EgoX-Data-6M, from which we curate the held-out
one-hour EgoX-Bench.
Trained on these annotations and harmonized public datasets,
EgoX jointly reconstructs cameras, dense depth, hands,
and rigid-object 6-DoF poses in a common metric world frame.
Experiments on EgoX-Bench and public benchmarks demonstrate
strong performance in hand and object reconstruction
and depth estimation.
Our current formulation assumes rigid objects and does not
predict their meshes.
Future work will explore object mesh prediction and
multiview inputs.

DUSt3R
[
60

predicts pairwise pointmaps, while

Ω
\Omega

costs with scene registers. EgoX combines register-mediated and

scenes, MonST3R
[
69
]
reconstructs moving content,
and St4RTrack
[
18
]
tracks 3D points in a common world
frame. Dynamic Point Maps
[
55
]
recovers rigid-object motion
through masked point alignment, V-DPM
[
54

extends

[
67
]
predicts 3D points
conditioned on source, target, and camera-reference times. EgoX

[
14
]
combines human meshes
with scene and camera reconstruction, while IGGT
[
35
]
jointly learns geometry and instance segmentation. HGGT
[
37
]
uses hand tokens to estimate MANO parameters and cameras from
uncalibrated views of a fixed hand configuration. Unlike these methods,
EgoX jointly reconstructs the camera, depth, and moving hands and
objects over time.

[
63
]
uses a motion prior and test-time guidance but requires object templates
and a metric camera trajectory. EgoX jointly predicts cameras, depth,
hands, and objects from RGB video and initial object masks, without
either external input. Its reconstruction losses evaluate hand, object,
and depth predictions through the predicted camera, providing training
signals for camera estimation.

Modular reconstruction also provides a source of training annotations.
MegaSaM
[
36
]
and ViPE
[
26

combine learned
geometry with camera and depth optimization. Metric3D
[
64
]
and UniDepth
[
46
]
predict metric depth from single
images, while MapAnything
[
29
]
predicts metric
geometry from multiple views. HaWoR uses metric depth to scale its
SLAM trajectory. EgoX instead learns a scale per window shared by
depth and camera, hand, and object translations, though shared scale
alone does not ensure geometric consistency.
MegaPose
[
31
]
requires a CAD model,
FoundationPose
[
62
]
accepts a model or
reference images, and Any6D
[
32

uses an RGB-D reference.
Their camera-relative poses can be mapped to world coordinates using
a camera trajectory. EgoX likewise transforms predictions into a
common frame, but learns camera and object estimates jointly. These
methods also differ in their requirements for depth, pose
initialization, scale, and masks.

varied capture protocols. ARCTIC includes articulated objects, and
HOT3D provides motion-capture reference poses. However, capture
volumes or clip protocols often limit evaluation of continuous camera
travel between workspaces.
More recent datasets broaden the settings. SHOW3D

Large collections such as Ego4D

indoor workspaces, and outdoor locomotion, with hand, object, and scene
annotations. This enables evaluation across camera displacement,
capture setting, and sequence duration using camera, depth, and
world-space interaction errors.
Appendix B
Public Dataset Cleaning and Geometric Alignment
We systematically clean HOT3D, HOI4D, H2O, H2O-3D, HO-Cap,
and DexYCB before joint training. We discard frames with erroneous
hand annotations and remove spurious points from depth-derived
point clouds. We further align depth-derived geometry, MANO hand
meshes, and object meshes in a common 3D coordinate system,
correcting inconsistencies in their relative placement and scale.
These steps reduce erroneous labels and conflicting geometric
supervision across reconstruction tasks.
Appendix C
Evaluation Protocol
Datasets and splits.
We evaluate on four sequence-disjoint benchmarks: HaWoR’s validation
split of HOT3D
[
68
]

EgoX-Bench, the official H2O test split, and our sequence-level
HOI4D validation split. Evaluation sequences are excluded from EgoX
training. All methods use identical sequence lists and matched
150-observation clips.
Inputs and matched protocol.
EgoX receives RGB and optional first-frame object masks.
Object-pose baselines additionally use DA3 Nested depth and intrinsics,
per-frame masks, or metric CAD assets as required; their runtimes
include any required DA3 preprocessing. Any6D receives DA3 Nested depth
and intrinsics together with per-frame object masks, but no CAD asset.
FoundationPose receives DA3 Nested depth and intrinsics together with
the metric CAD asset. GigaPose + MegaPose receives DA3 Nested
intrinsics, the metric CAD asset, and per-frame object masks.
Ground-truth camera poses and scale are not supplied as reconstruction
inputs in the main comparisons.
For HandFlow, we follow the released right-hand-only protocol by
mirroring left-hand inputs and mapping recovered joints back to the
original camera frame. HandFlow and WiLoR are paired with the same
DROID-SLAM camera trajectory; neither receives ground-truth camera
poses, depth, or hand annotations. Results are averaged over matched
clips after applying common annotation-validity masks.

scale. VGGT and VGGT-

article.headline: 统一重建相机、场景与手物的第一视角范式
article.lede: EgoXperience 把数据采集、自动标注、统一建模与评测打包成一套流程，单次前向即可重建第一视角视频中的相机、深度
article.problem: 从第一视角视频重建人类活动，不只是分别恢复各个三维部件：观察者的运动、周围几何以及手与物体的交互必须落在同一个一致的世界里。现有方法与数据集要么只恢复其中一部分，要么依赖多相机标定或动捕等专门设施，难以规模化，不同方法输出的尺度和坐标系也常常对不上。
article.method: 作者搭建了自动标注引擎 EgoX-Engine，用立体深度和 SLAM 把场景、手、物体对齐到同一度量坐标系，物体部分靠预扫描模型加 FoundationPose 跟踪，并用观测深度做几何校验。在此之上构建 50 小时、101 个刚性物体、270 个任务脚本的 EgoX-Data-6M，并留出 1 小时作为 EgoX-Bench。模型 EgoX 以 DINOv3 特征为输入，通过相机、手、物体 token 的视图内与跨视图注意力形成联合表示，再由预测的相机位姿和共享尺度头把各部件组合到首帧相机定义的世界坐标系中联合监督。
article.results: 在四个基准上，EgoX 在深度、手、物体指标上均排第一：相对最强基线，HOI4D 上相机 nATE 降低 68.9%，EgoX-Bench 上手 W-MPJPE 与深度 AbsRel 分别降低 65.6% 和 42.9%，HOT3D 上物体 AUC-S50 提升 28.0%；例如 EgoX-Bench 的 W-MPJPE 从 WiLoR + SLAM 的 328.81 mm 降到 113.24 mm，AUC-S50 为 76.59 对 59.80。消融显示去掉尺度头改用真值尺度后 W-MPJPE 反而从 38.89 mm 升至 40.67 mm、AUC-S50 从 73.71 降至 60.87；去掉深度头后 W-MPJPE 升至 67.53 mm、AUC-S50 降至 41.09。150 帧在单张 A800 上推理 14.60 s。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「相机—场景—手—物体」放进同一个度量世界坐标系，正是具身智能做示教学习与轨迹迁移时需要的那种对齐监督，且数据与模型均已公开。
article.limitations: 方法假设物体是刚性的且不预测物体网格，训练与标注还依赖专用的 HOMIE Gen2 头戴设备、31 相机穹顶扫描的物体模型与首帧掩码，跨环境的规模化采集成本仍然存在；相机精度上 VGGT-Ω 在 HOT3D 和 EgoX-Bench 上更好，DA3 Nested 在 H2O 上也领先，说明相机估计并非全面占优。
article.figure_caption_zh: EgoX 概览：共享的场景与实体特征支持联合重建，预测的相机与尺度把全部输出放回统一的度量世界坐标系。

journals.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03313-7

Large language models can mimic thought and feeling with uncanny skill. But evidence from neuroscience suggests that intelligence alone is not enough for subjective experience.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》刊文指出，大语言模型虽能逼真地模仿思考与情感，但神经科学证据显示，仅具备智能并不足以产生主观体验。作者据此提出三条理由，论证当前 AI 并不具有意识、且可能永远不会具有，并提醒研究者区分“能力表现”与“内在体验”。

journals.blurb: 《自然》在线简讯报道了一种快速化学指纹识别方法，用于追踪非法芬太尼供应中特定掺假物的兴起与消退。该工作强调对药物供应链中化学成分演变的持续监测。对机器学习研究生而言，这类随时间变化的指纹数据可为异常检测与趋势建模提供现实场景。
